title: Deductive reasoning defined
text: Deductive reasoning derives specific conclusions that follow necessarily from general premises. If the premises are true and the argument is valid, the conclusion must be true. Deduction preserves truth: it cannot introduce information not already contained, at least implicitly, in the premises.

title: Inductive reasoning defined
text: Inductive reasoning draws general conclusions from specific observations or a limited sample. Its conclusions are probable rather than certain, since the premises support but do not guarantee them. Induction is ampliative, meaning it extends beyond the information contained in the premises.

title: Abductive reasoning defined
text: Abductive reasoning, or inference to the best explanation, infers the most plausible cause or hypothesis that would account for a set of observations. It does not guarantee truth but selects the explanation that best fits the evidence, and is central to diagnosis, detective work, and scientific discovery.

title: Deduction versus induction
text: Deduction moves from general principles to specific certain conclusions, while induction moves from specific instances to general probable ones. Deductive validity concerns logical form; inductive strength concerns how well observed evidence supports a generalisation.

title: Certainty and defeasibility
text: Deductive conclusions are certain given true premises and cannot be overturned by new information. Inductive and abductive conclusions are defeasible: additional evidence can weaken or reverse them without any logical error having been made.

title: Ampliative inference
text: An ampliative inference is one whose conclusion contains more information than its premises. Induction and abduction are ampliative and therefore risky, whereas valid deduction is non-ampliative and merely makes explicit what the premises already entail.

title: Enumerative induction
text: Enumerative induction generalises from observed cases to a broader claim, such as concluding that all ravens are black after observing many black ravens. Its reliability depends on sample size, representativeness, and the absence of counterexamples.

title: Statistical induction
text: Statistical induction infers the proportion of a property in a population from its proportion in a sample. A well-chosen random sample allows quantified conclusions with measurable margins of error, unlike simple enumerative generalisation.

title: Analogical reasoning
text: Analogical reasoning infers that because two things share some known properties, they likely share a further property. Its strength depends on the relevance and number of shared features and the absence of relevant differences between the cases compared.

title: Abduction in diagnosis
text: In medicine and fault-finding, abduction proposes the condition or defect that best explains observed symptoms. Because several causes may fit the same symptoms, abductive conclusions require further tests to confirm or eliminate competing explanations.

title: Hypothetico-deductive method
text: The hypothetico-deductive method combines abduction and deduction: a hypothesis is proposed to explain observations, testable predictions are deduced from it, and experiments check those predictions. Failed predictions count against the hypothesis.

title: Deductive chains
text: A deductive chain links several inferences so that the conclusion of one step becomes a premise of the next. A long chain is only as reliable as its weakest link, since a single false premise or invalid step can undermine the final conclusion.

title: Inference to best explanation
text: Inference to the best explanation selects among rival hypotheses the one that, if true, would best account for the evidence. Criteria for the best explanation include simplicity, scope, coherence with background knowledge, and explanatory power.

title: Reasoning and uncertainty
text: Everyday reasoning blends deduction with induction and abduction. A conclusion may be deductively drawn from premises that were themselves established inductively, so the overall confidence in the conclusion cannot exceed confidence in those premises.

title: Prediction and retrodiction
text: Prediction infers future observations from a hypothesis, while retrodiction infers past states or events. Both test explanatory theories, and a theory that successfully retrodicts independent facts gains support just as one that predicts new observations does.

title: What an argument is
text: In logic, an argument is a set of statements in which some, the premises, are offered as reasons to accept another, the conclusion. An argument is not a quarrel but a structured attempt to support a claim with evidence or reasons.

title: Premises and conclusion
text: The premises of an argument are the statements offered as support, and the conclusion is the statement they are meant to establish. Identifying which claim is the conclusion is the first step in evaluating any argument.

title: Indicator words
text: Words such as because, since, and for typically introduce premises, while therefore, thus, hence, and so typically introduce conclusions. These indicator words help identify the logical structure of an argument, though they are not infallible signals.

title: Validity defined
text: An argument is valid when its conclusion follows necessarily from its premises: it is impossible for all the premises to be true while the conclusion is false. Validity concerns the form of the argument, not whether the premises are actually true.

title: Soundness defined
text: An argument is sound when it is both valid and has all true premises. A sound argument guarantees a true conclusion. Validity alone does not, because a valid argument can have false premises and thus a false conclusion.

title: Validity versus truth
text: Validity is a property of arguments, while truth is a property of statements. A valid argument can contain false statements, and a set of true statements can form an invalid argument, so the two must not be confused.

title: Cogency in induction
text: For inductive arguments, the counterpart of soundness is cogency. A cogent argument is strong and has all true premises. Strength measures how probable the premises make the conclusion, since inductive conclusions are never guaranteed.

title: Strong and weak induction
text: An inductive argument is strong when its true premises would make the conclusion highly probable, and weak when they would not. Strength is a matter of degree, unlike deductive validity, which is all or nothing.

title: Enthymemes
text: An enthymeme is an argument with an unstated premise or conclusion that the audience is expected to supply. Uncovering hidden premises is essential to evaluating everyday arguments, which are often stated incompletely.

title: Deductive argument forms
text: Deductive arguments share recognisable valid forms, and any argument fitting a valid form is valid regardless of subject matter. This is why logicians study form abstractly, using letters to stand for the component statements.

title: Counterexample method
text: To show an argument form is invalid, one constructs a counterexample: an argument of the same form with obviously true premises and an obviously false conclusion. A single such instance proves the form does not guarantee truth.

title: Necessary conditions
text: A necessary condition for an event is one without which the event cannot occur. Oxygen is necessary for fire. Denying a necessary condition lets one validly deny the outcome, but its presence alone does not ensure the outcome.

title: Sufficient conditions
text: A sufficient condition for an outcome is one whose presence guarantees the outcome. Being a square is sufficient for being a rectangle. A sufficient condition need not be necessary, since other conditions may also produce the outcome.

title: Necessary and sufficient
text: A condition is necessary and sufficient for an outcome when the outcome occurs if and only if the condition holds. Such biconditional relationships allow inference in both directions between condition and outcome.

title: Premise acceptability
text: Evaluating an argument requires judging whether its premises are acceptable, not merely whether the reasoning is valid. Premises may be accepted on the basis of observation, testimony, prior argument, or established knowledge.

title: Convergent and linked premises
text: Premises are linked when they work together and none supports the conclusion alone, and convergent when each independently supports the conclusion. Distinguishing the two shows whether refuting one premise collapses the whole argument.

title: Categorical syllogism
text: A categorical syllogism is a deductive argument with two premises and a conclusion, each a categorical statement relating two classes. It contains exactly three terms, and its validity depends on how those terms are distributed.

title: Categorical statements
text: Categorical statements assert relations between classes and come in four standard forms: universal affirmative (all S are P), universal negative (no S are P), particular affirmative (some S are P), and particular negative (some S are not P).

title: Major, minor, middle terms
text: In a categorical syllogism the major term is the predicate of the conclusion, the minor term is its subject, and the middle term appears in both premises but not the conclusion, linking the other two terms together.

title: Classic syllogism example
text: The classic valid syllogism runs: all men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal. Here mortal is the major term, Socrates the minor, and man the middle term shared by both premises.

title: Figure of a syllogism
text: The figure of a categorical syllogism is determined by the position of the middle term in the two premises. There are four figures, and together with mood they fix whether a given syllogism is valid.

title: Mood of a syllogism
text: The mood of a categorical syllogism is the sequence of the types of its three statements, such as AAA or EIO, using the letters A, E, I, and O for the four categorical forms. Mood and figure jointly determine validity.

title: Distribution of terms
text: A term is distributed in a statement when the statement refers to every member of the class it names. Universal statements distribute their subject, and negative statements distribute their predicate. Distribution governs syllogistic validity.

title: Undistributed middle fallacy
text: The fallacy of the undistributed middle occurs when the middle term of a syllogism is not distributed in either premise, so the premises fail to connect the major and minor terms. Such an argument is invalid despite appearing plausible.

title: Illicit major and minor
text: The fallacy of illicit major or illicit minor occurs when a term distributed in the conclusion was not distributed in its premise. Drawing a conclusion about a whole class from a premise about only part of it is invalid.

title: Two negative premises
text: A valid categorical syllogism cannot have two negative premises. If both premises deny a relationship, they provide no positive link between the major and minor terms from which any conclusion could follow.

title: Hypothetical syllogism
text: A pure hypothetical syllogism chains conditionals: if P then Q, and if Q then R, therefore if P then R. This valid form underlies transitive reasoning through a series of linked conditional statements.

title: Disjunctive syllogism
text: A disjunctive syllogism reasons from a disjunction and the denial of one disjunct to the affirmation of the other: either P or Q; not P; therefore Q. It is valid provided the disjunction is genuinely exhaustive.

title: Modus ponens
text: Modus ponens is the valid argument form: if P then Q; P; therefore Q. Affirming the antecedent of a true conditional lets one validly infer its consequent, and it is among the most basic rules of deductive inference.

title: Modus tollens
text: Modus tollens is the valid form: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P. Denying the consequent of a conditional lets one validly deny its antecedent, a pattern used constantly in testing and eliminating hypotheses.

title: Affirming the consequent
text: Affirming the consequent is an invalid form: if P then Q; Q; therefore P. Because Q may have causes other than P, its truth does not establish P. This fallacy resembles valid modus ponens but reverses it.

title: Denying the antecedent
text: Denying the antecedent is an invalid form: if P then Q; not P; therefore not Q. Since Q may hold for reasons besides P, the falsity of P does not establish the falsity of Q. It superficially resembles modus tollens.

title: Sorites
text: A sorites is a chain of categorical syllogisms in which the conclusion of each links to the next, stated compactly with intermediate conclusions omitted. It allows several premises to be marshalled toward a single final conclusion.

title: Existential import
text: Traditional logic treats universal statements as carrying existential import, implying their subject class has members, while modern logic does not. This difference affects which syllogisms involving universal premises are counted valid.

title: Venn diagram testing
text: Venn diagrams test categorical syllogisms by representing the three classes as overlapping circles, shading empty regions and marking occupied ones for the premises. If the conclusion is already depicted, the syllogism is valid.

title: Formal versus informal fallacies
text: A formal fallacy is an error in the logical structure of an argument, making it invalid regardless of content. An informal fallacy involves faults in content, language, or relevance that undermine an argument without violating its form.

title: Ad hominem
text: The ad hominem fallacy attacks the person making an argument rather than addressing the argument itself. Even if the person has flaws, those flaws are usually irrelevant to whether their claim is true or their reasoning sound.

title: Straw man
text: The straw man fallacy misrepresents an opponent's position as weaker or more extreme than it is, then refutes the distorted version. Defeating this caricature leaves the actual argument untouched while creating an illusion of victory.

title: False dilemma
text: The false dilemma, or false dichotomy, presents only two options as if they were the only possibilities when others exist. It forces a choice between extremes and ignores middle grounds or alternative solutions.

title: Slippery slope
text: The slippery slope fallacy claims that one step will inevitably lead through a chain of events to an extreme outcome, without establishing that each link is likely. It substitutes fear of a distant result for evidence about the first step.

title: Circular reasoning
text: Circular reasoning, or begging the question, assumes the conclusion within its own premises, so the argument proves nothing. The premise and conclusion may be worded differently but assert the same claim, offering no independent support.

title: Appeal to authority
text: The fallacious appeal to authority cites an authority whose expertise is irrelevant, disputed, or nonexistent to support a claim. Legitimate appeals to genuine, relevant expertise are reasonable; the fallacy lies in misusing authority.

title: Appeal to ignorance
text: The appeal to ignorance treats the absence of evidence against a claim as proof of it, or absence of evidence for it as proof of its falsity. Not having disproved something is not the same as having proved it.

title: Hasty generalisation
text: A hasty generalisation draws a broad conclusion from a sample too small or unrepresentative to support it. Concluding a trait applies to a whole group after seeing only a few members is a common source of stereotypes and error.

title: Post hoc fallacy
text: The post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy infers that because one event followed another, the first caused the second. Temporal sequence alone does not establish causation, which requires ruling out coincidence and common causes.

title: Equivocation
text: Equivocation trades on a word used with two different meanings within one argument, creating an illusion of valid inference. The argument only appears to connect its premises because the shifting meaning is overlooked.

title: Appeal to emotion
text: The appeal to emotion substitutes feelings such as fear, pity, or pride for relevant evidence. While emotions can accompany good arguments, using them in place of reasons to support a conclusion is fallacious.

title: Appeal to popularity
text: The appeal to popularity, or bandwagon fallacy, argues that a claim is true or an action right because many people accept or do it. Widespread belief is not evidence of truth, since majorities can be mistaken.

title: Appeal to tradition
text: The appeal to tradition argues that something is correct or good simply because it has long been done or believed. Age and custom are not evidence of truth or value, and long-standing practices can be mistaken or harmful.

title: Appeal to novelty
text: The appeal to novelty argues that something is better simply because it is new or modern. Newness is not evidence of superiority, just as age is not; each claim must be judged on its actual merits.

title: Red herring
text: A red herring introduces an irrelevant topic to divert attention from the issue under discussion. It may be interesting or emotionally charged, but it does not address the original question and derails reasoning.

title: Tu quoque
text: The tu quoque, or appeal to hypocrisy, deflects criticism by charging the critic with the same fault. Even if the critic is hypocritical, that does nothing to show the original criticism is mistaken.

title: Genetic fallacy
text: The genetic fallacy evaluates a claim solely by its origin or source rather than its current merits. Where an idea came from is usually irrelevant to whether it is true, though origins can occasionally bear on reliability.

title: False cause
text: The false cause fallacy attributes a causal relationship where none has been established, whether by confusing correlation with causation, reversing cause and effect, or overlooking a common underlying cause.

title: Correlation and causation
text: Correlation between two variables does not by itself establish that one causes the other. The link may be coincidence, reverse causation, or the result of a third factor influencing both, and only controlled study can distinguish these.

title: Composition fallacy
text: The fallacy of composition infers that what is true of the parts must be true of the whole. That each brick is light does not mean the wall is light, and properties of components need not carry over to the assembled whole.

title: Division fallacy
text: The fallacy of division infers that what is true of a whole must be true of its parts. That a team is excellent does not mean every player is, and properties of a whole need not distribute to its individual components.

title: Loaded question
text: A loaded question, such as asking whether someone has stopped a bad habit, smuggles in an unproven assumption. Any direct answer concedes the assumption, so the fallacy lies in the presupposition rather than the answer.

title: Gambler's fallacy
text: The gambler's fallacy is the mistaken belief that past outcomes of independent random events change the probability of future ones, as in expecting a coin due to land heads after several tails. Independent events have no memory.

title: Sunk cost reasoning
text: The sunk cost fallacy continues an endeavour because of resources already invested rather than future prospects. Because past costs cannot be recovered whatever one now decides, rational choice should weigh only future costs and benefits.

title: No true Scotsman
text: The no true Scotsman fallacy defends a generalisation against a counterexample by redefining the category to exclude it. This ad hoc move makes the claim unfalsifiable rather than answering the counterexample honestly.

title: Appeal to nature
text: The appeal to nature argues that something is good or right because it is natural, or bad because it is unnatural. Natural things can be harmful and artificial ones beneficial, so naturalness alone settles no question of value.

title: Moving the goalposts
text: Moving the goalposts is the tactic of demanding new, higher standards of proof once the original standard has been met. It allows a claim to be indefinitely resisted no matter how much evidence is supplied.

title: Special pleading
text: Special pleading applies a general principle to others while exempting oneself or a favoured case without a relevant justification. The double standard is disguised as though the exception were principled rather than arbitrary.

title: False equivalence
text: False equivalence treats two things as morally or logically equal when relevant differences of degree or kind separate them. It flattens important distinctions, often by comparing a minor fault with a serious one.

title: Middle ground fallacy
text: The middle ground fallacy assumes the truth must lie between two positions. Compromise is sometimes reasonable, but a claim can be wholly true or wholly false, and splitting the difference can land far from the facts.

title: Appeal to consequences
text: The appeal to consequences argues that a claim is true or false because of the desirability of its implications. Whether a belief is comforting or distressing has no bearing on whether it corresponds to reality.

title: Fallacy of the single cause
text: The fallacy of the single cause, or causal oversimplification, attributes an outcome to one cause when many factors contributed. Complex events usually have multiple interacting causes that a single-cause account overlooks.

title: Cherry picking
text: Cherry picking presents only evidence that supports a conclusion while ignoring evidence against it. A fair assessment must weigh the full body of relevant data rather than a selectively chosen subset.

title: Texas sharpshooter
text: The Texas sharpshooter fallacy finds a pattern after the fact by selecting data that clusters and ignoring the rest, like drawing a target around bullet holes. It mistakes coincidental clustering for a meaningful trend.

title: Fallacy fallacy
text: The fallacy fallacy, or argument from fallacy, concludes that a claim is false because an argument for it was fallacious. A poor argument does not make its conclusion false; the claim may still be true on other grounds.

title: Appeal to force
text: The appeal to force, or argumentum ad baculum, uses threats or coercion in place of reasons to gain acceptance of a conclusion. Compelling agreement does nothing to show the conclusion is actually true.

title: Appeal to pity
text: The appeal to pity, or argumentum ad misericordiam, urges acceptance of a claim by evoking sympathy rather than providing relevant support. Compassion may be warranted, but it does not bear on the truth of the claim.

title: Non sequitur
text: A non sequitur is an argument whose conclusion does not follow from its premises. The term covers any inference where the stated reasons fail to support the conclusion, even if both premises and conclusion happen to be true.

title: Fallacy of accent
text: The fallacy of accent arises when the meaning of a statement changes depending on which words are stressed or on selective quotation. Emphasis can distort a claim while leaving the literal words unchanged.

title: Amphiboly
text: Amphiboly is a fallacy of ambiguous grammatical structure, where a sentence can be read in more than one way because of its construction rather than a single ambiguous word. The argument exploits the unintended reading.

title: Weak analogy
text: The weak analogy fallacy rests an argument on a comparison between things that are not alike in the relevant respects. When the shared features are irrelevant to the conclusion, the analogy provides no real support.

title: Poisoning the well
text: Poisoning the well is a pre-emptive ad hominem that discredits a source before it speaks, so that anything it says will be dismissed. It biases the audience against an argument rather than engaging its content.

title: Two wrongs make right
text: The two wrongs make a right fallacy justifies a wrongful act by pointing to another wrongful act. That someone else did wrong does not make a further wrong permissible or correct.

title: Appeal to the stone
text: The appeal to the stone dismisses a claim as absurd without giving any argument against it. Simply declaring a position ridiculous is not a refutation and leaves the claim unaddressed.

title: Ecological fallacy
text: The ecological fallacy infers characteristics of individuals from statistics about the group they belong to. Group averages need not describe any particular member, so aggregate data can mislead conclusions about individuals.

title: Reification fallacy
text: Reification treats an abstraction, such as a nation, an average, or the market, as if it were a concrete thing with intentions or powers. This can smuggle unjustified assumptions into an argument about real events.

title: Confirmation bias
text: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek, interpret, and recall information in ways that support existing beliefs while discounting contrary evidence. It leads people to overestimate the strength of their positions and resist correction.

title: Anchoring bias
text: Anchoring is the tendency to rely too heavily on the first piece of information encountered when making estimates. Subsequent judgements are adjusted from that anchor but typically remain biased toward it, even when it is arbitrary.

title: Availability heuristic
text: The availability heuristic judges the likelihood of events by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent, or emotionally charged instances are recalled more readily, causing systematic overestimation of memorable but rare events.

title: Survivorship bias
text: Survivorship bias arises from focusing on cases that passed a selection process while overlooking those that did not. Studying only successes or survivors distorts conclusions because the failures, which are invisible, carry crucial information.

title: Dunning-Kruger effect
text: The Dunning-Kruger effect describes how people with low competence in a domain often overestimate their ability, partly because the skills needed to perform well are also those needed to recognise poor performance.

title: Framing effect
text: The framing effect is the tendency to reach different decisions depending on how equivalent options are described, such as in terms of gains or losses. Logically identical choices can elicit opposite preferences based on wording alone.

title: Hindsight bias
text: Hindsight bias is the tendency, once an outcome is known, to see it as having been predictable all along. It distorts memory of prior uncertainty and can make past decisions look more foreseeable than they truly were.

title: Self-serving bias
text: The self-serving bias leads people to attribute their successes to their own qualities and their failures to external circumstances. It protects self-esteem but distorts accurate assessment of one's role in outcomes.

title: Fundamental attribution error
text: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to explain others' behaviour by their character while explaining one's own by the situation. It underestimates how strongly circumstances shape what people do.

title: Halo effect
text: The halo effect is the tendency for an overall impression of a person to colour judgements of their specific traits. Someone seen as likeable may be assumed competent or honest without any evidence of those particular qualities.

title: Loss aversion
text: Loss aversion is the tendency to feel the pain of a loss more strongly than the pleasure of an equivalent gain. It makes people disproportionately avoid losses, sometimes leading to overly cautious or inconsistent choices.

title: Optimism bias
text: Optimism bias is the tendency to overestimate the likelihood of positive events and underestimate that of negative ones happening to oneself. It can lead to inadequate preparation and underestimation of genuine risks.

title: Negativity bias
text: Negativity bias is the tendency for negative information, experiences, or events to have a greater effect on judgement and memory than equally intense positive ones. Bad impressions form quickly and are hard to overturn.

title: Recency bias
text: Recency bias is the tendency to give greater weight to recent events or information than to earlier ones when forming judgements. It can distort trend estimation and cause overreaction to the latest data point.

title: In-group bias
text: In-group bias is the tendency to favour members of one's own group over outsiders in perception, evaluation, and treatment. It can produce unfair judgements and blind spots toward the merits of those outside the group.

title: Illusory correlation
text: Illusory correlation is the perception of a relationship between two variables when none exists or when the relationship is weaker than believed. Distinctive co-occurrences are over-remembered, creating false impressions of association.

title: Clustering illusion
text: The clustering illusion is the tendency to see patterns in random data, perceiving streaks or clusters as meaningful when they are the expected product of chance. Truly random sequences often contain apparent structure.

title: Overconfidence effect
text: The overconfidence effect is a well-documented tendency for people's confidence in their judgements to exceed their accuracy. Calibration studies show that events people say are certain often fail to occur as often as expected.

title: Planning fallacy
text: The planning fallacy is the tendency to underestimate the time, costs, and risks of future actions while overestimating their benefits. Projects routinely run late and over budget partly because of this persistent bias.

title: Status quo bias
text: Status quo bias is a preference for the current state of affairs, so that changes are perceived as losses. It can cause people to stick with default options and resist beneficial change without a reasoned justification.

title: Endowment effect
text: The endowment effect is the tendency to value something more highly simply because one owns it. People often demand more to give up an item than they would pay to acquire the same item, distorting fair valuation.

title: Belief perseverance
text: Belief perseverance is the tendency to maintain a belief even after the evidence that formed it has been discredited. Once a conclusion is held, it can persist through rationalisation long after its original basis is gone.

title: Illusion of control
text: The illusion of control is the tendency to overestimate one's influence over outcomes governed largely by chance. People may act as if skill affects random events, such as choosing their own lottery numbers.

title: Representativeness heuristic
text: The representativeness heuristic judges probability by similarity to a stereotype rather than by base rates. It can lead people to ignore how common a category actually is, producing the conjunction fallacy and base rate neglect.

title: Conjunction fallacy
text: The conjunction fallacy is the mistake of rating a specific conjunction of events as more probable than one of its constituents alone. A combined event can never be more likely than either event it contains.

title: Blind spot bias
text: The bias blind spot is the tendency to recognise cognitive biases in others more readily than in oneself. People often believe they are less susceptible to bias than average, which is itself a bias.

title: Curse of knowledge
text: The curse of knowledge is the difficulty experts have in imagining what it is like not to know what they know. It causes them to overestimate how well others understand and to explain things assuming shared background.

title: Probability basics
text: Probability measures how likely an event is, expressed as a number from 0 for impossible to 1 for certain. The probabilities of all mutually exclusive and exhaustive outcomes of a situation sum to 1.

title: Classical probability
text: The classical interpretation assigns probability by counting equally likely outcomes: the probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of possible outcomes, when all are equally likely.

title: Frequentist probability
text: The frequentist interpretation defines probability as the long-run relative frequency of an event over many repeated trials. On this view, the probability of a coin landing heads is the limiting proportion of heads in endless tosses.

title: Bayesian probability
text: The Bayesian interpretation treats probability as a degree of belief that can be updated as evidence arrives. It allows probabilities to be assigned to one-off events and revised coherently in light of new information.

title: Base rate
text: A base rate is the underlying frequency of a characteristic or event in a population before any specific evidence is considered. Neglecting base rates is a common source of error in judging how likely a diagnosis or classification is.

title: Bayes theorem
text: Bayes' theorem describes how to update the probability of a hypothesis given new evidence. The posterior probability is proportional to the prior probability times the likelihood of the evidence under the hypothesis.

title: Prior and posterior
text: In Bayesian updating, the prior is the probability assigned to a hypothesis before new evidence, and the posterior is the revised probability after incorporating that evidence. Strong priors require stronger evidence to shift them much.

title: Likelihood in Bayes
text: The likelihood is the probability of the observed evidence assuming a hypothesis is true. Evidence supports a hypothesis to the extent it is more probable under that hypothesis than under its rivals.

title: Rare disease problem
text: In screening for a rare condition, even an accurate test yields many false positives because the healthy population vastly outnumbers the affected. A positive result may still leave the condition unlikely, illustrating base rate neglect.

title: Prosecutor's fallacy
text: The prosecutor's fallacy confuses the probability of the evidence given innocence with the probability of innocence given the evidence. A small chance of a random match does not mean a small chance the defendant is innocent.

title: Conditional probability
text: Conditional probability is the probability of one event given that another has occurred, written P of A given B. It generally differs from the unconditional probability of A and from the probability of B given A.

title: Independence of events
text: Two events are independent when the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other. For independent events, the probability that both occur equals the product of their individual probabilities.

title: Confusing the conditionals
text: A common probability mistake is assuming the probability of A given B equals the probability of B given A. These are usually different, and treating them as interchangeable produces serious errors, as in medical and legal reasoning.

title: Multiplication rule
text: The multiplication rule gives the probability that two events both occur. For independent events it is the product of their probabilities; in general it multiplies one event's probability by the other's conditional probability.

title: Addition rule
text: The addition rule gives the probability that at least one of two events occurs. For mutually exclusive events it is the sum of their probabilities; otherwise the probability of both occurring together must be subtracted to avoid double counting.

title: Expected value
text: The expected value of an uncertain quantity is the sum of its possible values each weighted by its probability. It represents the long-run average outcome and guides decisions among gambles with different payoffs and odds.

title: Law of large numbers
text: The law of large numbers states that as the number of independent trials grows, the average of the results tends toward the expected value. It explains why long-run frequencies stabilise even though single outcomes stay unpredictable.

title: Regression to the mean
text: Regression to the mean is the tendency for extreme measurements to be followed by ones closer to the average. Ignoring it can create the illusion that an intervention worked when only natural variation was at play.

title: Sample size and reliability
text: Small samples produce more variable results than large ones, so extreme outcomes appear more often in small groups. Failing to account for sample size leads to over-interpreting differences that are merely statistical noise.

title: Prior sensitivity
text: Bayesian conclusions depend on the prior probability chosen, so the same evidence can yield different posteriors for people who started with different priors. Substantial evidence tends to bring differing priors into closer agreement.

title: Odds and probability
text: Odds express likelihood as the ratio of an event happening to it not happening, while probability expresses it as a fraction of all outcomes. Odds of three to one against correspond to a probability of one quarter.

title: Diagnostic value of a test
text: A test's usefulness depends not only on its accuracy but on the base rate of what it detects. The same test result carries very different implications in a high-risk group than in the general low-risk population.

title: Occam's razor
text: Occam's razor is the principle that among competing explanations that account equally well for the evidence, the one requiring the fewest assumptions should be preferred. It is a guide to choosing hypotheses, not a proof of truth.

title: Parsimony in science
text: Parsimony is the preference for simpler theories with fewer entities or assumptions. Simplicity aids testability and reduces the chance of unsupported claims, though a simpler theory is not automatically the correct one.

title: Razor as heuristic
text: Occam's razor is a heuristic rather than a law of nature. It recommends the simplest adequate explanation as a starting point, but reality can be complex, so the razor must yield when a simpler account fails to fit the evidence.

title: Ad hoc hypotheses
text: An ad hoc hypothesis is an extra assumption introduced solely to save a theory from refutation, without independent support. Occam's razor counts against such additions because they multiply assumptions merely to protect a favoured view.

title: Explanatory adequacy first
text: Occam's razor applies only among explanations that fit the evidence equally well. A simpler theory that fails to account for the facts is not preferred; adequacy comes first, and simplicity decides between adequate rivals.

title: Scientific method overview
text: The scientific method is a systematic approach to acquiring knowledge through observation, hypothesis formation, prediction, experiment, and revision. Its power lies in testing ideas against evidence and discarding those that fail.

title: Forming a hypothesis
text: A hypothesis is a proposed, testable explanation for an observation. To be scientifically useful it must be specific enough to generate predictions that could, in principle, be shown false by observation or experiment.

title: Falsifiability
text: Falsifiability is the property of a claim that some possible observation could show it to be false. A hypothesis that no evidence could contradict is not scientifically testable, however plausible it may seem.

title: Testable predictions
text: A scientific hypothesis earns support by making predictions that can be checked against observation. Predictions that are risky, specific, and could easily fail provide stronger tests than vague ones that almost anything would satisfy.

title: Controlled experiment
text: A controlled experiment isolates the effect of one variable by holding others constant and comparing a treatment group with a control group. Control groups reveal what would have happened without the intervention being tested.

title: Confounding variables
text: A confounding variable is an unmeasured factor that influences both the presumed cause and the effect, creating a spurious association. Controlling for confounders is essential before inferring that one variable causes another.

title: Control group and placebo
text: A control group provides a baseline against which a treatment's effect is measured. A placebo control accounts for improvements arising from expectation alone, so that any additional effect can be attributed to the treatment itself.

title: Blinding
text: Blinding conceals which participants receive which treatment to prevent expectations from biasing results. In double-blind studies neither participants nor those assessing them know the assignments, reducing conscious and unconscious bias.

title: Replication
text: Replication is repeating a study to see whether its results hold. Because any single result may arise from chance or error, findings gain credibility only when independent researchers can reproduce them under similar conditions.

title: Peer review
text: Peer review is the evaluation of research by independent experts before publication. It aims to catch errors, weak methods, and overstated conclusions, though it is a filter for quality rather than a guarantee of truth.

title: Theory versus hypothesis
text: In science a theory is a well-substantiated explanation supported by a large body of evidence, not a mere guess. A hypothesis is a specific testable proposal, whereas a theory unifies and explains many confirmed observations.

title: Null hypothesis
text: The null hypothesis states that there is no real effect or difference, serving as the default to be tested against. Researchers assess whether observed data are unlikely enough under the null to justify rejecting it.

title: Statistical significance
text: Statistical significance indicates that an observed result would be unlikely if only chance were operating, according to a chosen threshold. It concerns the reliability of an effect, not its size or practical importance.

title: P-value meaning
text: A p-value is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis were true. A small p-value casts doubt on the null but does not measure the probability that the hypothesis is true.

title: Type I and Type II errors
text: A Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis, a false positive, while a Type II error is failing to reject a false null, a false negative. Study design trades off the risks of these two kinds of mistake.

title: Operational definitions
text: An operational definition specifies how a concept is measured in a study, translating an abstract idea into observable procedures. Clear operational definitions make findings interpretable and allow other researchers to replicate them.

title: Observation and theory-ladenness
text: Observations in science are often theory-laden, meaning what one notices and records is shaped by prior expectations. Recognising this guards against seeing only what a favoured theory predicts and overlooking anomalies.

title: Confidence intervals
text: A confidence interval is a range of values, computed from data, that is likely to contain the true quantity being estimated. It conveys the precision of an estimate, with wider intervals indicating greater uncertainty.

title: Direct versus circumstantial
text: Direct evidence establishes a fact without inference, such as an eyewitness to an event, while circumstantial evidence supports a conclusion through inference from related facts. Strong circumstantial evidence can be more reliable than weak direct evidence.

title: Weight of evidence
text: The weight of evidence refers to how strongly it supports a conclusion, considering its reliability, relevance, and quantity. Weighing evidence means assessing each item's quality, not merely counting how many items point one way.

title: Corroboration
text: Corroboration is independent evidence that confirms a claim already supported by other evidence. Multiple independent sources agreeing on a fact raise confidence far more than a single source or repeated claims from one origin.

title: Testimonial evidence
text: Testimonial evidence is information provided by a witness or informant based on their perception or knowledge. Its value depends on the witness's honesty, competence, opportunity to observe, and the accuracy of their memory.

title: Physical evidence
text: Physical evidence consists of tangible objects and traces connected to an event, such as materials, marks, or residues. Because it does not depend on human memory or honesty, it can provide especially durable and objective support.

title: Reliability of eyewitnesses
text: Eyewitness testimony is frequently persuasive but can be unreliable, since memory is reconstructive and subject to suggestion, stress, and the passage of time. Confidence expressed by a witness does not guarantee accuracy.

title: Anecdote versus data
text: An anecdote is a single reported instance, whereas data are systematically collected observations. Anecdotes can suggest hypotheses but cannot establish general patterns, because they are unrepresentative and prone to selective recall.

title: Relevance of evidence
text: Evidence is relevant when it makes a claim more or less probable than it would be otherwise. Irrelevant information, however striking, adds nothing to an argument and can distract from the facts that actually bear on it.

title: Chain of custody principle
text: Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken record of who handled an item of evidence and when. It supports the integrity of physical evidence by showing it was not altered, substituted, or contaminated between collection and analysis.

title: Independent lines of evidence
text: A conclusion supported by several independent lines of evidence is far stronger than one resting on a single line. When different methods or sources converge on the same answer, the chance that all share the same error is small.

title: Extraordinary claims
text: The principle that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence holds that the more a claim conflicts with established knowledge, the stronger the evidence needed to accept it. Ordinary evidence suffices for ordinary claims.

title: Absence of evidence
text: Absence of evidence is weak evidence of absence only when evidence would be expected if the claim were true. Where thorough search should have found something and did not, its absence can meaningfully count against the claim.

title: Documentary evidence
text: Documentary evidence consists of records, writings, and files that bear on a question. Its value depends on authenticity, the reliability of its source, and whether it can be shown to be genuine and unaltered.

title: Prior probability of claims
text: How much evidence a claim requires depends partly on its prior plausibility. A claim consistent with well-established knowledge starts with a higher prior and needs less confirmation than one that contradicts it.

title: Forensic science defined
text: Forensic science applies scientific methods and principles to questions arising in legal contexts. It seeks to analyse physical evidence objectively, linking or excluding people, objects, and events through reproducible techniques.

title: Locard's exchange principle
text: Locard's exchange principle holds that whenever two objects come into contact, there is a transfer of material between them. Every contact leaves a trace, which underlies the collection and analysis of trace evidence.

title: Individual versus class evidence
text: Class evidence narrows a source to a group sharing common characteristics, while individual evidence can be linked to a single source. Fingerprints tend toward individualising, whereas fibre type is usually class characteristic.

title: Fingerprint patterns
text: Fingerprints display friction ridge patterns broadly grouped into loops, whorls, and arches. These patterns form before birth and remain stable throughout life, providing a persistent basis for identification.

title: Fingerprint uniqueness
text: The detailed arrangement of friction ridge minutiae, such as ridge endings and bifurcations, is considered highly distinctive to each finger. This individuality and persistence make fingerprints a long-standing means of identification.

title: Latent fingerprints
text: Latent fingerprints are impressions left by the natural oils and sweat of the friction ridges, usually invisible until developed. Techniques such as powders and chemical reagents make them visible for recording and comparison.

title: Footwear impressions
text: Footwear impressions can link a shoe to a scene through the tread pattern, size, and wear characteristics. Class features identify the type of shoe, while accidental damage and wear can lend more individual character to an impression.

title: Tool mark analysis
text: Tool marks are impressions or striations left when a tool contacts a surface. Because tools acquire microscopic imperfections through use, their marks can sometimes be compared with a suspected tool to assess a possible link.

title: Trace evidence
text: Trace evidence consists of small quantities of material transferred during contact, such as fibres, hairs, glass fragments, soil, and paint. Its analysis can associate people, objects, and locations by comparing physical characteristics.

title: Questioned documents
text: Questioned document examination assesses the authenticity, source, or alteration of writings and printed materials. It considers handwriting, inks, paper, printing methods, and signs of erasure, insertion, or forgery.

title: Handwriting comparison
text: Handwriting comparison examines features such as letter form, spacing, slant, pressure, and connecting strokes. Because writing habits are individual yet variable, examiners assess consistencies and differences across known and questioned samples.

title: Ballistics basics
text: Firearms examination, sometimes called ballistics, studies firearms, ammunition, and the marks they leave. A barrel imparts characteristic striations to a fired bullet, which may be compared with test-fired samples from a suspected weapon.

title: Cartridge case marks
text: When a firearm is discharged, its mechanism can leave distinctive marks on the cartridge case, including firing pin impressions and breech face marks. These may help associate a fired case with a particular weapon.

title: Toxicology
text: Forensic toxicology detects and measures drugs, poisons, and other substances in body fluids and tissues. It considers dose, metabolism, and time since exposure to interpret whether a substance may have contributed to an outcome.

title: Blood typing
text: Blood can be classified into groups such as the ABO system based on antigens on red cells. Blood typing can exclude possible sources and narrow a group of contributors, though it is far less discriminating than modern profiling.

title: Bloodstain patterns
text: Bloodstain pattern analysis studies the size, shape, and distribution of stains to infer how blood was deposited. Droplet shape and spatter distribution can suggest the direction, force, and position associated with an event.

title: Time of death indicators
text: General indicators used to estimate time since death include body cooling, the onset and passing of rigidity, and the settling of blood, each of which changes over predictable but variable ranges influenced by conditions.

title: Rigor mortis principle
text: Rigor mortis is the temporary stiffening of muscles after death caused by chemical changes in muscle tissue. It typically appears within hours, reaches a peak, and then passes, and its progress helps roughly estimate elapsed time.

title: Livor mortis principle
text: Livor mortis is the pooling of blood under gravity after circulation stops, producing discolouration in the lowest parts of the body. Its onset, fixation, and position can indicate elapsed time and whether a body was moved.

title: Algor mortis principle
text: Algor mortis is the gradual cooling of a body toward the surrounding temperature after death. Because the rate depends on many factors, temperature-based estimates of elapsed time carry considerable uncertainty.

title: Impression evidence
text: Impression evidence records the shape of an object pressed into or onto a surface, including fingerprints, footwear marks, tyre tracks, and tool marks. Comparison assesses both class characteristics and any individualising detail.

title: Contamination control
text: Preventing contamination is central to forensic work, since introduced material can create false associations. Careful handling, protective equipment, and separation of items help ensure that analysed traces genuinely relate to the case.

title: Presumptive versus confirmatory tests
text: Presumptive tests give a quick, sensitive indication that a substance may be present but can yield false positives. Confirmatory tests are more specific and are used to establish identity after a presumptive screen suggests it.

title: Forensic comparison logic
text: Forensic comparison assesses whether a questioned item and a known sample could share a common source, weighing similarities against differences. A meaningful match reduces the pool of possible sources rather than proving a unique one.

title: Limits of forensic certainty
text: Most forensic comparisons yield probabilistic associations rather than absolute certainty. Responsible interpretation states the strength of an association and its limits, avoiding overstated claims of unique identification.

title: Observation versus seeing
text: Careful observation differs from merely seeing: it involves deliberate, systematic attention to detail and its significance. Trained observers notice and interpret features that casual viewers register but do not consciously process.

title: Inattentional blindness
text: Inattentional blindness is the failure to notice a fully visible but unexpected object because attention is focused elsewhere. It shows that seeing depends on attention, and that people miss things they are not looking for.

title: Change blindness
text: Change blindness is the difficulty people have in detecting changes to a scene, especially across interruptions. Substantial alterations can go unnoticed, revealing that perception retains far less detail than it subjectively seems to.

title: Selective attention
text: Selective attention is the capacity to focus on relevant information while filtering out distractions. It enables concentration but also causes people to overlook information outside their current focus, however visible it is.

title: Baseline and anomaly
text: Skilled observation involves knowing what is normal for a setting so that anomalies stand out. Recognising deviations from an established baseline is often more informative than cataloguing details that are entirely expected.

title: Systematic scanning
text: Systematic scanning examines a scene in a deliberate order rather than at random, reducing the chance of missing important features. A consistent method ensures coverage and makes it easier to detect what is absent as well as present.

title: Detail and significance
text: Observing detail is only useful when its significance is understood. The value of a noticed feature lies in the inferences it supports, so observation and reasoning must work together to yield conclusions.

title: Expectation shapes perception
text: Prior expectations strongly influence what people perceive, causing them to see what they anticipate and overlook what they do not. Awareness of this effect encourages checking observations against alternatives rather than assumptions.

title: Recording observations promptly
text: Observations should be recorded promptly, because memory fades and reconstructs. A contemporaneous note preserves detail more faithfully than later recollection, which is vulnerable to distortion and the influence of subsequent information.

title: Critical thinking defined
text: Critical thinking is the disciplined process of actively analysing, evaluating, and synthesising information to reach well-reasoned conclusions. It involves questioning assumptions, weighing evidence, and considering alternatives rather than accepting claims uncritically.

title: Charitable interpretation
text: The principle of charity requires interpreting an argument in its strongest reasonable form before criticising it. Engaging the best version of an opposing view leads to more honest and productive reasoning than attacking a weak version.

title: Steel-manning
text: Steel-manning is the practice of stating an opposing argument in its strongest form, the opposite of building a straw man. It tests one's own position against the best case for the other side and sharpens genuine disagreement.

title: Distinguishing fact and opinion
text: A fact is a claim that can in principle be verified against reality, while an opinion expresses a judgement or preference. Clear reasoning separates the two, since opinions can be reasonable or not but are not simply true or false.

title: Questioning assumptions
text: Assumptions are unstated beliefs taken for granted in reasoning. Making them explicit and examining them is central to critical thinking, because a conclusion can only be as sound as the assumptions on which it rests.

title: Considering alternatives
text: Good reasoning actively seeks alternative explanations and courses of action rather than settling on the first that comes to mind. Comparing rival possibilities guards against premature commitment and confirmation bias.

title: Suspending judgement
text: Suspending judgement means withholding a firm conclusion when the evidence is insufficient. Tolerating uncertainty rather than forcing a decision prevents error and keeps the mind open to further evidence.

title: Intellectual humility
text: Intellectual humility is recognising the limits of one's knowledge and the possibility of being wrong. It encourages seeking out disconfirming evidence and revising beliefs, which are essential to sound reasoning.

title: Separating claim from source
text: A claim's truth is independent of who makes it, so evaluating an argument means assessing the reasoning and evidence rather than the identity of the speaker. Conflating the two leads to both ad hominem and appeal to authority.

title: Defining terms clearly
text: Clear reasoning depends on defining key terms so that disputes are about substance rather than words. Many disagreements dissolve once the parties clarify that they are using a term in different senses.

title: Burden of proof
text: The burden of proof lies with the party asserting a claim, not with those who doubt it. Demanding that others disprove an unsupported assertion reverses this burden and is a common rhetorical error.

title: Distinguishing correlation questions
text: A critical thinker faced with a correlation asks whether it reflects causation, reverse causation, a common cause, or coincidence. Naming these possibilities prevents leaping from an association to an unwarranted causal claim.

title: Decision under uncertainty
text: Decision-making under uncertainty involves choosing among options whose outcomes are not known in advance. Good decisions weigh possible outcomes by their likelihood and value rather than judging solely by how things turn out.

title: Process versus outcome
text: A good decision is one made well given the information available, which is distinct from a good outcome. Because chance intervenes, sound decisions can lead to bad results and poor decisions to good ones; judging by outcome alone is misleading.

title: Expected value in decisions
text: Choosing by expected value means selecting the option with the highest average payoff across its possible outcomes weighted by probability. It is a rational baseline, though attitudes to risk can justify departing from it.

title: Opportunity cost
text: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone when a choice is made. Sound decisions account for what is given up, not only what is gained, since every commitment excludes other possibilities.

title: Risk versus uncertainty
text: Risk refers to situations where outcomes are unknown but their probabilities are, while uncertainty refers to cases where even the probabilities are unclear. The distinction affects which decision methods can reasonably be applied.

title: Decision trees
text: A decision tree maps choices and chance events as branches, with outcomes and probabilities at the ends. Working backward from the outcomes allows the expected value of each initial choice to be compared systematically.

title: Base rates in decisions
text: Sound decisions incorporate base rates, the general frequency of outcomes in similar situations, rather than relying only on the specifics of the case. The typical result for comparable cases is often a better guide than intuition alone.

title: Satisficing
text: Satisficing is choosing the first option that meets an acceptable threshold rather than searching for the optimal one. When information and time are limited, satisficing can be more efficient than exhaustive optimisation.

title: Reversible versus irreversible
text: Reversible decisions can be undone at little cost, while irreversible ones cannot. It is rational to decide quickly on reversible matters and to gather more information before committing to choices that cannot be reversed.

title: Premortem analysis
text: A premortem imagines that a decision has already failed and asks why, surfacing risks before they occur. By deliberately seeking reasons a plan might go wrong, it counters overconfidence and improves preparation.

title: Weighing costs and benefits
text: A cost-benefit approach lists the advantages and disadvantages of each option, ideally weighted by importance and likelihood, to compare them on a common footing. It makes trade-offs explicit rather than leaving them to intuition.

title: Precautionary reasoning
text: Precautionary reasoning favours caution when a decision carries a risk of serious or irreversible harm, even under uncertainty. It weighs the severity of possible harms heavily, though it must be balanced against the costs of inaction.

title: Method of loci
text: The method of loci is a memory technique that associates items to be remembered with locations along a familiar route or place. Mentally walking the route recalls the items in order, exploiting strong spatial memory.

title: Memory palace
text: A memory palace is a mental structure, often based on a familiar building, used with the method of loci to store information at imagined locations. Vivid images placed in each spot make abstract material easier to recall.

title: Mnemonics
text: Mnemonics are techniques that aid memory by linking new information to easily recalled cues such as rhymes, acronyms, or images. They work by giving otherwise arbitrary material a memorable structure or association.

title: Chunking
text: Chunking groups individual items into larger meaningful units so that more can be held in working memory. Remembering a long number as a few grouped segments illustrates how structure expands effective memory capacity.

title: Spaced repetition
text: Spaced repetition schedules reviews of material at increasing intervals to strengthen long-term retention. Reviewing just before information would be forgotten is more efficient than massed practice at combating the forgetting curve.

title: Elaborative encoding
text: Elaborative encoding improves memory by connecting new information to existing knowledge through meaning, imagery, or association. Material processed deeply for meaning is retained far better than material rehearsed by rote.

title: Reconstructive memory
text: Memory is reconstructive rather than a faithful recording: recall rebuilds events from fragments, filling gaps with inference and expectation. This makes memory prone to distortion and to incorporating misleading later information.

title: Testing effect
text: The testing effect is the finding that actively retrieving information from memory strengthens retention more than re-reading it. Self-testing produces more durable learning than passive review of the same material.

title: Association and vividness
text: Memory techniques exploit the mind's affinity for vivid, unusual, and emotionally charged images. Bizarre or striking associations are recalled more easily than bland ones, which is why mnemonic images are made distinctive.

title: Peg system
text: The peg system links numbers to fixed memorable images, or pegs, so ordered lists can be attached to them. Recalling the peg for each number retrieves the associated item, providing a reusable framework for sequences.

title: Purpose of note-taking
text: Note-taking captures information in a durable, retrievable form, offloading memory and imposing structure on it. Good notes record not only facts but their sources and relationships, so they support later reasoning and review.

title: Separating fact and inference
text: Careful notes distinguish observed facts from inferences drawn about them. Conflating the two can entrench an interpretation prematurely, whereas keeping them separate leaves room to revise conclusions as new facts arrive.

title: Recording sources
text: Noting the source of each piece of information allows its reliability to be judged and claims to be traced back. Undocumented facts are hard to verify, and their credibility cannot be assessed without knowing where they came from.

title: Organising by relevance
text: Organising notes so that related facts are grouped and their connections made explicit reveals patterns that scattered records obscure. Structure turns a heap of details into an argument or a picture of a situation.

title: Timelines
text: A timeline arranges events in chronological order, making sequences, gaps, and overlaps visible. Ordering facts by time can expose inconsistencies and clarify what could or could not have caused what.

title: Concept mapping
text: A concept map represents ideas as nodes and their relationships as labelled links, showing how facts connect. Making structure visual can reveal implications and gaps that a linear list of notes would hide.

title: Reviewing and revising notes
text: Notes are more useful when reviewed and revised, since early records may be incomplete or mistaken. Periodic revision consolidates understanding, corrects errors, and integrates new information with what was already recorded.

title: Distinguishing certain from tentative
text: Well-kept records mark which facts are firmly established and which are tentative or unconfirmed. Flagging uncertainty prevents provisional information from later being treated as settled and helps prioritise verification.

title: Open versus closed questions
text: Open questions invite detailed, unconstrained answers, while closed questions call for brief or yes-no responses. Open questions elicit fuller accounts and reduce the risk of leading, whereas closed questions confirm specific details.

title: Leading questions
text: A leading question suggests its own answer or presupposes disputed information, biasing the response. Because such questions can shape and distort recollection, reliable interviewing avoids them, especially when gathering an initial account.

title: Free recall first
text: Reliable interviewing begins with free recall, letting the person describe events in their own words before specific questions are asked. This yields fuller, less contaminated information than starting with pointed or leading questions.

title: Rapport in interviewing
text: Establishing rapport helps an interviewee feel at ease and communicate more openly. A cooperative atmosphere tends to produce more complete and accurate information than a hostile or hurried one.

title: Memory contamination
text: Interview questions can contaminate memory by introducing details the person then incorporates into their account. Because recollection is malleable, careful interviewers avoid suggesting information and record answers in the person's own words.

title: Corroborating accounts
text: Statements gathered from interviews gain reliability when corroborated by independent witnesses or physical evidence. A single uncorroborated account, however confident, should be weighed cautiously against the possibility of error.

title: Detecting inconsistency
text: Comparing an account against itself, against other accounts, and against known facts can reveal inconsistencies worth exploring. Inconsistency may signal error, deception, or misunderstanding, and calls for clarification rather than immediate conclusion.

title: Listening and silence
text: Attentive listening and tolerance of silence encourage fuller answers, since people often continue speaking to fill a pause. Interrupting or rushing can cut off valuable information the interviewee was about to provide.

title: Avoiding confirmation in questioning
text: An interviewer prone to confirmation bias may ask only questions that support a favoured theory. Deliberately seeking information that could disconfirm the working hypothesis leads to a more accurate and balanced account.

title: Lateral thinking
text: Lateral thinking is solving problems by approaching them from unexpected angles rather than step-by-step logic. It involves questioning assumptions and reframing a problem to find solutions that direct, conventional reasoning would miss.

title: Constraint identification
text: Many puzzles are solved by identifying the constraints that any solution must satisfy and using them to eliminate possibilities. Making implicit constraints explicit narrows the search and often reveals a forced answer.

title: Working backward
text: Working backward starts from the desired goal and reasons toward the present, which can be easier than working forward when the endpoint is well defined. It is a powerful strategy for mazes, proofs, and planning problems.

title: Process of elimination
text: The process of elimination solves problems by ruling out impossible options until only viable ones remain. When possibilities are finite and constraints clear, systematically removing what cannot be true isolates what must be.

title: Substitution cipher
text: A substitution cipher replaces each letter of a message with another symbol or letter according to a fixed scheme. Simple substitution preserves letter frequencies, which is why frequency analysis can often break it.

title: Caesar cipher
text: A Caesar cipher shifts each letter of the alphabet by a fixed number of positions. Because there are only a limited number of possible shifts, it is easily broken by trying each one or by frequency analysis.

title: Frequency analysis
text: Frequency analysis breaks substitution ciphers by comparing how often symbols appear with the known frequencies of letters in the language. In English, common letters such as e and t reveal likely substitutions.

title: Transposition cipher
text: A transposition cipher rearranges the letters of a message according to a system rather than replacing them. The letters themselves are unchanged, so the plaintext characters are all present but reordered.

title: Steganography
text: Steganography conceals the existence of a message rather than its content, hiding information within an innocuous carrier such as an image or text. It differs from cryptography, which scrambles a message whose presence is open.

title: Reframing a problem
text: Reframing restates a problem in different terms to reveal new approaches. A question that seems intractable in one formulation may become straightforward when its goal, assumptions, or representation are changed.

title: Decomposition
text: Decomposition breaks a complex problem into smaller, more manageable subproblems that can be solved separately and then combined. Tackling parts in isolation reduces difficulty and makes progress measurable.

title: Insight and incubation
text: Some problems are solved suddenly by insight, often after a period of incubation away from active effort. Stepping back can allow unhelpful assumptions to fade and a new framing to emerge, resolving an apparent impasse.

title: Pattern recognition
text: Recognising patterns lets a solver apply the solution of a familiar problem to a new one that shares its structure. Abstracting away surface details to see the underlying form is central to solving puzzles and proofs.

title: Checking the solution
text: A crucial final step in problem-solving is verifying that a candidate solution actually satisfies all the conditions. Confirming an answer against the original constraints guards against overlooked cases and careless errors.

title: Begging the Question
text: Begging the question (petitio principii) is an informal fallacy in which the conclusion of an argument is assumed, often covertly, within one of its premises. The argument thus offers no independent support for its claim, merely restating it in different words. For example, asserting that a text is trustworthy because it says so treats the very point in dispute as an established premise.

title: Complex Question
text: The complex question fallacy (plurium interrogationum) embeds a controversial or unproven assumption within a question so that any direct answer appears to concede it. The classic illustration, asking whether someone has stopped a wrongful habit, presupposes that the habit existed. Splitting the loaded question into its separate parts exposes and defuses the smuggled assumption.

title: False Analogy
text: The false analogy fallacy draws a conclusion by comparing two things that resemble each other in some respects while ignoring differences that are relevant to the point being argued. Because analogies support conclusions only insofar as the compared cases are alike in the pertinent features, an inference collapses when the similarities are superficial and the crucial disanalogies are overlooked.

title: Appeal to Fear
text: The appeal to fear (argumentum ad metum or ad baculum in its coercive form) attempts to establish a conclusion by arousing dread of a consequence rather than by supplying evidence for the claim. Because provoking anxiety about an outcome does not bear on whether a proposition is true, the emotional pressure substitutes for legitimate justification and constitutes an informal fallacy.

title: Appeal to Hypocrisy
text: The appeal to hypocrisy, or tu quoque, deflects criticism by charging that the critic fails to practice what they preach, rather than addressing the substance of the criticism. Because a claim's truth or an argument's soundness is independent of whether its advocate is consistent, pointing to the opponent's hypocrisy is a form of ad hominem that leaves the original point untouched.

title: Snob Appeal
text: Snob appeal is a persuasion tactic, a variety of the appeal to vanity, that recommends a claim, product, or course of action by associating it with elite status, exclusivity, or the tastes of a superior class. Because prestige and social cachet have no bearing on whether a proposition is true or a product genuinely worthwhile, the appeal replaces evidence with flattery of the audience's aspirations.

title: Appeal to Spite
text: The appeal to spite (argumentum ad odium) tries to win assent to a conclusion by stirring up bitterness, resentment, or malice toward a person or group rather than by presenting relevant evidence. By exploiting the audience's ill will, it substitutes a hostile emotion for rational grounds, and the negative feeling it provokes has no bearing on the truth of the claim being advanced.

title: Appeal to Flattery
text: The appeal to flattery (argumentum ad superbiam) seeks agreement by praising or complimenting the audience so that accepting the conclusion feels like confirmation of their good judgment. Because insincere or irrelevant praise does nothing to establish whether a claim is true, the flattery functions as a manipulative substitute for evidence and is a recognized informal fallacy.

title: Moralistic Fallacy
text: The moralistic fallacy infers that because a state of affairs ought to be a certain way, it therefore is that way, or that because a phenomenon would be undesirable it cannot be factually true. It reverses the direction of the naturalistic fallacy, illegitimately deducing statements of fact from moral preferences and treating what is ethically appealing as thereby empirically established.

title: Naturalistic Fallacy
text: The naturalistic fallacy, a term introduced by G. E. Moore, is the error of defining or identifying the moral property good with some natural property such as pleasure, desire, or evolutionary advantage. Moore argued that good is a simple, non-natural quality, so any attempt to reduce it to natural facts is illegitimate; the open-question argument is his central test for exposing it.

title: Is-Ought Problem
text: The is-ought problem, articulated by David Hume, observes that arguments frequently shift from purely descriptive premises about what is the case to prescriptive conclusions about what ought to be done, without justifying the transition. Hume noted that a normative conclusion cannot validly be derived from factual premises alone, so such a leap requires an additional evaluative premise to be legitimate.

title: Argument from Silence
text: The argument from silence (argumentum ex silentio) infers a conclusion from the absence of evidence, typically claiming that because a source does not mention something, that thing did not occur or was unknown. Such reasoning is reliable only when the source would very probably have recorded the matter had it existed; otherwise silence is uninformative and the inference is fallacious.

title: Argument from Incredulity
text: The argument from incredulity concludes that a claim must be false or impossible simply because one cannot imagine or understand how it could be true, or that another claim must be true because no alternative is conceivable. It mistakes a limit of personal imagination or knowledge for a fact about reality, and is a species of the argument from ignorance.

title: Appeal to Common Sense
text: The appeal to common sense asserts that a claim must be true because it is obvious or widely regarded as self-evident, rather than offering supporting evidence. While shared intuitions can be a starting point for inquiry, invoking common sense to shut down scrutiny is fallacious, since many propositions once deemed obvious have proven false and obviousness is no guarantee of truth.

title: Thought-Terminating Cliche
text: A thought-terminating cliche is a stock phrase, often folksy or reassuring, deployed to halt critical reflection and dismiss dissent without engaging its substance. Expressions of this kind foreclose analysis by offering a ready-made answer that discourages further questioning. The concept was popularized by Robert Jay Lifton in his study of ideological thought reform and manipulative rhetoric.

title: False Attribution
text: False attribution is the fallacy of supporting an argument by citing an irrelevant, unqualified, biased, fabricated, or misidentified source as if it were authoritative.
