Because the persuasive force depends on the credibility of the attributed authority, misrepresenting who said something, or crediting a claim to someone who never made it, undermines any legitimate appeal to testimony or expertise.

title: Quoting Out of Context
text: Quoting out of context, sometimes called contextomy, is a form of false attribution in which a passage is excerpted so as to distort the original speaker's intended meaning. By removing qualifying words or surrounding argument, the quoter can make a source appear to endorse a position it actually rejected, misrepresenting the author while retaining a superficial appearance of faithful citation.

title: Kettle Logic
text: Kettle logic denotes the use of multiple mutually inconsistent arguments to defend a single position, where the individual defenses cannot all be true at once. The term derives from Freud's example of a man who, accused of returning a borrowed kettle damaged, claims he returned it undamaged, that it was already damaged, and that he never borrowed it, each excuse undercutting the others.

title: Proof by Assertion
text: Proof by assertion is the fallacy of maintaining that a claim is true merely by stating it repeatedly and forcefully, regardless of contradiction or refutation. Because reiterating a proposition adds no evidential support, the persistence of the assertion cannot make it true; the tactic relies on dogged repetition to create an impression of certainty in place of genuine justification.

title: Ipse Dixit
text: Ipse dixit, Latin for he himself said it, refers to an unsupported assertion presented as though its truth were guaranteed solely by the speaker's say-so. Such bare dogmatic pronouncements offer no reasons or evidence and demand acceptance on the authority of the speaker alone. The phrase originates with followers of Pythagoras who settled disputes by invoking their master's word.

title: Argumentum ad Nauseam
text: Argumentum ad nauseam, the argument from repetition, is the fallacy of asserting a claim so often that the audience comes to accept it through sheer familiarity rather than through evidence. It exploits the tendency to mistake fluency and repetition for truth, and overlaps with proof by assertion; the frequency with which a statement is repeated has no bearing on its accuracy.

title: Guilt by Association
text: Guilt by association is the fallacy of rejecting a person's claim or discrediting them because of their real or alleged connection to a disreputable group or individual. Because the merit of an argument does not depend on the company its proponent keeps, tarring a position through its associations rather than examining it directly is a species of the association fallacy and ad hominem.

title: Association Fallacy
text: The association fallacy infers that two things sharing some property must therefore share another, often concluding that because a claim or person is linked to something regarded as good or bad, they inherit that evaluation. It underlies both guilt by association and honor by association, and its formal skeleton mirrors the invalid pattern of the undistributed middle term.

title: Chronological Snobbery
text: Chronological snobbery, a phrase coined by C. S. Lewis and Owen Barfield, is the fallacy of assuming that a belief or practice is discredited simply because it belongs to an earlier era, or vindicated because it is contemporary. The age of an idea is irrelevant to its truth; dismissing a view as outdated without examining the reasons it was once held or later abandoned is fallacious.

title: Appeal to Wealth
text: The appeal to wealth (argumentum ad crumenam) is the fallacy of concluding that a claim is true, or a person correct, because they are rich, or that something is better because it is more expensive. Since financial success is no measure of a proposition's truth or an argument's soundness, treating wealth as evidence of correctness substitutes affluence for reasoning.

title: Appeal to Poverty
text: The appeal to poverty (argumentum ad lazarum) is the fallacy of supposing that a conclusion is true, or a person more virtuous or trustworthy, simply because they are poor. The inverse of the appeal to wealth, it romanticizes deprivation as a mark of authenticity or wisdom, but economic circumstances have no bearing on the truth of a claim or the validity of an argument.

title: Gish Gallop
text: The Gish gallop is a rhetorical technique, named after creationist Duane Gish, in which a debater overwhelms an opponent with a rapid succession of many weak or misleading arguments. Because refuting each claim takes far longer than making it, the sheer volume leaves most points unanswered, creating a misleading impression of strength through quantity rather than quality of reasoning.

title: Motte-and-Bailey
text: The motte-and-bailey fallacy conflates two positions sharing a name: a controversial, ambitious claim (the bailey) and an easily defensible, modest one (the motte). An arguer advances the bold claim but, when challenged, retreats to the uncontroversial one, then reasserts the bold claim once the pressure eases. The term, from Nicholas Shackel, likens this to a fortified keep guarding open land.

title: Whataboutism
text: Whataboutism is a rhetorical maneuver that responds to a charge or difficult question by raising a counter-accusation, in effect asking what about some other wrongdoing, rather than answering the original point. A variant of the tu quoque fallacy, it deflects scrutiny by redirecting attention to an opponent's alleged faults, leaving the initial criticism unaddressed and unrefuted.

title: DARVO
text: DARVO is an acronym for Deny, Attack, and Reverse Victim and Offender, describing a response pattern in which an accused party denies the wrongdoing, attacks the credibility of the accuser, and recasts themselves as the true victim. Identified by psychologist Jennifer Freyd, it is a manipulative rhetorical and interpersonal strategy for evading accountability by inverting the roles in a dispute.

title: False Balance
text: False balance, sometimes called bothsidesism, is the practice of presenting opposing positions as equally credible when the available evidence in fact favors one side heavily. Common in journalism, it can mislead audiences into perceiving genuine controversy where scholarly consensus exists, by granting disproportionate attention or apparent legitimacy to a marginal or discredited view.

title: Spotlight Fallacy
text: The spotlight fallacy occurs when someone assumes that cases receiving disproportionate media attention are representative of a whole group or of reality generally. Because coverage is driven by novelty and drama rather than frequency, prominence in the spotlight distorts estimates of how common something is, leading to unwarranted generalizations from a skewed and unrepresentative sample.

title: Nirvana Fallacy
text: The nirvana fallacy, also called the perfect solution fallacy, rejects a realistic proposal by comparing it not to available alternatives but to an idealized, unattainable perfect solution. Because no practical option can meet an impossible standard, this comparison unfairly dismisses workable improvements, treating the failure to solve a problem completely as a reason to attempt nothing at all.

title: Continuum Fallacy
text: The continuum fallacy, also known as the line-drawing fallacy or the fallacy of the beard, argues that because no precise boundary can be drawn along a gradual spectrum, no meaningful distinction exists between its extremes. It exploits vagueness in sorites-style series, wrongly concluding that the absence of a sharp cutoff means the difference between clear cases is illusory.

title: Fallacy of Relative Privation
text: The fallacy of relative privation dismisses a problem or complaint by pointing out that other problems are worse, as if the existence of greater misfortunes rendered the lesser one unworthy of attention. Often summarized by the phrase about starving children elsewhere, it wrongly treats the mere existence of a graver issue as a reason to disregard a genuine, if smaller, concern.

title: Package-Deal Fallacy
text: The package-deal fallacy assumes that things habitually grouped together must always belong together, or share the same properties, simply because they are conventionally associated. It treats a customary bundle of ideas, traits, or policies as an indivisible unit, overlooking that the association may be contingent and that the components can be evaluated and separated independently.

title: Definist Fallacy
text: The definist fallacy, named by William Frankena, is the error of defining a term in a way that covertly builds a controversial conclusion into the definition itself, or of identifying one property with another by mere stipulation. By loading a definition to favor a particular position, an arguer can make a substantive claim appear true by fiat rather than establishing it through argument.

title: Retrospective Determinism
text: Retrospective determinism is the fallacy of arguing that because an event occurred, it was bound to occur, and so those involved were foolish or blameworthy for not having foreseen it. By treating hindsight as though the outcome were inevitable from the start, it ignores the genuine uncertainty faced at the time and unfairly judges past decisions against knowledge unavailable then.

title: Historian's Fallacy
text: The historian's fallacy, described by David Hackett Fischer, is the error of assuming that decision-makers in the past possessed the same information available to those analyzing the events later. It projects present hindsight onto historical actors, faulting them for not anticipating outcomes they had no way to foresee, and is closely related to hindsight bias in judgment.

title: Wishful Thinking
text: Wishful thinking, as a logical fallacy, is the error of accepting a claim as true, or acting as though it were, because one wishes it to be so rather than because the evidence supports it. Sometimes framed as the appeal to consequences of belief, it lets desire dictate belief, treating the pleasantness of a proposition as though it bore on its actual truth.

title: Appeal to Probability
text: The appeal to probability is the fallacy of treating something as certain or inevitable merely because it is possible or likely to happen. From the fact that an outcome could occur, or even that it is probable, one cannot validly infer that it will definitely occur; conflating possibility or high probability with certainty overstates what the premises actually warrant.

title: Base Rate Fallacy
text: The base rate fallacy is the error of ignoring the general prevalence of a condition (its base rate) when judging the probability of a specific case, focusing instead on individuating or vivid information. It commonly arises with imperfect diagnostic tests, where neglecting how rare a condition is leads people to badly overestimate the chance that a positive result is a true positive.

title: Masked Man Fallacy
text: The masked man fallacy, or intensional fallacy, is the invalid substitution of terms within contexts of belief or knowledge. From the premise that someone knows a certain person yet does not know a masked man, one cannot conclude that the masked man is not that person, even if he is; what a subject believes about a thing under one description need not hold under another.

title: Intentional Fallacy
text: The intentional fallacy, a concept from literary theory advanced by Wimsatt and Beardsley, is the mistake of judging the meaning or value of a work of art by reference to the author's private intentions rather than the work itself. On this view the author's aim is neither available nor decisive for interpretation, so appealing to it to settle a work's meaning is methodologically unsound.

title: Existential Fallacy
text: The existential fallacy is a formal error in categorical logic in which a conclusion asserting that something exists is drawn from two universal premises that assert no existence. Because universal statements do not, under modern logic, presuppose that their subject classes have members, inferring a particular, existence-claiming conclusion from wholly universal premises is invalid.

title: Four Terms Fallacy
text: The four terms fallacy (quaternio terminorum) is a formal error in which a categorical syllogism, which must contain exactly three terms, effectively contains four because a term is used with two different meanings. The equivocation breaks the logical connection the middle term is supposed to provide, so the premises fail to link the terms of the conclusion and the inference is invalid.

title: Fallacy of Exclusive Premises
text: The fallacy of exclusive premises is a formal error in categorical syllogisms committed whenever both premises are negative. Two negative premises deny relationships without establishing any positive connection between the terms, so they cannot jointly support any conclusion; a valid categorical syllogism therefore requires at least one affirmative premise.

title: Affirmative from Negative Premise
text: Drawing an affirmative conclusion from a negative premise is a formal error in categorical syllogisms. If either premise is negative, the conclusion must also be negative, because a negative premise severs a relationship among the terms and cannot support an affirmation. A syllogism that reaches a positive conclusion from any negative premise is therefore invalid.

title: Negative from Affirmative Premises
text: Drawing a negative conclusion from affirmative premises is a formal error in categorical syllogisms. If both premises are affirmative, asserting positive relationships among the terms, they cannot validly yield a conclusion that denies a relationship. A negative conclusion requires a negative premise, so inferring one from two affirmatives violates the rules of the syllogism.

title: Illicit Major
text: The fallacy of the illicit major is a formal error in categorical syllogisms in which the major term is distributed in the conclusion but not in the premise where it appears. A term may be treated as referring to an entire class in the conclusion only if it was so treated in the premises; distributing it more widely in the conclusion than in the premise makes the argument invalid.

title: Illicit Minor
text: The fallacy of the illicit minor is a formal error in categorical syllogisms in which the minor term is distributed in the conclusion but not in the premise in which it occurs. Because a conclusion cannot make a claim about a whole class when the premises spoke only of part of it, extending the minor term's reference beyond its premise renders the syllogism invalid.

title: Undistributed Middle
text: The fallacy of the undistributed middle is a formal error in categorical syllogisms in which the middle term, which links the two premises, is not distributed in either premise. Since the middle term must refer to an entire class in at least one premise to connect the other terms reliably, its failure to be distributed leaves the premises unlinked and the inference invalid.

title: Modal Fallacy
text: The modal fallacy is an error involving the illegitimate transfer of a modal operator such as necessity or possibility. A common instance reasons that because a conditional is necessarily true, its consequent is necessary given the antecedent; in fact the necessity attaches to the whole conditional, not to the consequent alone, so shifting the modal scope produces an invalid conclusion.

title: Quantifier Shift Fallacy
text: The quantifier shift fallacy is a formal error that arises from illegitimately reversing the order of two quantifiers. From the premise that everyone has some cause, it does not follow that there is some single cause everyone shares; swapping the universal and existential quantifiers changes the meaning, and the second statement does not follow from the first.

title: Denying a Conjunct
text: Denying a conjunct is a formal fallacy of propositional logic that reasons from the denial of a conjunction and the falsity of one conjunct to the truth of the other. From not both P and Q, together with not-P, it wrongly concludes Q. The pattern is invalid because the negated conjunction is compatible with both conjuncts being false, leaving Q unestablished.

title: Affirming a Disjunct
text: Affirming a disjunct is a formal fallacy of propositional logic that reasons from an inclusive disjunction and the truth of one disjunct to the falsity of the other. From P or Q, together with P, it wrongly concludes not-Q. The pattern is invalid because an inclusive or permits both disjuncts to be true, so affirming one gives no ground for denying the other.

title: Commutation of Conditionals
text: Commutation of conditionals is a formal fallacy that treats a conditional statement as though it were equivalent to its converse, inferring if Q then P from if P then Q. Because the truth of a conditional does not guarantee the truth of its converse, the antecedent and consequent cannot simply be swapped; doing so confuses a sufficient condition with a necessary one.

title: Improper Transposition
text: Improper transposition is a formal fallacy that misapplies the valid rule of contraposition by negating the antecedent and consequent of a conditional without also interchanging them. From if P then Q it wrongly derives if not-P then not-Q, which is the inverse rather than the logically equivalent contrapositive, if not-Q then not-P; the resulting inference is invalid.

title: Bandwagon Fallacy
text: The bandwagon fallacy urges acceptance of a claim or adoption of a practice on the ground that it is popular and growing in acceptance, appealing to the desire to conform. A variant of the appeal to popularity, it treats the momentum of a trend as though rising numbers confirmed correctness, when in fact the growth of a belief has no bearing on its truth.

title: Hasty Generalization
text: Hasty generalization is an informal fallacy in which a broad conclusion about a class is drawn from a sample that is too small, biased, or otherwise unrepresentative. Because a general claim is only as reliable as the evidence supporting it, inferring a sweeping rule from insufficient or atypical instances overreaches what the data can justify and courts error.

title: Accident Fallacy
text: The fallacy of accident, or sweeping generalization, applies a sound general rule to a specific case whose special features make it a legitimate exception. By ignoring the relevant peculiarities of the instance, it forces a rule meant for typical situations onto an atypical one; it is thus the converse of hasty generalization, misapplying a valid rule rather than overgeneralizing from cases.

title: Cum Hoc Fallacy
text: The cum hoc fallacy, from cum hoc ergo propter hoc, meaning with this therefore because of this, infers a causal relationship from the mere co-occurrence or correlation of two things. Because correlated variables may be linked by a third common cause, by chance, or by reverse causation, observing that two phenomena vary together does not establish that one produces the other.

title: Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy
text: The Texas sharpshooter fallacy occurs when someone fixes attention on a cluster of data points that appear meaningfully related while ignoring differences, imposing a pattern after the fact. Named for a marksman who fires at a barn and then paints a target around the tightest grouping, it mistakes clustering that would be expected by chance for evidence of a genuine effect.

title: Fallacy of Many Questions
text: The fallacy of many questions, closely related to the complex question, arises when a single question presupposes something that has not been established and cannot properly be answered with one response because it conflates several distinct issues. Answering as though it were a single simple question forces acceptance of the hidden presupposition, so the question must first be separated.

title: Loaded Language
text: Loaded language is the use of emotionally charged or prejudicial wording to sway an audience toward a conclusion without providing supporting evidence. By framing a subject with terms that carry strong positive or negative connotations, a speaker steers judgment through connotation rather than argument, making the persuasion a rhetorical device rather than a reasoned case.

title: Sunk Cost Fallacy
text: The sunk cost fallacy is the tendency to continue an endeavor because of resources already invested, even when abandoning it would be more rational going forward. Because past expenditures cannot be recovered and should not influence present decisions, letting them dictate whether to persist leads to throwing good resources after bad rather than judging future prospects on their own merits.

title: Suppressed Correlative
text: The suppressed correlative fallacy redefines one of two mutually exclusive alternatives so broadly that it absorbs the other, thereby making it impossible for the second category to apply. By expanding a term until its correlative has no cases left, the arguer renders a genuine distinction empty, so the redefinition wins the point by definition rather than by evidence.

title: Ignoratio Elenchi
text: Ignoratio elenchi, or irrelevant conclusion, is the fallacy of presenting an argument that, however sound in itself, establishes a conclusion different from the one actually at issue. The reasoning misses the point by proving something beside the question in dispute, so that even a valid demonstration fails to bear on the proposition it was meant to support.

title: Fallacy of Quoting
text: The fallacy of quoting, or appeal to the quote, treats a well-turned or memorable saying as though its rhetorical polish established its truth. Because a statement's eloquence, familiarity, or aphoristic form is unrelated to whether it is correct, citing a pithy quotation as if it settled a factual or moral question substitutes verbal appeal for genuine argument.

title: Style over Substance
text: The style over substance fallacy occurs when the manner in which a claim is presented, such as eloquence, confidence, or polish, is taken as evidence for its truth. Because the quality of delivery is independent of the quality of reasoning, a smoothly articulated argument is not thereby more likely to be correct, and judging content by presentation misplaces the relevant criterion.

title: Moralizing
text: Moralizing, as an argumentative flaw, substitutes expressions of moral disapproval or virtue for reasoned analysis of an issue, treating condemnation as though it settled a factual or practical question. By foregrounding ethical censure in place of evidence, it discourages examination of the actual claim and lets the appearance of righteousness stand in for justification.

title: Slothful Induction
text: Slothful induction is the fallacy of refusing to accept the conclusion that a body of strong inductive evidence clearly supports, attributing the pattern instead to coincidence or some other factor. The mirror image of hasty generalization, it errs by understating rather than overstating the force of the evidence, denying a well-supported conclusion against the weight of the data.

title: Base Details Distraction
text: The fallacy of misleading vividness overweights a dramatic, memorable anecdote against a much larger body of statistical evidence pointing the other way. Because a striking individual case is not representative and its emotional salience does not increase its evidential value, allowing one vivid instance to override aggregate data leads to distorted conclusions about likelihood.

title: Two Wrongs Make a Right
text: The two wrongs make a right fallacy attempts to justify a wrongful act by pointing to another wrongful act, as if a second offense could cancel or excuse the first. Because the existence of one wrong does not make another permissible, invoking someone else's misconduct as warrant for one's own supplies no valid justification and is closely allied to the tu quoque.

title: Fallacy of Anecdotal Evidence
text: The fallacy of anecdotal evidence relies on personal testimony or isolated examples to support a general claim, in preference to systematic data. Because individual stories are prone to bias, selective recall, and unrepresentativeness, and a few cases cannot reliably reveal a broad pattern, treating anecdotes as though they settled a general question overstates their evidential weight.

title: Circular Definition
text: A circular definition defines a term using the very term being defined, or by a chain of terms that ultimately refers back to it, so that no genuinely informative account is given. Because the definition presupposes an understanding of the word it purports to explain, it fails to convey meaning to anyone who does not already grasp it and cannot support a substantive argument.

title: Ad Hominem Circumstantial
text: The circumstantial ad hominem rejects a person's argument by alleging that their circumstances, such as their interests or affiliations, dispose them to hold that view. Even if a bias exists, it does not show the argument to be unsound; a claim must be judged on its own evidence, so pointing to the arguer's situation rather than their reasoning is a fallacy of relevance.

title: Faulty Comparison
text: The faulty comparison, or false equivalence, treats two things as though they were meaningfully equivalent when relevant differences make the equivalence unwarranted. By downplaying disparities in scale, kind, or context, an argument can suggest that because two cases share some feature they deserve the same evaluation, when the differences in fact defeat the intended inference.

title: Fallacy of Presumption
text: A fallacy of presumption is a broad category of informal fallacy in which an argument depends on an unjustified or hidden assumption smuggled into its premises. Because the questionable presupposition is taken for granted rather than argued for, the conclusion appears to follow only if the concealed assumption is granted; begging the question and complex question are notable examples.

title: Perfectionist Fallacy
text: The perfectionist fallacy, a form of the nirvana fallacy, rejects a proposal on the ground that it will not entirely eliminate a problem, as if only a complete solution were worth adopting. By demanding perfection as the condition of action, it dismisses partial but genuine improvements, treating the impossibility of a flawless remedy as a reason to reject any remedy.

title: Fallacy of the Beard
text: The fallacy of the beard, a version of the continuum fallacy, contends that because there is no single hair whose addition turns a clean-shaven face into a bearded one, no clear distinction between bearded and beardless can exist. It exploits the vagueness of a gradual boundary to deny a real difference between the extremes, a pattern the sorites paradox generalizes.

title: Argument to Moderation
text: The argument to moderation (argumentum ad temperantiam) holds that the correct position is necessarily the compromise between two extremes. Although moderation is often prudent, a claim is not made true merely by occupying a middle position; when one extreme is factually correct, treating the midpoint as automatically right yields an unjustified conclusion.

title: Regression Fallacy
text: The regression fallacy ascribes a causal explanation to a change that is in fact the result of regression toward the mean, the statistical tendency of extreme measurements to be followed by ones closer to the average. By crediting an intervention for an improvement that would have occurred anyway, it mistakes an artifact of natural variation for a genuine effect.

title: Fallacy of Equivocal Middle
text: In categorical syllogistic reasoning, using the middle term with two distinct senses produces an argument that only superficially connects its premises. This equivocation on the middle term is a species of the four terms fallacy, since the term that is supposed to link the premises effectively splits into two, leaving the major and minor terms unconnected and the inference invalid.

title: Fallacy of Converse Accident
text: The fallacy of converse accident, another name for hasty generalization, forms a general rule from cases that are exceptional or atypical. By generalizing from special instances that should not set the standard, it produces a rule that misdescribes the ordinary case; it stands as the mirror image of the fallacy of accident, which misapplies a general rule to an exception.

title: Onus Probandi
text: The fallacy of shifting the burden of proof (onus probandi) occurs when someone who advances a positive claim demands that others disprove it rather than supplying evidence themselves. Since the obligation to justify a claim rests with the party asserting it, requiring opponents to refute an unsupported assertion improperly reverses the burden and is a fallacy of relevance.

title: Argument from Authority of Many
text: The appeal to the authority of numbers combines features of the appeal to popularity and the appeal to authority, treating the sheer number of people who accept a claim as though that constituted expert endorsement. Because a multitude of non-experts is no more reliable on a specialized question than a few, the aggregation of lay opinion does not establish the claim's truth.

title: Fallacy of Misplaced Concreteness
text: The fallacy of misplaced concreteness, a term from Alfred North Whitehead, is the error of treating an abstract concept or model as if it were a concrete reality. Closely related to reification, it mistakes an analytical abstraction for the full, concrete thing it represents, so that the simplifications built into the abstraction are wrongly taken as features of the world itself.

title: Argument by Repetition
text: Argument by repetition, also known as ad nauseam, advances a position by asserting it over and over until listeners cease to challenge it. Because restating a claim provides no additional support, the impression of validity it creates rests on familiarity rather than evidence; the number of times an assertion is made is wholly unrelated to whether it is true.

title: Fallacy of Composition of Motives
text: The pathetic fallacy, in its logical rather than poetic sense, ascribes human feelings, intentions, or agency to inanimate objects or natural forces and then reasons as though those attributions were literally true. By projecting mental states onto things incapable of them, an argument can reach conclusions that depend on a metaphor being mistaken for fact.

title: Furtive Fallacy
text: The furtive fallacy, identified by David Hackett Fischer, is the assumption that significant historical outcomes must have been caused by hidden, sinister motives or deliberate concealment. By presuming that important events are the product of concealed malevolence rather than ordinary or accidental causes, it distorts explanation toward conspiracy without warrant from the evidence.

title: Appeal to Accomplishment
text: The appeal to accomplishment asserts that a claim should be accepted or rejected on the basis of the arguer's achievements or lack thereof, as if success in one domain guaranteed correctness in the matter at hand. Because accomplishment in an unrelated field does not confer authority on the specific question, using it to validate or dismiss an argument is a fallacy of relevance.

title: Argument from Repugnance
text: The argument from repugnance, or the wisdom of repugnance, treats a strong feeling of disgust toward something as sufficient reason to conclude that it is morally wrong. Because an emotional aversion is not itself a justification and disgust has historically attached to practices later judged harmless, relying on repugnance in place of ethical argument is fallacious reasoning.

title: Anchoring and Adjustment
text: Anchoring is the tendency for an initial reference value, even an arbitrary or irrelevant one, to unduly influence subsequent numerical estimates. People adjust away from the anchor but typically insufficiently, so final judgements remain biased toward the starting point. Demonstrated by Tversky and Kahneman, the effect appears in pricing, negotiation, and probability estimation.

title: Affect Heuristic
text: The affect heuristic is the tendency to rely on immediate emotional responses when making judgements and decisions. When a good or bad feeling toward something is strong, people judge its risks as low and benefits as high, or vice versa, letting affect stand in for more effortful analysis of costs and probabilities.

title: Decoy Effect
text: The decoy effect, or asymmetric dominance effect, occurs when adding a third inferior option changes preferences between two original options. The decoy is dominated by one target but not the other, making the target appear more attractive by comparison. It is exploited in pricing and menu design to steer choices toward higher-margin items.

title: Contrast Effect
text: The contrast effect is the enhancement or diminishment of a perception, judgement, or performance when compared with a recently encountered contrasting object. A moderately heavy object feels lighter after lifting a very heavy one, and an average candidate seems stronger after a weak one, because judgement is relative to salient references.

title: Priming
text: Priming is the phenomenon whereby exposure to one stimulus influences the response to a later stimulus without conscious guidance. Encountering a word, image, or concept activates related mental associations, making them more accessible and speeding recognition or shaping subsequent behaviour and judgement, often outside of awareness.

title: Mere Exposure Effect
text: The mere exposure effect is the tendency for people to develop a preference for things merely because they are familiar with them. Repeated exposure to a stimulus, such as a face, melody, or symbol, increases liking even without conscious recognition, up to a point of satiation. It was documented extensively by Robert Zajonc.

title: Serial Position Effect
text: The serial position effect is the tendency to recall the first and last items in a list better than those in the middle. It combines a primacy advantage, attributed to greater rehearsal into long-term memory, and a recency advantage, attributed to items still held in short-term memory. It was described by Hermann Ebbinghaus.

title: Primacy Effect
text: The primacy effect is the superior recall of items presented early in a sequence relative to those in the middle. It is generally attributed to earlier items receiving more rehearsal and better transfer into long-term memory. In impression formation, early information also carries disproportionate weight in shaping overall judgements.

title: Recency Effect
text: The recency effect is the superior recall of the most recently presented items in a sequence. It is attributed to those items still residing in short-term or working memory at the time of retrieval, and it is typically reduced or eliminated by a delay or distractor task between presentation and recall.

title: Peak-End Rule
text: The peak-end rule is a heuristic by which people judge an experience largely by how it felt at its most intense moment and at its end, rather than by the sum or average of every moment. Documented by Kahneman and colleagues, it means duration is often neglected and a painful episode ending mildly can be remembered more favourably.

title: Zero-Risk Bias
text: Zero-risk bias is the preference for completely eliminating one small risk over achieving a larger overall reduction across multiple risks. People place special value on reducing a hazard to zero, even when reallocating the same effort would prevent more harm in total, because certainty of elimination is disproportionately reassuring.

title: Ambiguity Aversion
text: Ambiguity aversion is the tendency to prefer options with known probabilities over options with unknown or vague probabilities, even when expected values are comparable. People dislike not knowing the odds and treat missing information as a threat, distinguishing ambiguity aversion from ordinary risk aversion over known gambles.

title: Allais Paradox
text: The Allais paradox is a choice pattern, described by Maurice Allais, that violates the independence axiom of expected utility theory. When a common outcome is added to two gambles, people often reverse their preferences, revealing that certainty and the framing of probabilities affect choices in ways standard utility theory cannot accommodate.

title: Ellsberg Paradox
text: The Ellsberg paradox demonstrates ambiguity aversion through choices over urns containing balls in known versus unknown proportions. People systematically prefer betting on known probabilities, and their choices cannot be reconciled with any single consistent set of subjective probabilities, challenging the assumptions of subjective expected utility.

title: Certainty Effect
text: The certainty effect is the tendency to overweight outcomes that are certain relative to outcomes that are merely probable. People value the reduction of probability from certainty to near-certainty far more than an equivalent reduction between two uncertain probabilities, a central feature of prospect theory's probability weighting.

title: Pseudocertainty Effect
text: The pseudocertainty effect is the tendency to perceive an outcome as certain when it is actually contingent on an earlier uncertain stage. In multi-stage decisions, framing later choices as if the earlier uncertainty were resolved makes a conditionally sure outcome feel guaranteed, altering risk preferences relative to an equivalent single-stage gamble.

title: Hot-Hand Fallacy
text: The hot-hand fallacy is the belief that a person who has experienced success in a random or largely chance-based sequence has a greater probability of continued success. Observers infer streaks of skill or momentum from runs that are statistically consistent with independent trials, though the effect's status in some sports remains debated.

title: Base-Rate Neglect
text: Base-rate neglect is the tendency to ignore or underweight general prevalence information in favour of specific, individuating evidence when estimating probabilities. When judging whether a description fits a category, people focus on how representative it seems and disregard how common the category is, producing systematic errors in Bayesian reasoning.

title: Conservatism Bias
text: Conservatism bias in belief revision is the tendency to update beliefs insufficiently when presented with new evidence, clinging too closely to prior estimates. Unlike base-rate neglect, it involves underweighting the diagnostic value of new data, so posterior probabilities are revised in the correct direction but by too small an amount.

title: Congruence Bias
text: Congruence bias is the tendency to test hypotheses exclusively through direct testing of the favoured hypothesis, rather than by also testing alternative hypotheses. By examining only whether predicted outcomes occur, reasoners neglect tests that could distinguish their hypothesis from rivals, leaving competing explanations unexamined.

title: Choice-Supportive Bias
text: Choice-supportive bias is the tendency to retrospectively ascribe positive attributes to an option one has chosen and negative attributes to rejected options. After a decision, memory is reconstructed to favour the selected alternative, inflating its remembered merits and thereby reducing dissonance and justifying the choice already made.

title: IKEA Effect
text: The IKEA effect is the tendency for people to place a disproportionately high value on products they partially created or assembled themselves. Labour invested in constructing an object increases attachment and perceived worth, so self-made items are valued more highly than identical items made by others, regardless of the quality of the result.

title: Unit Bias
text: Unit bias is the tendency to regard a single presented unit of an item, such as one serving or one portion, as the appropriate amount to consume, regardless of its actual size. Because the unit is treated as a natural quantity, larger standard portions lead to greater consumption, contributing to overeating when portion sizes increase.

title: Denomination Effect
text: The denomination effect is the tendency to be less likely to spend money represented by a large single denomination than an equivalent sum in smaller units. A large bill feels more like a whole to be preserved, so people spend more readily from many small notes and coins than from a single note of the same total value.

title: Money Illusion
text: Money illusion is the tendency to think about money in nominal rather than real terms, neglecting the effect of inflation on purchasing power. People perceive a nominal wage increase as a gain even when prices rise faster, and react differently to nominally versus really equivalent changes, because face values dominate their judgements.

title: Hyperbolic Discounting
text: Hyperbolic discounting is the tendency to discount the value of future rewards by an amount that decreases sharply for near delays and more gently for distant ones. This produces preference reversals: a person may prefer a larger later reward when both are far off, yet flip to a smaller sooner reward as the earlier one becomes imminent.

title: Present Bias
text: Present bias is the tendency to give stronger weight to immediate payoffs relative to future ones, overvaluing the present moment when trading off costs and benefits over time. It leads to procrastination, undersaving, and impulsive consumption, and it is closely associated with the steep near-term discounting seen in hyperbolic models.

title: Projection Bias
text: Projection bias is the tendency to overestimate how much one's future preferences, tastes, or states will resemble one's current ones. People project present hunger, mood, or values onto their future selves, leading to choices, such as grocery shopping while hungry, that poorly serve their preferences when the future arrives.

title: Empathy Gap
text: The empathy gap is the difficulty of accurately predicting or understanding behaviour and preferences across differing emotional or physiological states. In a cool, calm state people underestimate the influence of hot states such as hunger, anger, or arousal, and vice versa, leading to systematic errors in forecasting their own and others' actions.

title: Restraint Bias
text: Restraint bias is the tendency to overestimate one's capacity to control impulsive behaviour. People who feel confident in their self-control expose themselves to greater temptation, believing they can resist, which paradoxically increases the likelihood of succumbing to impulses such as cravings, distractions, or addictive urges.

title: Impact Bias
text: The impact bias is the tendency to overestimate the intensity and duration of one's future emotional reactions to events. People predict that positive outcomes will make them happier for longer and that negative outcomes will be more devastating than they actually prove, partly because they neglect their own capacity to adapt and rationalise.

title: Focusing Illusion
text: The focusing illusion is the tendency to place too much weight on one salient factor when predicting the effect of a change on overall well-being. By concentrating on a single vivid attribute, such as climate or income, people overestimate its importance to happiness and neglect the many other aspects of life that remain unchanged.

title: Telescoping Effect
text: The telescoping effect is a distortion in the remembered timing of past events. Backward telescoping places recent events further in the past than they occurred, while forward telescoping perceives distant events as more recent. This misdating affects survey responses and autobiographical memory, especially for the timing of notable episodes.

title: Rosy Retrospection
text: Rosy retrospection is the tendency to remember past events as more positive than they were actually experienced at the time. Negative details fade and pleasant impressions are emphasised, so trips, relationships, and earlier eras are recalled through a favourable filter that can inflate nostalgia and idealise the past.

title: Declinism
text: Declinism is the tendency to view the past favourably and the future negatively, believing that a society, institution, or the world in general is in decline. It draws on nostalgic memory and pessimistic forecasting, so recent conditions are judged worse than earlier ones despite objective evidence that may indicate improvement.

title: Normalcy Bias
text: Normalcy bias is the tendency to underestimate the likelihood of a disaster and its potential effects, assuming that because something has not happened before it will not happen now. This can cause people to disregard warnings and fail to prepare or evacuate, treating an emerging threat as within the range of ordinary experience.

title: Ostrich Effect
text: The ostrich effect is the tendency to avoid exposure to information that is expected to be unpleasant or anxiety-provoking. Named for the myth of burying one's head in the sand, it describes behaviours such as declining to check a falling investment portfolio, so as to avoid confronting bad news even when awareness would aid decisions.

title: Moral Luck
text: Moral luck refers to the tendency to assign moral judgement to an agent based on outcomes that were partly beyond their control. Two people who act identically may be blamed differently if chance produces harm in one case and not the other, revealing that consequences influence moral evaluation despite equivalent intentions and conduct.

title: Just-World Hypothesis
text: The just-world hypothesis is the tendency to believe that the world is fundamentally fair, so that people generally get what they deserve and deserve what they get. This belief can lead observers to derogate or blame victims of misfortune, inferring that sufferers must somehow have merited their fate in order to preserve a sense of order.

title: Defensive Attribution
text: Defensive attribution is the tendency to assign blame for an accident in a way that protects the observer from feeling vulnerable. As the severity of an outcome or the observer's similarity to the victim increases, attributions shift to reduce personal threat, either blaming the victim more or excusing them, depending on identification.

title: Group Attribution Error
text: The group attribution error is the tendency to assume that the characteristics or attitudes of an individual group member reflect the group as a whole, or that a group's decisions mirror the preferences of each member. It conflates individual and collective properties, ignoring internal diversity and the effects of group decision procedures.

title: Ultimate Attribution Error
text: The ultimate attribution error is the tendency to attribute negative behaviour by outgroup members to their disposition and positive behaviour to situational factors, while doing the reverse for the ingroup. It extends the fundamental attribution error to intergroup perception, reinforcing prejudice by explaining away disconfirming conduct.

title: Outgroup Homogeneity Bias
text: Outgroup homogeneity bias is the tendency to perceive members of an outgroup as more similar to one another than members of one's own ingroup. People see their own group as rich in individual variation while regarding others as interchangeable, which supports stereotyping and coarse generalisations about groups to which one does not belong.

title: Cross-Race Effect
text: The cross-race effect is the tendency to recognise and distinguish faces of one's own racial or ethnic group more accurately than faces of other groups. Attributed to greater perceptual experience and differential encoding of own-group faces, it has significant implications for the reliability of eyewitness identification across racial lines.

title: Cheerleader Effect
text: The cheerleader effect is the tendency for individuals to appear more attractive when seen in a group than when seen alone. The visual system averages the faces in a group, and averaged faces tend to look more appealing, so a person's features are perceived more favourably in the context of surrounding faces.

title: Attractiveness Halo
text: The physical attractiveness stereotype is the tendency to assume that physically attractive people also possess other desirable traits such as intelligence, kindness, and competence. Often summarised as what is beautiful is good, it is a specific instance of the halo effect and influences hiring, judicial, and social evaluations.

title: Authority Bias
text: Authority bias is the tendency to attribute greater accuracy and to be more influenced by the opinion of a perceived authority figure, independent of the content of the message. Deference to titles, uniforms, and credentials can lead people to comply with or accept claims they would otherwise scrutinise, as illustrated in obedience research.

title: Social Desirability Bias
text: Social desirability bias is the tendency to answer questions in a manner that will be viewed favourably by others, over-reporting approved behaviours and under-reporting disapproved ones. It distorts self-report data on sensitive topics such as voting, income, health habits, and prejudice, complicating survey and interview research.

title: False Consensus Effect
text: The false consensus effect is the tendency to overestimate the extent to which other people share one's own beliefs, values, and behaviours. People assume their choices are more common and appropriate than they are, projecting their own perspective onto the population and misjudging how typical their attitudes really are.

title: False Uniqueness Effect
text: The false uniqueness effect is the tendency to underestimate the extent to which others share one's desirable traits and abilities. People regard their positive qualities and successes as rarer than they are, which supports a sense of distinctiveness and self-esteem, complementing the false consensus effect for negative or common attributes.

title: Pluralistic Ignorance
text: Pluralistic ignorance is a situation in which most members of a group privately reject a norm but incorrectly assume that most others accept it, and therefore go along with it. Because each person misreads others' outward conformity as genuine belief, a norm that few actually endorse is sustained through mutual misperception.

title: Spotlight Effect
text: The spotlight effect is the tendency to overestimate how much others notice and attend to one's appearance, mistakes, and behaviour. Because people are the centre of their own experience, they assume they are more conspicuous than they are, exaggerating the degree to which a blemish, gaffe, or outfit registers with observers.

title: Illusion of Transparency
text: The illusion of transparency is the tendency to overestimate the degree to which one's internal mental states are apparent to others. Speakers believe their nervousness is obvious and liars think their deceit shows, because privileged access to their own feelings makes those states seem more visible externally than they actually are.

title: Naive Realism
text: Naive realism is the conviction that one perceives the world objectively and that others who disagree must be uninformed, irrational, or biased. It assumes one's own view is the direct, unfiltered truth, leading people to underappreciate how construal shapes perception and to misattribute disagreement to others' failings.

title: Naive Cynicism
text: Naive cynicism is the tendency to expect that others are more self-interested and egocentrically biased than they actually are. In contrast to viewing oneself as objective, people assume others' judgements are motivated by self-serving distortion, which can breed distrust and overcorrection in interpreting others' behaviour.

title: Reactive Devaluation
text: Reactive devaluation is the tendency to devalue a proposal or concession simply because it originated from an adversary or disliked source. The same offer is rated less favourably when attributed to an opponent than to a neutral or allied party, which obstructs negotiation and conflict resolution independent of the offer's actual merits.

title: Reactance
text: Reactance is the motivational reaction to offers, rules, or persuasion that threaten or eliminate perceived behavioural freedoms. When people feel their autonomy is constrained, they experience an urge to reassert it, often by doing the opposite of what is urged or by valuing the forbidden option more highly.

title: Escalation of Commitment
text: Escalation of commitment is the tendency to increase investment in a failing course of action to justify prior decisions, rather than cutting losses. Prior expenditure of money, effort, or reputation pressures the decision maker to persist, so resources continue to flow into ventures whose prospects no longer warrant them.

title: Pro-Innovation Bias
text: Pro-innovation bias is the tendency of an innovation's proponents to hold excessive optimism about its usefulness and adoptability, while overlooking its limitations and the barriers to widespread use. Advocates assume the innovation should be diffused to all and adopted rapidly, discounting legitimate reasons for rejection or adaptation.

title: Semmelweis Reflex
text: The Semmelweis reflex is the tendency to reject new evidence or knowledge because it contradicts established norms, beliefs, or practices. Named after Ignaz Semmelweis, whose findings on handwashing were dismissed by his contemporaries, it describes reflexive resistance to information that challenges accepted paradigms.

title: Myside Bias
text: Myside bias is the tendency to generate, evaluate, and test evidence in a manner biased toward one's own prior opinions and attitudes. Closely related to confirmation bias, it specifically concerns reasoning about propositions on which one already holds a position, producing one-sided argument generation and asymmetric standards of proof.

title: Motivated Reasoning
text: Motivated reasoning is the tendency for goals, preferences, and emotions to shape the processing of information, so that people arrive at conclusions they are motivated to reach. Desired conclusions are held to weaker evidential standards than undesired ones, and evidence is selectively scrutinised, recalled, and weighted to favour the preferred outcome.

title: Disconfirmation Bias
text: Disconfirmation bias is the tendency to apply more critical scrutiny to evidence that contradicts one's beliefs than to evidence that supports them. Congenial information is accepted readily while uncongenial information is subjected to rigorous counterargument, so the same data can strengthen opposing positions on each side of a debate.

title: Backfire Effect
text: The backfire effect is a proposed phenomenon in which corrections to a mistaken belief cause people to hold that belief even more strongly. Once influential in accounts of misinformation, its generality is now debated, as many studies find that corrections usually reduce false beliefs and that robust backfire is relatively rare.

title: Continued Influence Effect
text: The continued influence effect is the tendency for misinformation to keep affecting reasoning and memory even after it has been clearly and credibly retracted. People continue to rely on the discredited information when drawing inferences, particularly when no alternative explanation is provided to fill the gap left by the correction.

title: Illusory Truth Effect
text: The illusory truth effect is the tendency to rate statements as more true simply because they have been encountered before. Repetition increases processing fluency, which is misread as a signal of accuracy, so repeated claims, including false ones, come to feel more believable regardless of their actual veracity.

title: Source Amnesia
text: Source amnesia is the inability to remember where, when, or how previously learned information was acquired while retaining the factual content. Because the memory of the source is lost, people may accept a claim as true without recalling that it came from an unreliable origin, contributing to the persistence of misinformation.

title: Cryptomnesia
text: Cryptomnesia is a memory error in which a forgotten memory returns without being recognised as a memory, so it is experienced as an original idea. It can lead to inadvertent plagiarism, where a person genuinely believes they have created something new that was in fact previously encountered and then forgotten as an external source.

title: Misinformation Effect
text: The misinformation effect is the tendency for memory of an event to be altered by misleading information encountered afterward. Post-event suggestions, leading questions, or exposure to inaccurate accounts can be incorporated into recollection, degrading the accuracy of eyewitness memory, as shown in the work of Elizabeth Loftus.

title: Zeigarnik Effect
text: The Zeigarnik effect is the tendency to remember interrupted or incomplete tasks better than completed ones. Named after Bluma Zeigarnik, it suggests that an unfinished task maintains a state of tension or heightened accessibility in memory, which is released once the task is completed, reducing its subsequent recall.

title: Generation Effect
text: The generation effect is the finding that information is better remembered when it is actively generated by the learner than when it is simply read or received. Producing an answer, word, or solution oneself engages deeper processing and creates more retrieval cues than passively encountering the same material.

title: Picture Superiority Effect
text: The picture superiority effect is the tendency for images to be remembered more readily than words. Pictures are thought to be encoded both visually and verbally, giving them a dual route to later retrieval, so concepts presented as pictures are recognised and recalled better than the same concepts presented only as text.

title: Von Restorff Effect
text: The von Restorff effect, or isolation effect, is the tendency for an item that stands out from its surroundings to be remembered better than more homogeneous items. A distinctive entry in a list, differing in colour, size, or category, captures attention and is preferentially encoded, boosting its recall relative to neighbouring items.

title: Levels of Processing
text: The levels-of-processing framework holds that memory retention depends on the depth at which information is processed rather than on rehearsal time alone. Semantic, meaning-based encoding produces more durable memories than shallow processing of surface features such as appearance or sound, as proposed by Craik and Lockhart.

title: Gain-Loss Framing
text: Gain-loss framing is a specific framing manipulation in which the same outcome is described either as a gain or as an equivalent loss. Because losses loom larger than gains, people tend to be risk-averse when options are framed as gains and risk-seeking when the same options are framed as losses, altering their choices.

title: Mental Accounting
text: Mental accounting is the tendency to treat money differently depending on subjective categories such as its source, intended use, or the account it is assigned to. Because funds are not treated as fungible, people may simultaneously save at low interest and borrow at high interest, or spend windfalls more freely than earned income.

title: Prospect Theory
text: Prospect theory is a descriptive account of decision under risk developed by Kahneman and Tversky. It holds that people evaluate outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point, that losses loom larger than equivalent gains, that sensitivity to changes diminishes with magnitude, and that probabilities are weighted nonlinearly.

title: Diminishing Sensitivity
text: Diminishing sensitivity is the principle that the subjective impact of a change decreases as one moves further from the reference point. The difference between gaining ten and twenty feels larger than the difference between gaining one hundred ten and one hundred twenty, producing the concave value function for gains and convex for losses.

title: Reference Dependence
text: Reference dependence is the principle that people evaluate outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point rather than in terms of absolute final states. The chosen reference, often the status quo or an expectation, determines whether the same objective outcome is coded as a satisfying gain or a disappointing loss.

title: Probability Weighting
text: Probability weighting is the tendency, formalised in prospect theory, to transform stated probabilities into decision weights nonlinearly. Small probabilities are typically overweighted while moderate and large probabilities are underweighted, which helps explain the simultaneous appeal of lotteries and insurance.

title: Overestimation Bias
text: Overestimation is a subtype of overconfidence in which people believe their actual performance, ability, or level of control is higher than it truly is. It concerns the absolute assessment of one's own attributes, distinct from comparisons with others, and it tends to be larger for difficult tasks.

title: Overplacement Bias
text: Overplacement is a subtype of overconfidence in which people rate themselves as better than others to an unjustified degree. Reflected in the better-than-average effect, most individuals place themselves above the median on desirable traits, which is statistically impossible for the whole population.

title: Overprecision Bias
text: Overprecision is a subtype of overconfidence in which people are excessively certain that their beliefs are correct. It is measured by confidence intervals that are too narrow to contain the true value at the stated rate, so ninety-percent intervals capture the correct answer far less than ninety percent of the time.

title: Hard-Easy Effect
text: The hard-easy effect is the tendency to be overconfident on difficult tasks and underconfident on easy tasks. As questions become harder, people fail to lower their confidence enough, producing overconfidence, whereas on very easy items they may express less certainty than their high accuracy warrants.

title: Barnum Effect
text: The Barnum or Forer effect is the tendency for individuals to accept vague, general personality descriptions as uniquely applicable to themselves. Statements crafted to fit almost anyone are rated as highly accurate personal insights, which underlies the perceived validity of astrology, cold reading, and generic personality tests.

title: Subjective Validation
text: Subjective validation is the tendency to perceive a statement or piece of information as accurate because it holds personal meaning or significance for the individual. A claim is judged true if it resonates with one's beliefs or expectations, which reinforces the Barnum effect and the acceptance of pseudoscientific readings.

title: Apophenia
text: Apophenia is the tendency to perceive meaningful connections or patterns among unrelated or random things. It encompasses seeing structure where none exists, from imagined correlations to conspiratorial links, and reflects the mind's disposition to impose coherence and meaning on ambiguous or noisy information.

title: Pareidolia
text: Pareidolia is the tendency to perceive a specific, often meaningful image, typically a face, in ambiguous or random visual stimuli. Seeing a face in a cloud, a rock formation, or an electrical outlet is a common example, arising from the brain's strong specialisation for detecting faces and familiar forms.

title: Insensitivity to Sample Size
text: Insensitivity to sample size is the tendency to neglect the effect of sample size when judging the probability of obtaining a given result. People expect small samples to resemble the population as closely as large ones, ignoring that extreme outcomes are far more likely in small samples than in large ones.

title: Misconceptions of Chance
text: Misconceptions of chance describe the expectation that a sequence of random events will locally represent the essential characteristics of the process that generated it. People expect short random sequences to appear irregular and balanced, so they judge a run that looks orderly as unlikely, even when all sequences are equally probable.

title: Regression Neglect
text: Regression neglect is the failure to anticipate regression toward the mean, the tendency for extreme measurements to be followed by more average ones. Ignoring this statistical inevitability, people invent causal explanations for the return toward average, such as crediting punishment or blaming praise for subsequent performance changes.

title: Illusion of Validity
text: The illusion of validity is the tendency to be overconfident in the accuracy of one's judgements, especially when available information is coherent or fits a consistent pattern. Consistency among inputs boosts subjective confidence even when the inputs have little predictive power, so plausibility is mistaken for accuracy.

title: Dread Risk Perception
text: Dread risk perception is the tendency to fear rare, catastrophic, uncontrollable, or dreaded hazards more than common, familiar risks that cause far more total harm. Psychometric research shows that perceived risk is driven by qualities such as dread and unfamiliarity rather than by statistical fatality rates alone.

title: Availability Cascade
text: An availability cascade is a self-reinforcing process in which a belief gains increasing plausibility through its rising repetition in public discourse. As a claim is repeated, it becomes more available in memory and more socially acceptable, prompting further repetition, which can amplify collective concern beyond what evidence supports.

title: Information Cascade
text: An information cascade occurs when individuals, observing the actions of those before them, follow suit and disregard their own private information. Because each person rationally infers that predecessors possessed good reasons, a sequence of imitative choices can propagate even if it is based on scant or mistaken initial signals.

title: Herd Behaviour
text: Herd behaviour is the tendency for individuals to align their actions and beliefs with those of a larger group, often without independent evaluation. It arises from social proof, informational influence, and the safety of conformity, and it can drive phenomena such as speculative bubbles, panics, and fads.

title: Groupthink
text: Groupthink is a mode of group decision making in which the desire for harmony and conformity leads to irrational or dysfunctional outcomes. Members suppress dissent, self-censor doubts, and cultivate an illusion of unanimity and invulnerability, so alternatives are inadequately examined, as analysed by Irving Janis.

title: Group Polarization
text: Group polarization is the tendency for group discussion to strengthen the average pre-existing inclination of its members, producing a more extreme collective position. After deliberating, groups often adopt riskier or more cautious stances than individuals held beforehand, driven by persuasive arguments and social comparison.

title: Shared Information Bias
text: Shared information bias is the tendency for groups to spend more discussion time on information that all members already possess and less on information held by only some members. Because commonly known facts are raised and validated more often, unique knowledge is underused, degrading the quality of collective decisions.

title: Default Effect
text: The default effect is the tendency for people to accept a pre-selected option rather than actively changing it. Because switching requires effort and defaults are read as recommendations, chosen or automatic settings strongly influence outcomes in areas such as retirement enrolment and organ donation registration.

title: Omission Bias
text: Omission bias is the tendency to judge harmful actions as worse than equally harmful inactions. People prefer to cause harm through omission rather than commission and blame acts more than failures to act, even when the consequences are identical, which shapes attitudes toward risks such as vaccination and intervention.

title: Action Bias
text: Action bias is the tendency to favour taking action over inaction, even when doing nothing would be at least as beneficial. In situations of uncertainty or pressure, people feel compelled to be seen to act, so decisions to intervene are made where waiting would serve equally well, as observed among goalkeepers facing penalty kicks.

title: Actor-Observer Bias
text: The actor-observer bias is the tendency to attribute one's own behaviour to situational causes while attributing others' behaviour to dispositional causes. Because actors focus on the situation they face and observers focus on the actor, the same conduct is explained differently depending on whose behaviour is being judged.

title: Horn Effect
text: The horn effect is the negative counterpart of the halo effect, in which one unfavourable trait leads to an overall negative evaluation. A single disliked characteristic colours perception of a person's unrelated qualities, so an individual judged poorly on one dimension is presumed deficient on others as well.

title: Bandwagon Effect
text: The bandwagon effect is the tendency to adopt beliefs or behaviours because many others have already done so. As a position gains adherents, its perceived correctness and social acceptability grow, prompting further adoption, which can inflate trends, opinions, and voting intentions independent of underlying merit.

title: Bizarreness Effect
text: The bizarreness effect is the tendency for bizarre or unusual material to be remembered better than common material. Odd images and improbable sentences attract attention and are distinctively encoded, giving them a recall advantage over ordinary content, particularly when mixed together in the same list.

title: Anchoring in Negotiation
text: In negotiation, the first offer often functions as an anchor that shapes the final agreement. Because subsequent counteroffers adjust insufficiently from the opening figure, the party who states an ambitious first number tends to pull the settlement toward it, making initial demands an influential strategic lever.

title: Fluency Effect
text: The processing fluency effect is the tendency to judge information that is easy to process as more true, likeable, or valuable. Ease of perception or comprehension, arising from clarity, familiarity, or repetition, is misattributed to properties of the stimulus itself, influencing judgements of truth, risk, and preference.

title: Recognition Heuristic
text: The recognition heuristic is a decision rule by which, when comparing two objects on some criterion, the one that is recognised is judged to have the higher value. It can yield accurate inferences when recognition correlates with the criterion, allowing decisions based on partial ignorance to outperform more informed strategies.

title: Less-Is-More Effect
text: The less-is-more effect is the counterintuitive finding that having less information can sometimes yield more accurate inferences. When recognition is diagnostic, a person who recognises only some objects may outperform one who recognises them all, because partial ignorance enables the recognition heuristic to discriminate.

title: Framing by Attribute
text: Attribute framing is a form of framing in which a single characteristic of an object is described in either positive or negative terms. Meat labelled seventy-five percent lean is rated more favourably than the same meat labelled twenty-five percent fat, showing that the valence of a descriptor shapes evaluation of the identical item.

title: Goal Framing
text: Goal framing is a form of framing that emphasises either the benefits of performing a behaviour or the costs of not performing it. Because losses tend to be more persuasive than gains, messages stressing what will be lost by inaction are often more influential than equivalent messages stressing what will be gained by action.

title: Sample Space
text: In probability theory, the sample space is the set of all possible distinct outcomes of a random experiment, conventionally denoted by the symbol omega or S. Each individual outcome is an element of this set, and every event is a subset of the sample space. The sample space may be finite, countably infinite, or uncountable depending on the experiment considered.

title: Event
text: An event is any subset of the sample space, that is, a collection of one or more outcomes to which a probability can be assigned. An elementary event contains exactly one outcome, while the entire sample space is the certain event and the empty set is the impossible event. Events can be combined using set operations such as union, intersection, and complement.

title: Kolmogorov Axioms
text: The Kolmogorov axioms are three conditions that define a probability measure P on a sample space. First, non-negativity: P(A) is greater than or equal to zero for every event A. Second, normalization: the probability of the whole sample space equals one. Third, countable additivity: for mutually exclusive events, the probability of their union equals the sum of their probabilities.

title: Probability of Certain Event
text: The probability of the certain event, which is the entire sample space, equals exactly one under the Kolmogorov normalization axiom. This reflects that some outcome in the sample space must occur whenever the experiment is performed. A probability of one indicates certainty in the mathematical model, though it does not always mean physical impossibility of the alternative in infinite spaces.

title: Probability of Impossible Event
text: The probability of the impossible event, represented by the empty set, equals zero because it contains no outcomes of the sample space. This follows from the axioms since the empty set is disjoint from itself and additivity forces its measure to be zero. In continuous spaces a probability of zero does not necessarily imply the event is logically impossible.

title: Complement Rule
text: The complement rule states that for any event A, the probability that A does not occur equals one minus the probability that A occurs: P(not A) = 1 - P(A). This follows because an event and its complement are mutually exclusive and their union is the entire sample space, whose total probability is one. It is often easier to compute a complement than the event directly.

title: Mutually Exclusive Events
text: Two events are mutually exclusive, or disjoint, when they cannot both occur in the same trial, meaning their intersection is empty. For such events the probability of their union equals the sum of their individual probabilities, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Mutual exclusivity concerns whether events can co-occur and is distinct from statistical independence.

title: Independence Versus Exclusivity
text: Mutual exclusivity and independence are different concepts often confused. Mutually exclusive events have empty intersection, so they never co-occur, and knowing one occurred makes the other impossible. Independent events can co-occur, and one occurring gives no information about the other. Two events with nonzero probability cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent simultaneously.

title: Addition Rule Disjoint
text: The addition rule for mutually exclusive events states that the probability that either of two disjoint events occurs equals the sum of their separate probabilities: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). This is a direct consequence of the countable additivity axiom applied to two disjoint sets, and it generalizes to any finite collection of pairwise disjoint events.

title: General Addition Rule
text: The general addition rule computes the probability of a union of two events that may overlap: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). The subtraction corrects for the intersection, which would otherwise be counted twice. When the events are mutually exclusive the intersection term is zero and this reduces to the simple addition rule.

title: General Multiplication Rule
text: The general multiplication rule expresses the joint probability of two events as P(A and B) = P(A given B) times P(B), or equivalently P(B given A) times P(A). It follows directly from the definition of conditional probability and holds without assuming independence. This rule is fundamental for chaining probabilities in sequential experiments and building probability trees.

title: Joint Probability
text: A joint probability is the probability that two or more events occur together, written P(A and B) for two events. It corresponds to the probability of the intersection of the events within the sample space. For independent events the joint probability factorizes into the product of marginals, while in general it is obtained from the multiplication rule using a conditional probability.

title: Marginal Probability
text: A marginal probability is the probability of a single event without reference to any other, obtained by summing or integrating a joint distribution over all values of the other variables. For example, the marginal probability of A equals the sum over all B of P(A and B). It is called marginal because such totals were historically written in the margins of a joint probability table.

title: Marginal Conditional Joint
text: In a multivariable setting these three quantities are distinct: the joint probability P(A and B) is the chance both occur, the marginal probability P(A) is the chance of one ignoring the other, and the conditional probability P(A given B) is the chance of one within the subset where the other holds. They are related by P(A and B) = P(A given B) times P(B).

title: Law of Total Probability
text: The law of total probability states that if events B1 through Bn form a partition of the sample space, each with positive probability, then for any event A the probability P(A) equals the sum over i of P(A given Bi) times P(Bi). It decomposes an event's probability across mutually exclusive and exhaustive cases, providing the denominator used in Bayes' theorem.

title: Partition Sums to One
text: If a collection of events forms a partition of the sample space, meaning they are pairwise mutually exclusive and their union is the whole space, then their probabilities sum to exactly one. This is a consequence of the additivity and normalization axioms and underlies the law of total probability and the normalization step in Bayesian updating.

title: Prior Probability
text: In Bayesian reasoning the prior probability is the probability assigned to a hypothesis before observing new evidence, denoted P(H). It encodes existing knowledge, base rates, or subjective belief about the hypothesis. The prior is combined with the likelihood of the observed evidence to produce the posterior probability through Bayes' theorem.

title: Likelihood Term
text: In Bayes' theorem the likelihood is P(E given H), the probability of observing the evidence assuming the hypothesis is true. It measures how well the hypothesis predicts the data.
