Considered as a function of the hypothesis for fixed evidence, the likelihood is generally not itself a probability distribution over hypotheses and need not sum to one across them.

title: Evidence Marginal
text: In Bayes' theorem the evidence, also called the marginal likelihood or normalizing constant, is P(E), the total probability of observing the evidence across all hypotheses. It is computed by the law of total probability as the sum of P(E given Hi) times P(Hi). Dividing by this constant ensures the posterior probabilities of the competing hypotheses sum to one.

title: Posterior Probability
text: The posterior probability P(H given E) is the updated probability of a hypothesis after taking new evidence into account, produced by Bayes' theorem. It is proportional to the prior times the likelihood. The posterior from one round of evidence can serve as the prior for the next, allowing sequential and coherent updating of belief as data accumulate.

title: Odds Form of Bayes
text: The odds form of Bayes' theorem states that the posterior odds equal the prior odds multiplied by the likelihood ratio. Writing odds as the ratio of two hypotheses' probabilities, P(H given E)/P(not H given E) = [P(E given H)/P(E given not H)] times [P(H)/P(not H)]. This formulation avoids computing the marginal evidence explicitly.

title: Likelihood Ratio
text: The likelihood ratio for two competing hypotheses is P(E given H1) divided by P(E given H2), measuring how much more probable the observed evidence is under one hypothesis than the other. In the odds form of Bayes' theorem this ratio multiplies the prior odds to give the posterior odds. A ratio far from one indicates evidence that strongly favors one hypothesis.

title: Bayes Factor
text: A Bayes factor is the ratio of the marginal likelihoods of two competing models or hypotheses given the observed data, quantifying the strength of evidence one provides over the other. It multiplies the prior odds to yield the posterior odds. Unlike a simple likelihood ratio for point hypotheses, a Bayes factor averages the likelihood over each model's parameter prior.

title: Base Rates
text: A base rate is the underlying prevalence or unconditional probability of a characteristic in a population before any individuating evidence is considered. Base rates function as prior probabilities in Bayesian updating. Ignoring them leads to systematic errors in probability judgment, because the informativeness of any test or cue depends heavily on how common the target condition is.

title: False Positive Paradox
text: The false positive paradox occurs when a test with a low false positive rate still produces more false positives than true positives, because the condition being tested is rare. When prevalence is very low, the large population of unaffected individuals generates many false alarms that can outnumber the few genuine detections, making a positive result weak evidence on its own.

title: Sensitivity
text: Sensitivity, also called the true positive rate, is the probability that a test correctly returns a positive result for individuals who truly have the condition, equal to true positives divided by all actual positives. A highly sensitive test rarely misses true cases, so a negative result from such a test is strong evidence of absence. Sensitivity is a property of the test independent of prevalence.

title: Specificity
text: Specificity, also called the true negative rate, is the probability that a test correctly returns a negative result for individuals who do not have the condition, equal to true negatives divided by all actual negatives. A highly specific test rarely produces false alarms, so a positive result from such a test strongly indicates the condition is present. Specificity does not depend on prevalence.

title: Positive Predictive Value
text: The positive predictive value is the probability that a person actually has the condition given that the test returned positive, computed as true positives divided by all positive results. Unlike sensitivity and specificity, it depends strongly on the prevalence of the condition in the tested population. For rare conditions the positive predictive value can be surprisingly low despite good test accuracy.

title: Negative Predictive Value
text: The negative predictive value is the probability that a person is truly free of the condition given a negative test result, computed as true negatives divided by all negative results. Like the positive predictive value, it depends on prevalence as well as on the test's sensitivity and specificity, and it tends to be high when the condition is rare in the population.

title: Prevalence Effect on PPV
text: Prevalence, the proportion of a population with a condition, strongly affects predictive values even when a test's sensitivity and specificity are fixed. As prevalence rises, the positive predictive value increases because true positives grow relative to false positives; as prevalence falls, positive predictive value declines. This is why the same test performs differently across populations with different base rates.

title: Monty Hall Problem
text: In the Monty Hall problem a contestant picks one of three doors hiding one prize; the host, who knows the locations, opens a different door revealing no prize, then offers a switch. Switching wins with probability two thirds while staying wins with probability one third. The host's informed choice conveys information, making the remaining unchosen door twice as likely to hide the prize.

title: Birthday Problem
text: The birthday problem asks how many people are needed so that two share a birthday with probability at least one half; the answer is only twenty three. The result seems paradoxical because it counts pairs rather than matches to a fixed date: with n people there are n(n-1)/2 pairs, and the number of comparisons grows quickly enough to make a coincidence likely.

title: Simpson's Paradox
text: Simpson's paradox occurs when a trend that appears in several groups of data reverses or disappears when the groups are combined. It arises from a lurking confounding variable and unequal group sizes that distort the aggregated comparison. The paradox shows that aggregated statistics can mislead, and that the correct interpretation depends on which variables are controlled or partitioned.

title: Berkson's Paradox
text: Berkson's paradox is a form of selection bias in which two traits that are unrelated, or even positively related, in the general population appear negatively correlated within a selected subsample. It commonly arises when the selection criterion is satisfied if either trait is present, as in hospital admission studies, creating a spurious inverse association among those selected.

title: Variance
text: The variance of a random variable measures the average squared deviation from its mean, quantifying how spread out the distribution is. It is defined as the expected value of the squared difference between the variable and its mean, and equivalently equals the mean of the square minus the square of the mean. Variance is always non-negative and has squared units.

title: Standard Deviation
text: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance and measures the typical distance of values from the mean in the same units as the data itself. It is a widely used summary of dispersion because it is expressed on the original scale rather than in squared units. A larger standard deviation indicates greater variability around the central value.

title: Central Limit Theorem
text: The central limit theorem states that the sum or average of a large number of independent, identically distributed random variables with finite variance is approximately normally distributed, regardless of the original distribution's shape. This explains why the bell curve arises so often in nature and underlies many statistical inference procedures that assume approximate normality of sample means.

title: Correlation Coefficient
text: The Pearson correlation coefficient is a number between minus one and plus one that measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables. A value near plus one indicates a strong positive linear association, near minus one a strong negative one, and near zero the absence of a linear relationship. It does not capture nonlinear associations or imply causation.

title: Correlation Not Causation
text: A statistical correlation between two variables does not by itself establish that one causes the other. An observed association may reflect reverse causation, a common cause or confounder influencing both, coincidence, or selection effects. Establishing causation typically requires controlled experiments or careful causal inference beyond the mere presence of a correlation in observational data.

title: Spurious Correlation
text: A spurious correlation is a statistical association between two variables that does not reflect a direct causal link, arising instead from a confounding third variable, a shared time trend, or pure coincidence in the data. With enough variables compared, some will correlate strongly by chance alone. Recognizing spurious correlations guards against unfounded causal conclusions.

title: Confounding Variable
text: A confounding variable is an extraneous factor that is associated with both the supposed cause and the observed effect, potentially producing a misleading association between them. Failure to account for confounders can create the false appearance of a causal relationship. Techniques such as randomization, stratification, and statistical adjustment aim to control confounding in study design and analysis.

title: Bernoulli Trial
text: A Bernoulli trial is a single random experiment with exactly two possible outcomes, conventionally labeled success and failure, with a fixed probability p of success. Repeated independent Bernoulli trials with the same success probability form the building blocks of the binomial distribution. The variance of a single Bernoulli trial equals p times one minus p.

title: Binomial Distribution
text: The binomial distribution gives the probability of obtaining exactly k successes in n independent Bernoulli trials, each with the same success probability p. Its probability mass function is the binomial coefficient n choose k times p to the k times (1-p) to the n minus k. Its mean is n times p and its variance is n times p times one minus p.

title: Poisson Situation
text: The Poisson distribution models the number of independent rare events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space when events happen at a constant average rate. It is characterized by a single parameter lambda, which equals both its mean and its variance. It arises as a limiting case of the binomial distribution when the number of trials is large and success probability small.

title: Uniform Distribution
text: A uniform distribution assigns equal probability to all outcomes in its range. In the discrete case each of a finite set of outcomes has the same probability, as with a fair die. In the continuous case the probability density is constant over an interval and zero elsewhere, so the probability of any subinterval is proportional to its length relative to the whole interval.

title: Normal Distribution
text: The normal, or Gaussian, distribution is a continuous symmetric bell-shaped distribution fully specified by its mean and standard deviation. About sixty-eight percent of its probability lies within one standard deviation of the mean, about ninety-five percent within two, and about ninety-nine point seven percent within three. It is central to statistics due to the central limit theorem.

title: Permutations
text: A permutation is an ordered arrangement of objects, where the order of selection matters. The number of ways to arrange r objects chosen from n distinct objects is n factorial divided by (n minus r) factorial, written P(n, r). When all n objects are arranged the count is n factorial. Permutations are used whenever different orderings count as different outcomes.

title: Combinations
text: A combination is a selection of objects in which order does not matter. The number of ways to choose r objects from n distinct objects is the binomial coefficient n choose r, equal to n factorial divided by r factorial times (n minus r) factorial. Combinations are used for unordered selections and equal the number of permutations divided by r factorial.

title: Permutations Versus Combinations
text: Permutations and combinations both count selections from a set, but they differ in whether order matters. Permutations treat different orderings as distinct outcomes and yield larger counts, while combinations treat any two selections with the same members as identical. The number of combinations equals the number of permutations of the same size divided by the factorial of that size.

title: Fundamental Counting Principle
text: The fundamental counting principle states that if one task can be done in m ways and a second independent task in n ways, then the two tasks together can be performed in m times n ways. It extends to any number of successive choices by multiplying the counts. This multiplication rule underlies the derivation of permutation and combination formulas.

title: Inclusion Exclusion Principle
text: The inclusion-exclusion principle counts the size of a union of sets by adding the sizes of the individual sets, subtracting the sizes of all pairwise intersections, adding back triple intersections, and so on with alternating signs. For probabilities it gives P(A or B or C) as the sum of single probabilities minus pairwise joint probabilities plus the triple joint probability.

title: Conditional Independence
text: Two events A and B are conditionally independent given a third event C when, once C is known, learning about A gives no information about B: P(A and B given C) = P(A given C) times P(B given C). Conditional independence is distinct from unconditional independence; events can be dependent overall yet independent within each level of a conditioning variable, and vice versa.

title: Defence Attorney's Fallacy
text: The defence attorney's fallacy dismisses incriminating evidence by noting that many people in a large population share the matching trait, implying the defendant is just one of many and therefore probably innocent. The error ignores how the shared evidence combines with other independent facts of the case to sharply narrow the pool of plausible suspects and raise the posterior probability of guilt.

title: Subjective Versus Objective Probability
text: Objective probability interprets probability as a property of the world, such as a long-run relative frequency or a physical symmetry, existing independently of any observer. Subjective, or Bayesian, probability interprets it as a degree of rational belief that can be updated with evidence. Both interpretations obey the same mathematical axioms but differ in what the numbers are taken to represent.

title: Proposition
text: In logic a proposition is a declarative statement that is either true or false but not both, and it carries a definite truth value. Questions, commands, and exclamations are not propositions because they cannot be assigned a truth value. Propositions are the basic units combined by logical connectives to form compound statements in propositional logic.

title: Truth Value
text: A truth value is the designation of a proposition as either true or false in classical two-valued logic. Every proposition has exactly one truth value, and the truth value of a compound statement is determined by the truth values of its component propositions together with the connectives joining them. Truth tables systematically record these determinations.

title: Logical Conjunction
text: Logical conjunction is the connective corresponding to and, written A and B, which is true exactly when both of its component propositions are true and false otherwise. It corresponds to set intersection and to the minimum of the two truth values. Conjunction is commutative and associative, and it distributes over disjunction in propositional logic.

title: Logical Disjunction
text: Logical disjunction is the inclusive-or connective, written A or B, which is true when at least one component proposition is true and false only when both are false. It corresponds to set union and to the maximum of the two truth values. This inclusive sense differs from exclusive or, which is true only when exactly one component is true.

title: Logical Negation
text: Logical negation is the unary connective corresponding to not, written not A, which reverses the truth value of its operand: it is true when A is false and false when A is true. Applying negation twice returns the original proposition in classical logic, a property called double negation elimination. Negation interacts with conjunction and disjunction through De Morgan's laws.

title: Material Conditional
text: The material conditional, written if A then B, is a connective that is false only when the antecedent A is true and the consequent B is false, and true in all other cases. In particular it is vacuously true whenever the antecedent is false. This truth-functional definition captures implication in classical logic but diverges from some intuitive causal or relevance senses of if-then.

title: Biconditional
text: The biconditional, written A if and only if B, is a connective that is true exactly when both propositions share the same truth value, that is, both true or both false. It expresses logical equivalence between the two statements and is equivalent to the conjunction of the conditional from A to B and its converse. It corresponds to the negation of exclusive or.

title: Truth Table
text: A truth table is a systematic tabulation that lists every possible combination of truth values for a compound statement's component propositions and gives the resulting truth value of the whole. For n distinct propositions there are two to the n rows. Truth tables provide a mechanical method to determine logical equivalence, validity, tautology, contradiction, and satisfiability.

title: Tautology
text: A tautology is a compound proposition that is true under every possible assignment of truth values to its components, such as A or not A. Tautologies are the logical truths of propositional logic and correspond to statements true purely by their logical form. An argument is valid precisely when the conditional from its conjoined premises to its conclusion is a tautology.

title: Contradiction
text: A contradiction is a compound proposition that is false under every possible assignment of truth values to its components, such as A and not A. Contradictions are logically false by form alone. A statement is a contradiction exactly when its negation is a tautology, and an unsatisfiable formula is one whose truth table contains no true row.

title: Contingency
text: A contingency is a compound proposition that is neither a tautology nor a contradiction, meaning it is true under some truth-value assignments and false under others. Most ordinary compound statements are contingent, their truth depending on the actual values of their components. In a truth table a contingency shows at least one true row and at least one false row.

title: Logical Equivalence
text: Two propositions are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value under every possible assignment of truth values to their components, so their truth-table columns match. Equivalent statements can be substituted for one another without changing overall truth values. Logical equivalence holds precisely when the biconditional joining the two statements is a tautology.

title: De Morgan's Laws
text: De Morgan's laws describe how negation interacts with conjunction and disjunction: the negation of a conjunction equals the disjunction of the negations, not (A and B) equals (not A) or (not B), and the negation of a disjunction equals the conjunction of the negations, not (A or B) equals (not A) and (not B). They are fundamental equivalences in logic and set theory.

title: Contrapositive
text: The contrapositive of a conditional statement if A then B is the statement if not B then not A. A conditional and its contrapositive are logically equivalent, always sharing the same truth value. This equivalence underlies proof by contrapositive, in which one proves a conditional by instead proving its logically equivalent contrapositive form.

title: Converse
text: The converse of a conditional statement if A then B is the statement if B then A, obtained by swapping the antecedent and consequent. A conditional and its converse are not logically equivalent in general, so the truth of one does not guarantee the truth of the other. Mistakenly treating a conditional as equivalent to its converse is a common reasoning error.

title: Inverse Statement
text: The inverse of a conditional statement if A then B is the statement if not A then not B, obtained by negating both the antecedent and the consequent. The inverse is not logically equivalent to the original conditional, but it is equivalent to the converse. Assuming a conditional implies its inverse is a formal fallacy known as denying the antecedent.

title: Constructive Dilemma
text: Constructive dilemma is a valid rule of inference that combines two conditionals with a disjunction of their antecedents. From if A then B, if C then D, and A or C, one may conclude B or D. It effectively applies modus ponens across a disjunction of cases, yielding a disjunctive conclusion, and is a standard pattern in argument by cases.

title: Simplification Rule
text: Simplification is a valid rule of inference stating that from a conjunction A and B one may infer either conjunct separately, that is A, and also B. Because a conjunction is true only when both parts are true, each part must individually be true. This rule allows extracting components from a compound conjunctive premise during a proof.

title: Conjunction Rule
text: The conjunction rule of inference states that from two separately established premises A and B one may infer their conjunction A and B. Since both premises are asserted as true, their combination is likewise true. This rule is the inferential counterpart to simplification, allowing established statements to be joined into a single compound assertion.

title: Addition Rule Logic
text: The addition rule of inference states that from a single premise A one may validly infer the disjunction A or B for any proposition B. Because a disjunction is true whenever at least one disjunct is true, the truth of A alone guarantees the truth of the whole disjunction. This rule introduces a disjunction and is truth preserving despite weakening information.

title: Universal Quantifier
text: The universal quantifier, symbolized by an inverted A, expresses that a predicate holds for every element in the domain of discourse; the statement for all x, P(x) asserts P is true of each object. Its negation is an existential claim: not for all x P(x) is equivalent to there exists x such that not P(x). Universal statements are falsified by a single counterexample.

title: Existential Quantifier
text: The existential quantifier, symbolized by a reversed E, expresses that a predicate holds for at least one element of the domain; the statement there exists x such that P(x) asserts P is true of some object. Its negation is a universal claim: not there exists x P(x) is equivalent to for all x, not P(x). An existential statement is verified by exhibiting one witness.

title: Predicate Logic
text: Predicate logic, also called first-order logic, extends propositional logic by analyzing the internal structure of statements using predicates, variables, quantifiers, and relations. It can express general claims about objects and their properties, such as all humans are mortal, which propositional logic cannot capture. It is more expressive and forms the standard foundation for mathematical reasoning.

title: Law of Non-Contradiction
text: The law of non-contradiction states that a proposition and its negation cannot both be true at the same time and in the same respect; formally, not (A and not A) is a logical truth. It is one of the classical laws of thought and expresses that contradictions are always false. This principle underlies the coherence of classical deductive systems.

title: Law of Excluded Middle
text: The law of excluded middle states that for any proposition either it or its negation is true, so A or not A holds as a logical truth with no third option. Together with the law of non-contradiction it characterizes classical two-valued logic. Some non-classical systems, such as intuitionistic logic, reject the unrestricted form of this law.

title: Law of Identity
text: The law of identity states that every thing is identical to itself and every proposition is equivalent to itself, often expressed as A is A or A if and only if A. It is one of the three classical laws of thought and asserts that a term retains a consistent meaning throughout an argument. Violating it produces equivocation and invalid reasoning.

title: Reductio Ad Absurdum
text: Reductio ad absurdum is a method of argument that establishes a claim by showing that assuming its negation leads to a contradiction or absurd consequence. Since a true premise cannot yield a contradiction, the assumed negation must be false and the original claim true. It is the reasoning form underlying proof by contradiction in mathematics.

title: Proof by Contradiction
text: Proof by contradiction establishes a statement by assuming its negation and deriving a logical contradiction, thereby showing the negation is untenable and the original statement must hold. It relies on the law of excluded middle and non-contradiction. Classic examples include the proof that the square root of two is irrational and that there are infinitely many primes.

title: Direct Proof
text: A direct proof establishes a conditional statement if A then B by assuming the hypothesis A and applying definitions, axioms, and previously proven results through valid inference steps until the conclusion B is reached. It proceeds forward from premises to conclusion without assuming the negation of the goal. Direct proof is the most straightforward standard proof technique.

title: Proof by Contrapositive
text: Proof by contrapositive establishes a conditional if A then B by instead proving its logically equivalent contrapositive, if not B then not A. Because a conditional and its contrapositive always share the same truth value, proving one proves the other. This technique is useful when the negated statements are easier to reason about than the originals.

title: Counterexample
text: A counterexample is a specific instance that satisfies the hypothesis of a universal statement but violates its conclusion, thereby demonstrating the statement is false. A single valid counterexample suffices to refute a universally quantified claim. Searching for counterexamples is a standard way to test conjectures before attempting a general proof.

title: Soundness
text: In logic, soundness is the property of a deductive system in which every statement provable within the system is actually true under the intended interpretation, so its inference rules preserve truth. An argument is sound when it is both valid and has all true premises. Soundness guarantees that proofs yield only genuine truths, never false conclusions.

title: Completeness
text: In logic, completeness is the property of a deductive system in which every statement that is true in all models, that is every logical consequence of the axioms, is provable within the system. Completeness and soundness are complementary: soundness says provable implies true, while completeness says true implies provable. First-order logic is both sound and complete.

title: Logical Consistency
text: A set of statements is consistent when it is possible for all of them to be true simultaneously, meaning no contradiction can be derived from them. An inconsistent set entails a contradiction and, in classical logic, entails every proposition. Consistency is a minimal requirement for a useful axiom system, since an inconsistent system proves everything and distinguishes nothing.

title: Logical Entailment
text: Logical entailment holds when a conclusion is true in every interpretation in which all the premises are true, written premises entail conclusion. It captures the semantic notion of following logically. Entailment corresponds to validity of the associated argument and, in a sound and complete system, coincides with provability from the premises using the inference rules.

title: Satisfiability
text: A formula is satisfiable when there exists at least one assignment of truth values to its variables, or an interpretation, that makes it true. A formula that is true under no assignment is unsatisfiable and equivalent to a contradiction. Satisfiability is dual to validity: a formula is valid exactly when its negation is unsatisfiable, a relationship central to logic and computation.

title: Validity of Argument
text: An argument is valid when it is impossible for its premises to all be true while its conclusion is false, so the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises by logical form alone. Validity concerns the structure of the reasoning, not the actual truth of the premises. A valid argument with all true premises is sound and guarantees a true conclusion.

title: Fallacy of Affirming Consequent
text: Affirming the consequent is a formal fallacy that invalidly infers A from the premises if A then B and B. The error lies in treating the conditional as if it also asserted its converse. The pattern is not truth preserving because B may hold for reasons other than A, so the conclusion can be false even when both premises are true.

title: Fallacy of Denying Antecedent
text: Denying the antecedent is a formal fallacy that invalidly infers not B from the premises if A then B and not A. The error mistakenly treats the conditional as equivalent to its inverse. It is not truth preserving because B may still be true through some cause other than A, so the negation of the antecedent does not establish the negation of the consequent.

title: Exclusive Or
text: Exclusive or, often written XOR, is a binary connective that is true when exactly one of its two component propositions is true and false when they are both true or both false. It differs from inclusive disjunction, which is also true when both components are true. Exclusive or is equivalent to the negation of the biconditional between the same propositions.

title: Random Variable
text: A random variable is a function that assigns a numerical value to each outcome in a sample space, translating the results of a random experiment into numbers. Discrete random variables take countably many values with a probability mass function, while continuous ones take values in a continuum described by a probability density function. Random variables enable computation of expectation and variance.

title: Probability Distribution
text: A probability distribution specifies how probability is allocated over the possible values of a random variable. For a discrete variable it is given by a probability mass function assigning probabilities that sum to one, and for a continuous variable by a probability density function that integrates to one. The distribution fully determines quantities such as the mean, variance, and percentiles.

title: Complementary Events Sum
text: For any event and its complement, the two probabilities always sum to exactly one because together they exhaust the sample space and are mutually exclusive. This relationship, P(A) + P(not A) = 1, follows from the additivity and normalization axioms and provides the basis for the complement rule used to compute one probability from the other.

title: Chain Rule of Probability
text: The chain rule of probability expresses a joint probability of several events as a product of conditional probabilities, for example P(A and B and C) = P(A) times P(B given A) times P(C given A and B). It generalizes the multiplication rule to any number of events by conditioning each successive event on all the preceding ones, and holds without independence assumptions.

title: Bernoulli Versus Binomial
text: A Bernoulli trial describes a single experiment with two outcomes and success probability p, whereas the binomial distribution describes the count of successes across a fixed number n of independent, identical Bernoulli trials. A Bernoulli variable is the special case of a binomial variable with n equal to one, and summing n such independent variables produces a binomial variable.

title: Frequentist Interpretation
text: The frequentist interpretation defines the probability of an event as the limiting relative frequency with which it occurs in a large number of repeated, independent trials under identical conditions. Under this view probability is an objective feature of a repeatable process, and it is not meaningful to assign probabilities to one-time unrepeatable events except through such reference classes.

title: Predicate and Domain
text: In predicate logic a predicate is an expression that becomes a proposition when its variables are assigned values from a domain of discourse, expressing a property of or relation among objects. The domain is the set of objects over which the quantified variables range. The truth of a quantified statement depends on both the predicate and the chosen domain.

title: Argument Form Validity
text: The validity of a deductive argument depends only on its logical form, not on the specific content of its propositions. Any argument sharing the form of a valid pattern is itself valid, and any sharing an invalid form is invalid. This is why validity can be checked by examining structure through truth tables or recognized inference rule schemas.

title: Well-Formed Formula
text: A well-formed formula is a finite string of logical symbols assembled according to the formation rules of a formal language, so that it has a definite grammatical structure and a determinable meaning. Only well-formed formulas can be assigned truth values or serve as premises and conclusions. The formation rules ensure unambiguous parsing of connectives and quantifiers.

title: Vacuous Truth
text: A vacuously true statement is a conditional whose antecedent is never satisfied, making the whole conditional true regardless of the consequent. In the material conditional if A then B, whenever A is false the statement counts as true by definition. Universally quantified claims over an empty domain are likewise vacuously true because there is no instance that could falsify them.

title: Bayesian Updating
text: Bayesian updating is the process of revising the probability of a hypothesis as new evidence arrives, by applying Bayes' theorem to combine the current probability, treated as the prior, with the likelihood of the new data. The resulting posterior becomes the prior for subsequent evidence. This iterative procedure yields coherent, order-independent beliefs when evidence is conditionally independent.

title: Mutually Exclusive Exhaustive
text: A collection of events is mutually exclusive and exhaustive when no two can occur together and at least one must occur, so the events partition the sample space. Their probabilities sum to exactly one. Such a partition is the setting for the law of total probability and for the denominator of Bayes' theorem, ensuring all possibilities are accounted for without overlap.

title: Expected Value Linearity
text: Expectation is a linear operator: for any random variables and constants, the expected value of a linear combination equals the same linear combination of the expected values, so E(aX + bY) equals a times E(X) plus b times E(Y). Crucially this linearity holds whether or not the variables are independent, which makes expectation especially convenient in calculations.

title: Variance of Sum
text: For two random variables the variance of their sum equals the sum of their variances plus twice their covariance. When the variables are independent, or more generally uncorrelated, the covariance is zero and the variance of the sum reduces to the sum of the variances. Unlike expectation, variance is not linear and requires independence for this additive simplification.

title: Ridge Ending Minutia
text: A ridge ending is a point where a friction ridge terminates or abruptly stops along its length. It is one of the fundamental minutiae, or Galton points, used in fingerprint comparison. The relative position, orientation, and spatial relationship of ridge endings to other minutiae contribute to the overall ridge detail that examiners assess when evaluating whether two impressions share a common source.

title: Bifurcation Minutia
text: A bifurcation is a point at which a single friction ridge divides into two ridges that continue onward. Along with ridge endings, bifurcations are among the most common and reliable minutiae used in comparison. Their location and orientation relative to neighbouring features form part of the ridge configuration examiners rely upon when assessing the likelihood of a shared source between two prints.

title: Dot Ridge Feature
text: A dot is a very short friction ridge feature whose length is approximately equal to its width, appearing as an isolated small unit within the ridge flow. Dots are counted among the recognised minutiae in fingerprint analysis. Because their placement is not systematically arranged, their positions add to the distinctiveness of a ridge arrangement used in comparison.

title: Island Ridge Minutia
text: An island, sometimes called an enclosure or lake, is formed where a single ridge bifurcates and then rejoins after a short separation, enclosing a small area. It is treated as a distinct minutia type in friction ridge analysis. The size, shape, and location of an enclosure contribute to the constellation of features examiners evaluate during comparison.

title: Spur Ridge Feature
text: A spur, or hook, is a bifurcation in which one of the resulting branches is notably short before ending. It is recognised as a specific minutia type within friction ridge examination. Like other minutiae, its value in comparison derives from its position and orientation relative to the surrounding ridge detail rather than from the feature type alone.

title: Loop Pattern Type
text: A loop is a fingerprint pattern in which one or more ridges enter from one side, curve around, and exit from the same side, passing near a central point. Loops are generally the most frequently occurring of the broad pattern classes. They are subdivided by the direction of ridge flow, which supports classification but not individualisation on its own.

title: Ulnar and Radial Loops
text: Loops are subdivided into ulnar and radial types according to the direction in which the ridges flow relative to the bones of the forearm. In an ulnar loop the ridges open toward the little-finger side, and in a radial loop they open toward the thumb side. This distinction is a class characteristic useful for classification rather than for establishing individual identity.

title: Whorl Pattern Type
text: A whorl is a fingerprint pattern characterised by ridges that form circular, spiral, or oval configurations around a central region, typically featuring two delta points. Whorls are one of the three broad pattern classes and occur less commonly than loops. Their subtypes describe overall ridge flow and serve as class characteristics for classification purposes.

title: Whorl Subtypes
text: Whorl patterns are commonly subdivided into plain whorls, central pocket loop whorls, double loop whorls, and accidental whorls, based on the arrangement of ridges and the relationship of delta points to the pattern core. These subtypes assist in systematic classification of prints but describe general ridge flow rather than the individual detail used for identification.

title: Arch Pattern Type
text: An arch is a fingerprint pattern in which ridges enter from one side, rise toward the centre, and exit the opposite side without forming a loop or whorl. Arches are the least common of the three broad pattern classes. They are divided into plain and tented forms, providing a class-level descriptor useful for classification.

title: Plain and Tented Arches
text: Arch patterns are subdivided into plain arches, where ridges rise in a gentle wave across the pattern, and tented arches, where ridges near the centre thrust upward sharply, sometimes with an angle or an upthrusting ridge. This distinction is a class characteristic that aids classification but does not by itself establish that two impressions share a common origin.

title: Delta and Core Points
text: The delta is a triangular ridge formation, or the point of divergence of ridge flows, while the core is the approximate centre of a recurving ridge pattern. These reference points are used to orient a print and to classify its pattern type. Counting ridges between delta and core supports classification systems but is a class-level rather than individualising measure.

title: Latent Prints
text: A latent print is a friction ridge impression that is not readily visible and is deposited when perspiration, oils, or other residues transfer from the ridges onto a surface. Such prints generally require development through physical or chemical means to be visualised. Latent impressions are among the most commonly encountered forms of fingerprint evidence at scenes.

title: Patent Prints
text: A patent print is a friction ridge impression that is visible to the unaided eye because the ridges have transferred a coloured or contaminating substance, such as blood, ink, dust, or grease, onto a surface. Because these impressions are already visible, they are typically documented photographically before any further processing is attempted.

title: Plastic Prints
text: A plastic print is a three-dimensional friction ridge impression left when the ridges press into a soft, pliable material such as wax, putty, or fresh paint, which then retains the moulded shape. These impressions are visible and are usually recorded through photography using oblique lighting to emphasise the ridge detail before any casting is considered.

title: Powder Development
text: Fingerprint powders adhere to the moist or oily residues of a latent print, rendering it visible against a contrasting background, chiefly on smooth, non-porous surfaces. The powder is applied lightly with a soft brush and the developed print is then photographed and often lifted with adhesive material. Colour and composition are chosen to contrast with the underlying surface.

title: Ninhydrin On Porous Surfaces
text: Ninhydrin is a chemical reagent used to develop latent prints on porous surfaces such as paper and cardboard, where it reacts with amino acids present in print residue to produce a purple coloured product. Gentle heat and humidity can accelerate the reaction. Because it targets amino acids absorbed into the substrate, it is particularly suited to documents and other absorbent materials.

title: Cyanoacrylate Fuming
text: Cyanoacrylate fuming develops latent prints on non-porous surfaces by exposing evidence to the vapours of a fast-curing adhesive within an enclosed chamber. The vapour polymerises on the moisture and other constituents of the print residue, forming a stable white deposit along the ridges. The hardened result can then be photographed or enhanced with dyes or powders.

title: Iodine Fuming
text: Iodine fuming is an older technique in which iodine vapour temporarily colours the fatty and oily components of a latent print a brownish hue, making it visible for a limited time. Because the developed print fades as the iodine sublimes away, it is typically photographed promptly. The method can be applied to a range of surfaces, including some porous materials.

title: Silver Nitrate Development
text: Silver nitrate develops latent prints on porous surfaces by reacting with chloride salts present in perspiration residue to form silver chloride, which darkens on exposure to light and reveals the ridge detail. Because the reaction targets salts rather than amino acids or oils, it can complement other porous-surface techniques applied in sequence.

title: Fingerprint Persistence
text: Friction ridge patterns form during foetal development and, barring deep scarring or certain diseases, remain unchanged in their arrangement throughout life, growing only in overall size. This persistence is a foundational premise of fingerprint identification, since it allows an impression to be meaningfully compared against a reference taken at a different time.

title: Ridge Individuality Premise
text: Friction ridge examination rests on the premise that the detailed arrangement of ridges and minutiae is highly variable between individuals, including between identical twins, making close correspondence in fine detail strongly associative. Modern practice frames conclusions in terms of the probability of a shared source rather than as claims of absolute mathematical certainty.

title: Palm Print Comparison
text: The friction ridge skin of the palms bears ridge detail and minutiae comparable to that of the fingertips and can be used for comparison in the same manner. Palm impressions include distinctive regions and flexion creases that aid orientation. Because palms frequently contact surfaces, their impressions can provide associative evidence alongside or instead of fingertip prints.

title: Bare Footprint Ridges
text: The soles of the feet, like the palms and fingertips, are covered in friction ridge skin bearing minutiae that can be compared between a questioned impression and a reference. Bare footprint ridge detail follows the same principles of persistence and variability. Such impressions may be relevant where individuals have been unshod at a location of interest.

title: Footwear Class Characteristics
text: Footwear impressions carry class characteristics, such as the overall size, tread pattern, and design features shared by all shoes of a given model and manufacture. These features allow an impression to be associated with a category of footwear. On their own, class characteristics support inclusion within a group rather than identification of one specific shoe.

title: Footwear Individual Characteristics
text: Individual characteristics of footwear arise from randomly acquired features such as cuts, nicks, embedded debris, and wear that develop uniquely during use. When such acquired features correspond in detail between a questioned impression and a suspected shoe, they can strongly support the conclusion that the specific shoe made the impression, expressed as an association rather than absolute proof.

title: Wear And Acquired Features
text: As footwear and tyres are used, their contact surfaces accumulate wear patterns and randomly acquired marks that reflect the particular history of the item. Because these features develop by chance and change over time, close correspondence between them and a questioned impression carries substantial associative value, while their gradual evolution is considered when assessing timing.

title: Tyre Track Impressions
text: Tyre impressions display class characteristics in their tread design, width, and circumference, and may display individual characteristics from cuts, wear, and embedded material acquired during use. Comparison proceeds much as for footwear, associating a track first with a tread category and, where acquired features correspond, potentially with a specific tyre.

title: Impressed Tool Marks
text: An impressed tool mark is formed when a tool is pressed into a softer surface with little or no lateral movement, leaving a negative impression of the tool's contacting shape. Such marks can reproduce both the general form of the tool and finer surface irregularities. Comparison focuses on whether corresponding detail supports an association with a particular tool.

title: Striated Tool Marks
text: A striated tool mark consists of a series of fine parallel scratches produced when a tool moves across a surface under pressure, transferring irregularities of the tool edge as lines. The pattern of striations reflects microscopic imperfections of the tool. Correspondence of striation detail between a questioned mark and test marks can associate the mark with a particular tool.

title: Toolmark Comparison Microscopy
text: Toolmark comparison typically employs a comparison microscope, which places a questioned mark and a mark made by a suspected tool side by side within a single field of view. The examiner assesses the agreement of individual surface features between the two. Conclusions are framed as associative, reflecting the degree of correspondence rather than absolute identification.

title: Locard Exchange Principle
text: Locard's exchange principle holds that whenever two objects or surfaces come into contact, there is a mutual transfer of material between them, so that a person or object bringing something to a scene also takes something away. This principle underlies the collection and interpretation of trace evidence, though the transferred traces may be minute, fragile, or difficult to detect.

title: Trace Transfer And Persistence
text: Trace evidence analysis considers both how readily material transfers between surfaces and how long transferred material persists before being lost. Persistence is influenced by the nature of the material, the receiving surface, and subsequent activity. Because traces are shed over time, their quantity and distribution are interpreted with the dynamics of transfer and loss in mind.

title: Hair Morphology Structure
text: A hair shaft is composed of an outer cuticle of overlapping scales, an inner cortex containing pigment and structural detail, and, when present, a central medulla. These features vary in appearance and can be examined microscopically. Because such characteristics are shared among many hairs, morphological hair comparison is regarded as class evidence rather than a means of individual identification.

title: Hair As Class Evidence
text: Microscopic comparison of hairs assesses features such as colour, diameter, pigment distribution, and medullary appearance, which can indicate whether a questioned hair is consistent with a reference source. Because many individuals may share such features, a morphological association places a hair within a group and does not, by itself, identify a single specific source.

title: Natural And Synthetic Fibres
text: Fibres are broadly divided into natural fibres, derived from plant or animal sources, and manufactured fibres, produced by chemical or mechanical processes. Their type can be examined through optical and chemical means. Because large numbers of identical fibres are produced and worn, fibre comparison is treated as class evidence supporting association rather than unique identification.

title: Fibre Comparison Value
text: Fibre comparison evaluates characteristics such as type, colour, diameter, cross-sectional shape, and dye composition to determine whether a questioned fibre could share a common origin with a known source. Because mass production yields many indistinguishable fibres, a correspondence supports an associative inference whose strength depends on how common the fibre type is.

title: Glass Fracture Patterns
text: When a sheet of glass is broken by an impact, it commonly fractures into radial cracks that extend outward from the point of force and concentric cracks that encircle it. The configuration of these fractures can indicate the point and, in some circumstances, the direction of the applied force, based on established principles of how brittle sheets fail.

title: Radial And Concentric Cracks
text: Radial fractures radiate outward from an impact point like spokes, while concentric fractures form roughly circular arcs around it. Examination of the edges of these cracks can indicate which side of the glass received the force, since characteristic stress markings on the broken edges relate systematically to the sequence and direction of fracturing.

title: Glass Refractive Index
text: Glass fragments can be compared by measuring their refractive index, the extent to which they bend transmitted light, often determined by immersion in a liquid of matched properties. Correspondence in refractive index indicates that two fragments could share a common source. Because many objects are made from similar glass, such a match is associative rather than uniquely identifying.

title: Soil Comparison Principles
text: Soil can be compared by examining colour, texture, mineral content, and included particles to assess whether samples could share a common origin. Because soil composition varies from place to place yet similar soils exist over broad areas, a correspondence supports an associative inference. Its strength depends on how distinctive the observed characteristics are for a location.

title: Paint Layer Analysis
text: Paint evidence is examined by comparing colour, composition, and the sequence and thickness of layers, since manufactured and repainted surfaces often build up characteristic layer structures. Correspondence in layer sequence and composition supports an association between a questioned fragment and a source. The strength of that inference reflects how common the layer arrangement is.

title: Gunshot Residue Concept
text: The discharge of a firearm can deposit residue composed of particles from the primer and propellant onto nearby surfaces, including the hands and clothing. Detection of such particles can indicate proximity to a discharge, but their presence may also arise from handling contaminated items or environments, so results are interpreted cautiously and in context rather than as conclusive of who fired a weapon.

title: Firearm Rifling Basics
text: The interior of a rifled firearm barrel bears helical grooves cut into it, leaving raised lands between them, which impart spin to a projectile for stability. As a bullet passes through, the lands and grooves engrave corresponding marks on its surface. The number, width, and direction of twist of these features constitute class characteristics of the barrel.

title: Bullet Striation Marks
text: As a fired bullet travels through a rifled barrel, microscopic imperfections on the barrel's interior scratch fine striations onto the bullet's bearing surface. Because these imperfections arise partly at random and change slowly, correspondence of striation detail between a questioned bullet and test-fired bullets can associate the bullet with a particular firearm, expressed as a probabilistic conclusion.

title: Class Versus Individual Firearm Marks
text: Firearm marks are divided into class characteristics, such as calibre and the number and twist of rifling grooves shared by all arms of a type, and individual characteristics arising from unique wear and manufacturing irregularities. Class features narrow the field of possible sources, while corresponding individual features can support an association with one specific firearm.

title: Firing Pin Impression
text: The firing pin strikes the primer of a cartridge to initiate discharge, leaving an impression whose shape and surface detail reflect the pin and the surrounding breech. Both the general form and finer irregularities of this impression are examined in comparison, contributing to conclusions about whether a questioned cartridge case was fired in a particular weapon.

title: Breech Face Marks
text: During firing, the pressure of discharge drives the cartridge case head back against the breech face of the firearm, transferring the microscopic texture of that surface onto the case head. Because the breech face bears manufacturing and wear irregularities, correspondence of these marks between a questioned case and test firings can support an association with a specific firearm.

title: Extractor And Ejector Marks
text: The mechanisms that withdraw a cartridge case from the chamber and expel it can leave characteristic marks on the case, respectively from the extractor gripping the rim and the ejector striking the case. Such marks carry both class and individual detail and are examined alongside firing pin and breech face impressions when associating a case with a firearm.

title: Trajectory Reasoning
text: The path of a projectile can be reconstructed by examining the marks it left, such as perforations and impact damage, and relating them through their alignment. Establishing the line connecting entry and impact points allows inferences about the direction and, sometimes, the approximate origin of a shot. Such reconstructions carry uncertainty and are expressed as ranges rather than exact paths.

title: Bloodstain Pattern Basics
text: Bloodstain pattern analysis interprets the size, shape, distribution, and location of bloodstains to infer the events and actions that produced them. It applies principles of fluid behaviour to distinguish, for example, passive drops from projected patterns. Conclusions describe the mechanisms consistent with a pattern and are framed with attention to the range of possible causes.

title: Passive Blood Drops
text: Passive bloodstains are formed by the action of gravity alone, as when blood drips from a source without additional applied force. The size and shape of a passive drop are influenced by the falling distance and the nature of the receiving surface. Recognising passive patterns helps distinguish them from stains produced by impact or projection.

title: Blood Spatter Formation
text: Spatter is produced when a force acts on a liquid blood source, breaking it into droplets that travel and deposit as a pattern. The size distribution of the resulting stains relates broadly to the amount of energy involved. Interpretation associates a spatter pattern with a general category of causative mechanism rather than pinpointing a single precise event.

title: Stain Directionality
text: The shape of an individual bloodstain records the direction in which its droplet was travelling, since a droplet striking a surface at an angle tends to elongate and leave a narrower tail pointing away from the origin. Assessing the directionality of multiple stains allows an analyst to reason about where droplets came from within a scene.

title: Angle Of Impact
text: The angle at which a blood droplet strikes a surface can be estimated from the ratio of the width to the length of the resulting elliptical stain, using an established trigonometric relationship. Combining the impact angles and directions of several stains allows estimation of a region of origin. Such estimates carry uncertainty and are expressed as approximate areas.

title: Void Patterns
text: A void is a gap or absence within an expected bloodstain pattern, created when an object or person intercepts droplets before they reach a surface and is later removed. Recognising void patterns can indicate the former presence and approximate position of an intervening object, offering information about the arrangement of a scene at the time stains were deposited.

title: Serology Presumptive Tests
text: Presumptive serological tests provide a rapid preliminary indication of whether a stain may be a particular body fluid, typically by producing a colour change or luminescence in the presence of a target substance. Because other materials can yield similar reactions, a positive presumptive result is not conclusive and must be followed by more specific confirmatory testing.

title: ABO Blood Grouping
text: The ABO system classifies blood according to the presence or absence of certain antigens on red cells, yielding recognised groups. Historically, determining the ABO group of a stain could exclude some individuals as its source or place the source within a broad population sharing that group. As shared class evidence, it associates rather than uniquely identifies.

title: Secretor Status Concept
text: In some individuals, known as secretors, blood group substances are present in body fluids such as saliva besides the blood itself, whereas in non-secretors they are not. Whether a person is a secretor is an inherited characteristic. This concept historically allowed blood group information to be recovered from certain fluid stains, adding to class-level associative evidence.

title: Toxicology ADME
text: Forensic toxicology considers how a substance is absorbed into the body, distributed among tissues, metabolised into other compounds, and eliminated over time. These processes govern the concentration of a substance and its breakdown products in different samples at different times. Understanding them is essential for interpreting analytical results in terms of dose and timing.

title: Postmortem Redistribution
text: After death, the concentration of some substances measured in blood can change as they move between tissues and the blood, a phenomenon known as postmortem redistribution. Because a measured level may not reflect the concentration at the time of death, interpretation of postmortem toxicology accounts for the sampling site and the potential for such shifts.

title: Poisons General Principles
text: A poison is any substance capable of causing harm to the body, with its effect depending on dose, route of exposure, and individual factors. The long-standing principle that the dose determines whether a substance acts as a poison underlies toxicological interpretation. Detecting a substance is distinct from establishing that its quantity was sufficient to cause harm.

title: Algor Mortis Cooling
text: Algor mortis refers to the cooling of a body after death as it tends toward the surrounding temperature. Under stable conditions the decline in body temperature can offer a rough indication of the interval since death, but the rate is affected by body size, clothing, environment, and other factors, so any resulting estimate is broad and approximate.

title: Livor Mortis Lividity
text: Livor mortis is the settling of blood under gravity after death, producing a discolouration in the dependent parts of the body that eventually becomes fixed. Its development and pattern can offer clues about the interval since death and whether a body was moved after death, though as with other markers it yields approximate rather than precise timing.

title: Stomach Contents Timing
text: The extent to which food in the stomach has been digested and emptied can offer a rough indication of the time elapsed since a person's last meal, and thereby loosely constrain the time of death. Because digestion and gastric emptying vary considerably between individuals and circumstances, such estimates are broad and treated with caution.

title: Forensic Entomology Succession
text: Forensic entomology uses the predictable colonisation of remains by successive insect species, and the developmental stages of those insects, to estimate the minimum time since death. The sequence of arriving species and their growth rates depend strongly on temperature and environment, so estimates are given as ranges and interpreted against local conditions.

title: Decomposition Stages
text: After death, a body generally passes through recognisable stages of decomposition, from early changes through bloating and active breakdown to advanced skeletal reduction. The progression is strongly influenced by temperature, moisture, and environment. Observing the stage reached can loosely indicate the interval since death, but the timing is variable and approximate.

title: Questioned Document Examination
text: Questioned document examination compares disputed writings, printings, and materials against known standards to address issues of authorship, authenticity, and alteration. It considers features of the ink, paper, and production method as well as the writing itself. Conclusions are expressed as degrees of support for or against a proposition rather than as absolute certainties.

title: Indented Writing And ESDA
text: When writing is produced on an upper sheet of a pad, impressions can be left on underlying sheets. Electrostatic detection methods can reveal such indented writing by developing a visible image from the disturbed surface, without requiring visible ink. Recovered indentations can indicate the content of writing that was made on a sheet since removed.

title: Ink And Paper Analysis
text: The inks and papers used in a document can be examined for colour, composition, and other properties to assess consistency between parts of a document or against a purported origin. Differences may indicate additions or alterations. Because materials are mass produced, correspondence supports associative inferences whose strength depends on how distinctive the materials are.

title: Alterations And Obliterations
text: Documents may be altered by adding, erasing, or overwriting material, or obliterated by covering original writing. Examination using varied lighting and imaging can reveal traces of the original content or the fact that a change was made. Detecting such changes distinguishes the original entries from later modifications without necessarily recovering every altered detail.

title: Handwriting Individuality
text: Handwriting develops individual characteristics through habit, so that no two writers form all features identically, yet each writer also exhibits a degree of natural variation from one specimen to another. Comparison weighs the consistency of individual habits against expected variation. Conclusions about authorship are expressed as levels of support rather than absolute proof.

title: Natural Variation In Writing
text: Every writer produces a range of naturally varying forms rather than perfectly repeated ones, so genuine writings by one person differ slightly among themselves. Recognising the normal scope of a writer's variation is essential to comparison, since differences within that range are consistent with common authorship while differences beyond it may indicate another writer.

title: Forgery Types
text: Fraudulent writing is often categorised into freehand simulation, in which a writer copies the general appearance of another's writing by eye; tracing, in which an outline is followed; and freehand invention without a model. Each method tends to leave characteristic signs, such as unnatural hesitation or tremor, that examiners look for when assessing genuineness.

title: Anthropology Sex Estimation
text: Forensic anthropology estimates biological sex from skeletal remains chiefly by examining features of the pelvis and skull that tend to differ between populations of males and females. Because these features overlap and vary, sex estimation is expressed as a probability or a range of confidence rather than a certain determination, and is most reliable with well-preserved remains.

title: Anthropology Age Estimation
text: Age at death can be estimated from the skeleton using indicators such as the development and eruption of teeth, the fusion of growth plates, and age-related changes at certain joint surfaces. Younger individuals can generally be aged more precisely than older adults. Estimates are given as ranges reflecting the biological variability of skeletal ageing.

title: Anthropology Stature Estimation
text: Living stature can be estimated from skeletal remains by measuring long bones and applying established relationships between bone length and height derived from reference populations. Because these relationships vary among populations and individuals, stature estimates are presented as ranges. Accuracy improves when complete long bones and appropriate reference data are available.

title: Forensic Odontology Comparison
text: Forensic odontology compares dental features, such as the arrangement, shape, and restorations of teeth, between recovered remains and dental records to support identification. Because dental configurations vary and dental work is individual, correspondence can strongly support an identification. Conclusions rest on the quality of the records and the correspondence of distinctive features.

title: Forensic Pathology Role
text: Forensic pathology examines the body after death to determine the medical findings relevant to how a person died, integrating external and internal examination with history and circumstances. It seeks to establish the cause of death and to inform the manner of death. Its conclusions are drawn from objective findings interpreted in the context of available information.

title: Sharp Force Injuries
text: Sharp force injuries are produced by objects with edges or points and are characterised clinically by relatively clean margins, in contrast to the features of blunt trauma. Their dimensions and characteristics may allow general inferences about the class of instrument involved. Such inferences describe categories of possible objects rather than identifying a single specific implement.

title: Blunt Force Injuries
text: Blunt force injuries result from impact with or against a broad, non-edged surface and tend to display features distinct from those of sharp force, such as irregular margins and associated bruising. The pattern of injury can sometimes suggest the general nature of the object or surface involved, while identifying a specific object usually requires additional corroborating evidence.

title: Wound Types General
text: Injuries are broadly categorised by the mechanism that produced them, including sharp force, blunt force, thermal, and other classes, each tending to leave characteristic features. Careful documentation of the appearance, location, and dimensions of injuries supports inferences about how they were caused, while such inferences describe categories of mechanism rather than exact reconstructions.

title: Cause Manner Mechanism Of Death
text: In forensic pathology the cause of death is the disease or injury that initiated the fatal sequence, the mechanism is the physiological derangement through which it produced death, and the manner is the broad category of circumstances under which death occurred. Distinguishing these related concepts is fundamental to describing a death accurately and consistently.

title: Hypothesis In Investigation
text: A hypothesis is a proposed explanation formulated so that its consequences can be tested against observation. In investigation, framing explicit hypotheses allows evidence to be evaluated for how well it supports or contradicts each one. A useful hypothesis makes predictions that could in principle be shown false, distinguishing it from an untestable assertion.

title: Controls In Testing
text: A control is a reference condition included in a test to provide a basis for comparison, such as a sample known to lack the target or a procedure run without the item of interest. Controls help distinguish genuine effects from artefacts of the method or contamination. Their use is central to ensuring that observed results are attributable to the intended cause.

title: Variables In Experiments
text: A variable is any factor that can change within an investigation. An independent variable is deliberately altered, a dependent variable is measured for its response, and other factors are ideally held constant or otherwise accounted for. Identifying and managing variables is essential so that observed differences can be attributed to the intended cause rather than confounders.

title: Bias Control Methods
text: Bias is a systematic tendency that distorts a result away from the truth. It is controlled through measures such as standardised procedures, controls, randomisation where applicable, and shielding examiners from potentially misleading information. Recognising and limiting sources of bias strengthens the reliability of conclusions drawn from evidence.

title: Blind Analysis
text: In blind analysis, the person performing or interpreting a test is kept unaware of information that could improperly influence the outcome, such as the expected or desired result. This separation reduces the risk that expectation shapes a judgement. Blinding is a general safeguard for the objectivity of measurements and comparisons in forensic work.

title: Error Rates
text: The reliability of a method is characterised in part by its error rates, meaning how often it yields false positive or false negative results under defined conditions. Knowing a method's error rates allows its conclusions to be weighed appropriately. A technique with poorly characterised error rates offers weaker grounds for confident interpretation.

title: Validation Of Methods
text: Validation is the process of demonstrating, through systematic testing, that a method performs reliably and as intended for its purpose before it is used on casework. Validation establishes the conditions under which a method is dependable and characterises its limitations. Using only validated methods is a foundation of sound forensic practice.

title: Reproducibility
text: Reproducibility is the extent to which a result can be obtained again when a procedure is repeated, whether by the same analyst or by others. A finding that can be reproduced under stated conditions carries greater weight than one that cannot. Assessing reproducibility helps distinguish reliable observations from those arising by chance or from uncontrolled factors.

title: Class Versus Individual Characteristics
text: A class characteristic is a feature shared by all members of a group and can place an item within a category, while an individual characteristic arises from random events and may distinguish one item from others of its kind. This distinction underlies comparison across forensic disciplines, since only correspondence of individual features can support attribution to a single source.

title: Exclusion Versus Identification
text: In comparison, an exclusion is a determination that two items do not share a common source, while an identification is a conclusion that they do to a stated degree of confidence. Exclusions can often be reached with strong certainty from a single clear difference, whereas identifications rest on the accumulation of corresponding detail and are expressed probabilistically.

title: Elimination Of Alternatives
text: Sound investigation systematically considers and, where possible, rules out alternative explanations rather than fixing on a single hypothesis prematurely. A conclusion is strengthened when competing explanations have been examined and found inconsistent with the evidence. This disciplined elimination guards against accepting an explanation merely because it was the first considered.

title: Occam's Razor In Investigation
text: Occam's razor is the heuristic that, among explanations consistent with the evidence, the one requiring the fewest unsupported assumptions is generally to be preferred. In investigation it discourages needlessly complicated accounts. It is a guide to provisional preference rather than a proof, and a simpler explanation is set aside when evidence favours a more complex one.

title: Base Rates In Identification
text: The base rate is the underlying frequency of a characteristic within a relevant population. Interpreting the significance of a matching feature requires attention to its base rate, since a common feature provides weaker discrimination than a rare one. Neglecting base rates can lead to overstating the weight of an observed correspondence.

title: Cognitive Bias In Examiners
text: Forensic examiners, like all people, are susceptible to cognitive biases that can influence perception and judgement without conscious awareness. Recognising this susceptibility motivates safeguards such as controlling exposure to extraneous information. Acknowledging the potential for bias is a precondition for designing procedures that limit its effect on conclusions.

title: Contextual Bias
text: Contextual bias occurs when information beyond the evidence itself, such as knowledge of other findings or expectations about a case, unduly shapes an examiner's interpretation. Because such extraneous context can steer a judgement toward an anticipated result, procedures that restrict an examiner's exposure to irrelevant information help preserve the objectivity of a comparison.

title: Expectation Effects
text: Expectation can influence what an observer perceives, so that anticipating a particular result may make ambiguous features appear to confirm it. This effect operates without deliberate intent and can affect careful examiners. Limiting foreknowledge of the desired outcome and documenting observations before conclusions help reduce the sway of expectation on findings.

title: Verification And Peer Review
text: Verification is the independent re-examination of a comparison or result by another qualified analyst to check whether the same conclusion is reached. Peer review more broadly subjects reasoning and findings to critical scrutiny by others. These practices help detect error and bias, strengthening confidence in conclusions beyond the judgement of a single examiner.

title: Documentation Practices
text: Thorough documentation records what was observed, done, and concluded, together with the conditions and reasoning involved, so that work can be reviewed and, where possible, reproduced. Contemporaneous and complete records support transparency and allow others to assess the basis for a conclusion. Poor documentation weakens the evidentiary value of otherwise sound work.

title: Chain Of Custody
text: Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken record of the handling of an item of evidence from collection through analysis and storage, identifying who had it and when. Maintaining this record supports the integrity of the evidence by demonstrating that it was not lost, altered, or substituted. Gaps in the chain can cast doubt on an item's reliability.

title: Contamination Avoidance
text: Contamination is the unwanted introduction or transfer of material that can distort analysis or create misleading associations. It is avoided through clean handling, appropriate protective measures, separation of samples, and controls that would reveal it. Because trace evidence can transfer readily, disciplined contamination control is essential to the trustworthiness of results.

title: Evidence Integrity
text: Evidence integrity is the preservation of an item in a condition that faithfully reflects its state when collected, protecting it from loss, degradation, alteration, and contamination. It is maintained through proper packaging, storage, and handling. Preserving integrity ensures that the material examined and presented remains a reliable representation of what was recovered.

title: Presumptive Versus Confirmatory Testing
text: A presumptive test gives a quick, sensitive but non-specific indication that a substance may be present, whereas a confirmatory test is more specific and establishes identity with greater certainty. Because presumptive results can arise from other substances, a positive presumptive finding is treated as preliminary and is followed by confirmatory analysis before firm conclusions are drawn.

title: Individual Evidence Concept
text: Individualising evidence is that which can, in principle, be associated with a single source to a high degree of confidence because it bears features arising from random processes. Forensic disciplines differ in how far they approach true individualisation.
