Modern practice tends to express even strong associations in probabilistic terms rather than as claims of absolute uniqueness.

title: Observation Versus Inference
text: An observation is a directly recorded feature of the evidence, whereas an inference is a conclusion reasoned from observations. Keeping these distinct clarifies which parts of an analysis rest on data and which on interpretation. Documenting observations separately from the inferences drawn from them supports transparent and defensible reasoning.

title: Sampling Considerations
text: Because analysis often examines only a portion of available material, the way a sample is selected affects how well it represents the whole. A sample chosen without regard to representativeness can mislead. Considering how samples are taken, and whether they reflect the material of interest, is important to interpreting analytical results appropriately.

title: Comparison Reference Standards
text: Meaningful comparison requires known reference standards of adequate quality and quantity against which questioned material is evaluated. The value of a comparison depends on the suitability of the standards, such as writing collected under comparable conditions or test firings from a recovered firearm. Inadequate standards limit the conclusions that can be responsibly drawn.

title: Negative Evidence Value
text: The absence of an expected trace can itself be informative, since some activities would be expected to leave detectable material. However, non-detection may reflect limited transfer, loss over time, or the limits of a method rather than the non-occurrence of an event. Interpreting negative findings therefore requires care and attention to alternative explanations.

title: Uniqueness Assumption Caution
text: Some forensic comparisons have historically rested on an assumption that natural features are effectively unique. Because such uniqueness is difficult to demonstrate empirically for a whole population, careful practice frames conclusions in terms of the strength of an association and the rarity of shared features rather than asserting uniqueness as an established fact.

title: Impression Evidence Overview
text: Impression evidence comprises marks left when one object contacts another, including friction ridge prints, footwear and tyre impressions, and tool marks. Its analysis shares a common logic of distinguishing class characteristics, which categorise a source, from individual characteristics acquired by chance, which can support association with a single specific source.

title: Comparison Microscope Function
text: A comparison microscope joins the fields of two microscopes so that two specimens can be viewed simultaneously side by side or in a single merged image. This allows an examiner to align and directly compare fine surface features of a questioned and a known item. It is a central instrument in firearms and toolmark examination for assessing correspondence.

title: Photographic Documentation
text: Photography records the appearance and location of evidence as found, before any processing that might alter it, and provides a durable image for later analysis and review. Techniques such as including a scale and using controlled lighting improve the usefulness of the record. Careful photographic documentation supports both interpretation and independent scrutiny of findings.

title: Casting Impressions
text: Three-dimensional impressions such as footwear, tyre, and tool marks in soft surfaces can be preserved by casting, in which a setting material is applied to capture the moulded detail. A cast reproduces the shape and fine features of the impression for later comparison. Casting complements photography by retaining depth information that a flat image cannot convey.

title: Lifting Latent Prints
text: After a latent print on a non-porous surface has been developed, it can be preserved by lifting, in which adhesive material is pressed onto the developed print to transfer the powdered ridge detail. The lift is then mounted on a contrasting backing. Lifting captures the print for comparison when the surface itself cannot be retained.

title: Sequential Processing
text: Where more than one development or analytical technique may be applied to an item, they are performed in a considered sequence so that earlier methods do not destroy detail needed by later ones. Ordering procedures thoughtfully allows the maximum information to be recovered from a single item of evidence without foreclosing subsequent examinations.

title: Refractive Index Concept
text: The refractive index of a transparent material describes how much it bends light passing through it and is a physical property useful for comparison. Because it can be measured precisely and varies with composition, refractive index is used to compare materials such as glass fragments. As a shared property of many products, correspondence is associative rather than unique.

title: Microscopy In Forensics
text: Microscopy magnifies small features beyond the resolution of the unaided eye and is used across forensic disciplines to examine hairs, fibres, marks, and other trace material. Different microscopic techniques reveal different properties, such as surface texture or optical behaviour. Careful microscopic observation underlies many comparisons of class and individual characteristics.

title: Physical Fit Analysis
text: A physical fit, or fracture match, is established when the irregular broken edges of two pieces are shown to align and interlock as parts of a formerly single object. Because such a break is highly individual, a demonstrated physical fit can strongly support the conclusion that the pieces shared a common origin, expressed with correspondingly high confidence.

title: Presumptive Colour Tests
text: Many presumptive tests rely on a reagent that produces a characteristic colour change in the presence of a target substance, offering a quick preliminary screen. Because unrelated substances can sometimes produce similar colours, a positive colour reaction indicates only the possible presence of the target and is confirmed by more specific methods before firm conclusions are drawn.

title: Elimination Prints Concept
text: Elimination samples, such as reference prints from persons known to have had legitimate access to a scene, are collected so that marks attributable to them can be distinguished from those of unknown origin. Accounting for expected contributors focuses attention on genuinely questioned material and reduces the risk of misattributing an innocent mark.

title: Scene Reconstruction Logic
text: Reconstruction interprets the combined physical evidence at a scene to infer the sequence and nature of events consistent with it. It integrates patterns such as impressions, stains, and the positions of items to build an account constrained by the evidence. A reconstruction describes what is compatible with the findings rather than proving a single certain narrative.

title: Toolmark Class Characteristics
text: The class characteristics of a tool mark reflect the general type and dimensions of the tool that produced it, such as the width of a blade or the shape of a working edge. These features can place a mark within a category of possible tools. Individual correspondence beyond class features is required before a mark can be associated with one specific tool.

title: Fibre Persistence Dynamics
text: Transferred fibres are progressively lost from a surface through ordinary activity and the passage of time, so the number recovered tends to decline after transfer. Because persistence depends on the fibre, the surface, and subsequent movement, the quantity and distribution of fibres are interpreted with these dynamics in mind rather than assumed to be stable.

title: Hair Growth Regions
text: A hair can be considered in regions along its length, including the root end nearest the follicle and the shaft extending outward. Certain features observable in these regions can indicate general characteristics of the hair. Because such morphological features are shared among many hairs, they support class-level comparison rather than identification of a single source.

title: Glass Fragment Transfer
text: When glass breaks, small fragments can travel backward toward and onto a person or object near the breaking surface, becoming trace evidence. The recovery of such fragments and comparison of their properties can associate them with a source. Because glass is manufactured in large quantities with similar properties, such associations are probabilistic rather than unique.

title: Trajectory And Angle Estimation
text: Estimating the angle of a projectile's path from the marks it left, such as elongated impact damage, allows partial reconstruction of its direction of travel. Combining angle estimates from multiple marks constrains the possible line of flight. Because measurements carry uncertainty, resulting trajectories are expressed as ranges rather than as single exact lines.

title: Region Of Origin Estimation
text: In bloodstain analysis, combining the directions and impact angles of multiple stains allows estimation of a three-dimensional region from which the droplets originated. This region of origin indicates approximately where a blood source was located when the stains were produced. Because the underlying measurements are imprecise, the estimate describes an area rather than a point.

title: Manner Of Death Categories
text: The manner of death classifies the broad circumstances surrounding a death into recognised categories used for record and analysis. It is distinct from the medical cause of death and is inferred from the combination of pathological findings and investigative information. Where the available evidence is insufficient to choose confidently, the manner may be recorded as undetermined.

title: Digestion And Timing Caution
text: Estimates of elapsed time based on the state of stomach contents rest on assumptions about rates of digestion and gastric emptying that vary widely with the individual, the meal, and physiological factors. Because of this variability, such estimates are treated as broad indicators to be weighed alongside other evidence rather than as precise measures of timing.

title: Presumptive Blood Testing
text: Presumptive tests for blood typically detect the activity of components present in blood by producing a colour change or light emission, providing a rapid screen for possible bloodstains. Because certain other substances can trigger similar reactions, a positive result indicates only that blood may be present and is followed by more specific testing before conclusions are drawn.

title: Antigen Antibody Grouping
text: Blood grouping relies on the specific interaction between antigens on cells and corresponding antibodies, which produces an observable reaction used to determine group membership. Historically this allowed a stain to be assigned to a blood group, thereby excluding some potential sources or associating it with a broad population sharing that group as class-level evidence.

title: Standardised Procedures
text: Following standardised, documented procedures helps ensure that analyses are performed consistently and that results are comparable and reviewable. Standardisation reduces variation arising from individual habit and limits opportunities for undisciplined judgement. Adherence to established procedures, together with records of any deviations, supports the reliability and transparency of forensic work.

title: Limitations Acknowledgement
text: Responsible forensic reporting acknowledges the limitations of the methods used and the uncertainty attaching to conclusions, rather than overstating what the evidence can support. Recognising the boundaries of a technique, the quality of the material, and the possibility of error allows conclusions to be weighed appropriately by those who rely upon them.

title: Falsifiability Principle
text: A claim is scientifically meaningful in part to the extent that it could, in principle, be contradicted by observation. Framing hypotheses so that they make testable predictions allows evidence to count for or against them. An assertion compatible with every conceivable outcome offers little because no observation could show it to be wrong.

title: Replication Value
text: Independent replication, in which a finding is obtained again by different people or under different conditions, strengthens confidence that a result is genuine rather than an artefact of particular circumstances. Findings that withstand replication are generally more trustworthy. The inability to replicate a result is itself informative and warrants caution in relying upon it.

title: Confounding Factors
text: A confounding factor is an influence, other than the one under study, that affects the outcome and can create a misleading appearance of a relationship. Identifying and accounting for potential confounders is necessary before attributing an observed effect to a particular cause. Overlooking confounding can lead to conclusions that do not reflect the true underlying relationship.

title: Deductive Reasoning
text: Deductive reasoning derives conclusions that follow necessarily from the premises; if the premises are true and the argument valid, the conclusion cannot be false. It is non-ampliative, meaning the conclusion contains no information beyond what the premises already imply, and it is truth-preserving rather than truth-generating.

title: Inductive Reasoning
text: Inductive reasoning draws general or probabilistic conclusions from specific observations, such as inferring that a pattern will continue. It is ampliative because the conclusion asserts more than the premises guarantee, so even strong inductive arguments can have true premises yet a false conclusion, making them fallible rather than certain.

title: Abductive Reasoning
text: Abductive reasoning, or inference to the best explanation, infers a hypothesis that would, if true, best account for a set of observations. Introduced by C. S. Peirce as a distinct mode alongside deduction and induction, it generates plausible explanatory hypotheses rather than guaranteeing them, and its conclusions remain tentative and revisable.

title: Defeasible Reasoning
text: Defeasible reasoning yields conclusions that are tentatively acceptable but can be withdrawn if new information comes to light. Unlike strict deduction, a defeasible inference holds only in the absence of defeaters, making it central to everyday and legal reasoning where conclusions are provisional and subject to revision.

title: Monotonic Versus Non-Monotonic
text: In monotonic reasoning, adding premises never removes previously derivable conclusions, a property of classical deductive logic. In non-monotonic reasoning, new information can invalidate earlier conclusions, modeling how commonsense inference and defeasible reasoning revise beliefs when additional facts become available.

title: Cogency of Arguments
text: A cogent argument is a strong inductive argument with all true premises, the inductive analogue of a sound deductive argument. Cogency requires both that the premises make the conclusion probable and that those premises actually hold; an argument can be strong yet not cogent if a premise is false.

title: Uniformity of Nature
text: The uniformity of nature is the assumption that unobserved cases resemble observed ones and that regularities holding in the past will continue to hold. This principle is often cited as the tacit premise that inductive inference relies upon, and its justification is a central concern in the philosophy of induction.

title: Problem of Induction
text: The problem of induction is the question of how, if at all, inductive inferences can be rationally justified, since past regularities do not logically guarantee future ones. Attempts to justify induction by appeal to its past success appear circular, because that appeal itself uses inductive reasoning.

title: Hume on Induction
text: David Hume argued that inductive inferences rest on the assumption that the future will resemble the past, an assumption that can be justified neither by demonstrative reason nor without circularity by experience. He concluded that induction is grounded in custom and habit rather than rational demonstration.

title: Premise and Conclusion
text: In an argument, premises are the statements offered as reasons or evidence, and the conclusion is the claim they are meant to support. The transition from premises to conclusion is the inference, and identifying which statement is the conclusion is the first step in analyzing any argument.

title: Inference in Arguments
text: An inference is the step of reasoning that moves from premises to a conclusion, asserting that accepting the premises gives grounds for accepting the conclusion. The quality of an argument depends on whether this inferential link is legitimate, distinct from whether the individual statements happen to be true.

title: Toulmin Argument Model
text: The Toulmin model analyzes arguments into six components: the claim being argued, the grounds or data offered as support, the warrant linking grounds to claim, the backing supporting the warrant, a qualifier expressing certainty, and a rebuttal noting conditions under which the claim fails.

title: Warrant in Argument
text: In the Toulmin model, the warrant is the general principle or inferential rule that licenses moving from the grounds to the claim, explaining why the evidence supports the conclusion. Warrants are often left implicit, and making them explicit is a key step in evaluating an argument's strength.

title: Backing and Qualifier
text: In Toulmin's scheme, backing is the further evidence or authority that supports a warrant when the warrant itself is questioned, while a qualifier is a word or phrase such as 'probably' or 'presumably' that indicates the degree of force with which the claim is asserted.

title: Rebuttal in Toulmin Model
text: A rebuttal in the Toulmin model specifies the circumstances under which the general warrant would not apply and the claim would fail to hold. Including a rebuttal acknowledges exceptions and limits, presenting the argument as defeasible rather than as an absolute or unconditional assertion.

title: Validity of Arguments
text: An argument is valid when its logical form guarantees that if all the premises are true, the conclusion must be true; validity concerns structure, not the actual truth of the statements. A valid argument can have false premises, and validity alone does not establish that the conclusion is true.

title: Soundness of Arguments
text: A deductive argument is sound when it is both valid and has all true premises, which together guarantee a true conclusion. Soundness is stronger than validity because it adds the requirement that the premises actually hold, not merely that the inference would be truth-preserving if they did.

title: Strength of Arguments
text: The strength of an inductive argument measures how probable its premises make its conclusion, ranging along a continuum rather than being all-or-nothing like validity. A strong argument is one whose true premises would render the conclusion highly likely, though not certain.

title: Conditional Statements
text: A conditional statement has the form 'if P then Q', where P is the antecedent and Q the consequent, asserting that Q holds whenever P does. In the conditional, the antecedent is a sufficient condition for the consequent, and the consequent is a necessary condition for the antecedent.

title: Explanatory Scope
text: Scope is a criterion for evaluating explanations, favoring hypotheses that account for a wider range of the observations and known facts. An explanation with greater scope leaves fewer phenomena unexplained, but scope must be weighed against other virtues such as simplicity to avoid ad hoc overreach.

title: Explanatory Simplicity
text: Simplicity, as a criterion for choosing explanations, favors hypotheses that posit fewer entities, causes, or assumptions to account for the evidence. Related to Occam's razor, it treats unnecessary complexity as a defect, though simplicity is one virtue among several and can conflict with breadth of scope.

title: Explanatory Coherence
text: Coherence is a criterion favoring explanations that fit well with established background knowledge and with one another, avoiding conflict with accepted facts. A hypothesis that coheres with what is already known is generally preferred over one that would require abandoning well-supported beliefs.

title: Testability Criterion
text: Testability is the degree to which a hypothesis yields observable consequences that could confirm or disconfirm it. Explanations that make specific, checkable predictions are preferred, because untestable hypotheses cannot be evaluated against evidence and add little to explanatory or predictive power.

title: Conservatism in Explanation
text: Conservatism is the explanatory virtue of preferring hypotheses that require the fewest changes to existing beliefs. When a new explanation would force wholesale revision of well-established knowledge, conservatism counts against it, favoring accounts that preserve as much prior understanding as possible.

title: Analogy Strength Factors
text: The strength of an analogical argument increases with the number and relevance of similarities between the cases, the diversity among the supporting instances, and the absence of relevant disanalogies. Similarities that bear causally on the inferred property matter more than superficial resemblances.

title: Mill's Method of Agreement
text: Mill's method of agreement identifies a probable cause by finding a single factor common to all instances in which an effect occurs. If two or more cases sharing only one circumstance all exhibit the phenomenon, that shared circumstance is inferred to be causally connected to it.

title: Mill's Method of Difference
text: Mill's method of difference compares a case where the effect occurs with an otherwise similar case where it does not; the single factor present in one and absent in the other is inferred to be the cause. It underlies controlled experiments that vary one condition at a time.

title: Mill's Joint Method
text: The joint method of agreement and difference combines Mill's first two methods, strengthening a causal inference by showing that a factor is present whenever the effect occurs and absent whenever it does not. This dual pattern gives stronger evidence of causation than either method used alone.

title: Mill's Method of Residues
text: Mill's method of residues isolates the cause of a residual effect by subtracting the portions of a complex phenomenon already known to result from established causes. Whatever effect remains unexplained is attributed to the remaining antecedent circumstances not previously accounted for.

title: Concomitant Variation
text: Mill's method of concomitant variation infers a causal connection when two phenomena vary together in a regular way, one changing as the other does. It is useful when a factor cannot be entirely removed, since consistent covariation still points toward a causal relationship between the varying quantities.

title: Scientific Method
text: The scientific method is a systematic approach in which observations prompt questions, hypotheses are proposed as tentative explanations, predictions are derived and tested through controlled experiment or observation, and results lead to confirmation, revision, or rejection. Findings are subject to replication and peer scrutiny.

title: Hypothesis in Science
text: A hypothesis is a proposed, testable explanation for an observation or phenomenon, framed so that it generates predictions that could turn out false. A useful scientific hypothesis is precise enough to be checked against evidence and to be distinguished from rival explanations.

title: Scientific Prediction
text: A prediction is a specific observable consequence deduced from a hypothesis under stated conditions, stating what should be found if the hypothesis is true. Comparing predictions with actual results provides the evidential test that supports, revises, or refutes the hypothesis that generated them.

title: Experimental Control
text: A control is a standard of comparison in an experiment, such as a group not receiving the treatment, used to isolate the effect of the variable under study. Controls help ensure that observed differences are attributable to the manipulated factor rather than to other influences.

title: Replication in Science
text: Replication is the repetition of a study or experiment, ideally by independent investigators, to determine whether its results hold consistently. Reproducible findings carry more evidential weight, whereas results that cannot be reproduced are regarded as unreliable or possibly artifacts of the original conditions.

title: Parsimony Principle
text: Parsimony is the methodological preference for the simplest adequate explanation, using the fewest assumptions or postulated causes. As a scientific value it guides model selection and hypothesis choice, favoring economy of explanation while recognizing that the simplest account is not always the correct one.

title: Heuristics Versus Algorithms
text: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure guaranteed to produce a correct solution if followed exactly, whereas a heuristic is a shortcut or rule of thumb that often finds a good solution quickly without guaranteeing correctness. Heuristics trade certainty for speed and reduced effort.

title: Means-Ends Analysis
text: Means-ends analysis is a problem-solving strategy that repeatedly compares the current state with the goal state, identifies the largest difference, and selects an operator to reduce it, creating subgoals when necessary. It is a general method used in both human problem solving and artificial intelligence.

title: Working Backward Strategy
text: Working backward is a problem-solving strategy that starts from the goal and reasons in reverse toward the initial state, applying operators that could have produced the goal. It is especially effective when the goal is well specified and the paths from the start are numerous or unclear.

title: Analogical Transfer
text: Analogical transfer is applying the solution or structure of a previously solved problem to a new, structurally similar problem. Successful transfer depends on recognizing the deep relational correspondence between problems rather than surface features, which is often the main obstacle to using relevant prior solutions.

title: Problem Decomposition
text: Decomposition is the strategy of breaking a complex problem into smaller, more manageable subproblems that can be solved individually and then combined. By reducing a large task to tractable parts, decomposition lowers cognitive load and clarifies the structure and dependencies of the overall problem.

title: Trial and Error
text: Trial and error is a problem-solving method that tries possible actions and retains those that work while discarding those that fail, without a guiding plan. It can succeed when the solution space is small or poorly understood, but is inefficient for large spaces where systematic methods are available.

title: Hill Climbing Strategy
text: Hill climbing is a heuristic search strategy that repeatedly moves toward states that appear closer to the goal, choosing at each step the option that most improves the current position. It can be efficient but may become stuck at a local optimum that is not the true goal.

title: Insight in Problem Solving
text: Insight is the sudden emergence of a solution that arrives seemingly all at once, often after an impasse, involving a restructuring of how the problem is represented. Insight problems are characterized by this abrupt reorganization rather than by gradual, step-by-step progress toward the answer.

title: Incubation Effect
text: Incubation is the phenomenon in which setting a problem aside for a period can improve the chance of solving it later. Proposed mechanisms include the weakening of misleading assumptions and unconscious processing, allowing a fresh approach when the solver returns to the problem.

title: Functional Fixedness
text: Functional fixedness is a cognitive bias that limits a person to using an object only in its customary way, hindering solutions that require using it in a novel role. It illustrates how prior experience with an object's typical function can block creative problem solving.

title: Mental Set
text: A mental set, or Einstellung effect, is the tendency to approach a problem using a strategy that worked before, even when a simpler or more effective solution exists. Habitual methods can block recognition of better alternatives, so prior success sometimes impairs performance on related problems.

title: Well-Defined Problems
text: A well-defined problem has a clearly specified initial state, goal state, and set of allowable operations, so that solvers know exactly what counts as a solution. Such problems are amenable to systematic search methods because the search space and success criteria are explicit and unambiguous.

title: Ill-Defined Problems
text: An ill-defined problem lacks a clear initial state, goal, or set of operations, or has criteria for success that are vague or contested. Many real-world problems are ill-defined, requiring the solver first to structure the problem before any solution procedure can be meaningfully applied.

title: Problem Representation
text: Problem representation is the way a problem is mentally structured, including how its elements, goals, and constraints are encoded. Because the chosen representation shapes which strategies seem available, re-representing a problem can transform an intractable one into a solvable one, a key element of insight.

title: Constraint Satisfaction
text: A constraint satisfaction problem seeks values for a set of variables that simultaneously satisfy all specified constraints. Solving it involves narrowing the possibilities by propagating the implications of each constraint, and such problems underlie many logic puzzles, scheduling tasks, and configuration challenges.

title: Expected Utility
text: Expected utility extends expected value by weighting outcomes according to their subjective utility rather than their raw monetary value, reflecting that the value of a gain or loss can vary with circumstances. Maximizing expected utility is a standard normative model for decision-making under risk.

title: Dominance in Decisions
text: One option dominates another when it is at least as good in every possible state of the world and strictly better in at least one, making the dominant option preferable regardless of which state occurs. Eliminating dominated options is a basic step in simplifying decisions under uncertainty.

title: Maximin Criterion
text: The maximin criterion chooses the option whose worst possible outcome is best among all options' worst outcomes, reflecting a cautious focus on guarding against the least favorable result. It is suited to decision-making when probabilities are unknown and the decision-maker is risk-averse.

title: Minimax Regret
text: The minimax regret criterion selects the option that minimizes the maximum possible regret, where regret is the difference between an outcome and the best outcome that could have been obtained in that state. It targets the decision least likely to produce severe hindsight disappointment.

title: Risk Versus Ambiguity
text: Risk refers to situations where the probabilities of outcomes are known, whereas ambiguity refers to situations where those probabilities are themselves unknown or uncertain. People often treat the two differently, tending to avoid ambiguous prospects even when a risky alternative offers comparable expected results.

title: Premortem Technique
text: A premortem is a decision-making exercise in which a team imagines that a planned course of action has already failed and works backward to identify plausible reasons for the failure. Conducted before committing, it surfaces risks and weaknesses that optimism might otherwise obscure.

title: Mnemonic Devices
text: Mnemonic devices are memory aids that impose structure or meaning on material to make it easier to encode and retrieve, such as rhymes, acronyms, and imagery. They work by linking new information to existing knowledge or memorable patterns, reducing the burden of rote memorization.

title: Acronyms and Acrostics
text: An acronym forms a memorable word from the initial letters of a series of items, while an acrostic uses the first letters to construct a memorable phrase or sentence. Both are mnemonic devices that encode order and content of a list through easily recalled letter cues.

title: Dual Coding
text: Dual coding is the principle that information encoded both verbally and visually is remembered better than information encoded in one form alone. Combining words with corresponding images provides two complementary retrieval routes, increasing the chance of successful recall.

title: Forgetting Curve
text: The forgetting curve describes how retention of newly learned material declines over time, typically dropping rapidly at first and then more gradually. Associated with Hermann Ebbinghaus's memory research, it illustrates why timely review is needed to counteract the natural loss of information.

title: Working Memory Limits
text: Working memory is the system that holds and manipulates a small amount of information over short intervals, and it has a limited capacity. Because only a few items can be actively maintained at once, strategies such as chunking and external notes help overcome this bottleneck.

title: Proactive Interference
text: Proactive interference occurs when previously learned information disrupts the recall of newly learned material, so that older memories intrude upon and impede the retrieval of more recent ones. It is one of two directions of interference that contribute to forgetting.

title: Retroactive Interference
text: Retroactive interference occurs when newly learned information disrupts the recall of previously learned material, so that recent learning impairs access to older memories. Together with proactive interference, it shows how competing memories can obstruct one another rather than fading independently.

title: Context-Dependent Memory
text: Context-dependent memory is the finding that recall is improved when the external environment at retrieval matches the environment at encoding. Cues from the original setting, such as the place or surrounding sounds, can facilitate access to memories formed in that context.

title: State-Dependent Memory
text: State-dependent memory is the finding that recall is enhanced when a person's internal physiological or emotional state at retrieval matches their state at the time of learning. The internal condition present during encoding can serve as a retrieval cue for the associated memories.

title: Recording Provenance
text: Provenance is the documented origin and chain of custody of a piece of information or evidence, including its source, date, and how it was obtained. Recording provenance allows claims to be traced back and verified, and it is essential to assessing reliability and detecting contamination.

title: Timelines in Investigation
text: A timeline arranges events in chronological order to clarify the sequence and timing of what occurred. Constructing one helps reveal gaps, overlaps, and inconsistencies, and it supports reasoning about which events could have caused or preceded others based on their temporal order.

title: Outlining Method
text: Outlining is a note-taking method that arranges information hierarchically, using indented headings and subpoints to show the relationships between main ideas and supporting details. Its structure clarifies organization and makes the relative importance and grouping of points easy to review.

title: Cornell Note System
text: The Cornell method divides a page into a narrow left cue column, a wider right column for notes taken during a session, and a summary area at the bottom. After the session, cue questions and a summary are added, and the notes column is covered to test recall.

title: Mind Mapping
text: A mind map is a diagram that begins with a central topic and radiates outward into branches of related subtopics and details. Its visual, associative structure mirrors how ideas connect and can aid brainstorming, organization, and recall by grouping related information around a central theme.

title: Cognitive Interview
text: The cognitive interview is a set of evidence-based techniques for improving accurate recall from cooperative witnesses. It encourages uninterrupted free reporting, mental reinstatement of the original context, and recalling events in varied orders and perspectives, aiming to increase detail without introducing distortion.

title: Free Recall
text: Free recall is an interviewing technique in which the respondent describes events in their own words and at their own pace, without interruption or specific prompts. It elicits an uncontaminated initial account, and interviewers reserve targeted questions until after this open narrative is complete.

title: Avoiding Contamination
text: Contamination in interviewing occurs when the interviewer's questions, assumptions, or disclosed information become incorporated into the respondent's account. Avoiding it requires using open prompts, withholding specific details, and not signaling expected answers, so that the account reflects the respondent's own memory.

title: Corroboration of Evidence
text: Corroboration is the confirmation of a claim by independent evidence or an additional source. Because a single account may be mistaken or biased, seeking corroborating information strengthens confidence in a conclusion, whereas the absence of corroboration signals a need for caution.

title: Funnel Questioning
text: The funnel approach to questioning begins with broad, open questions that elicit a general account and progressively narrows to specific, focused questions on points of interest. This sequence gathers an uncontaminated overview first before probing particular details, reducing the risk of leading the respondent.

title: Substitution Ciphers
text: A substitution cipher encrypts a message by replacing each letter or symbol of the plaintext with another according to a fixed rule, while preserving the positions of the units. Because the letter positions are unchanged, simple substitution ciphers remain vulnerable to analysis of letter frequencies.

title: Transposition Ciphers
text: A transposition cipher encrypts a message by rearranging the positions of its letters according to a system, without altering the letters themselves. The resulting ciphertext contains the same letters as the plaintext, so its letter frequencies match the original language, distinguishing it from substitution.

title: Polyalphabetic Ciphers
text: A polyalphabetic cipher uses multiple substitution alphabets in sequence, so that the same plaintext letter can be enciphered differently at different positions. By flattening letter frequencies, this approach resists simple frequency analysis; the Vigenere cipher is a well-known historical example.

title: Vigenere Cipher
text: The Vigenere cipher is a polyalphabetic substitution cipher that uses a repeating keyword to determine a series of shifting Caesar-style alphabets across the message. The repeating key length is its key weakness, since detecting the period reduces the cipher to several simple substitutions.

title: One-Time Pad
text: The one-time pad encrypts a message by combining it with a random key that is as long as the message, used only once and shared secretly. When the key is truly random, secret, and never reused, the scheme offers provable, unbreakable secrecy, but these strict requirements limit its practicality.

title: Steganography Versus Cryptography
text: Cryptography protects a message by scrambling its content so that it is unintelligible without a key, whereas steganography conceals the very existence of the message by hiding it within an innocuous carrier. The two techniques address different goals and can be combined for layered protection.

title: Keyword Cipher
text: A keyword cipher is a monoalphabetic substitution in which a keyword, with duplicate letters removed, begins the cipher alphabet, and the remaining letters follow in their normal order. This yields a mixed alphabet that is easier to remember than a random one but still vulnerable to frequency analysis.

title: Null Cipher
text: A null cipher hides a message among irrelevant filler text, so that only certain letters or words, selected by an agreed rule such as taking the first letter of each word, carry the true meaning. It is a form of steganography that conceals a message within ordinary-looking text.

title: Book Cipher
text: A book cipher encodes a message using references to words or letters in an agreed text, such as page, line, and word numbers, that both parties possess. Its security rests on the secrecy of which book is used as the key, since the ciphertext alone gives few clues.

title: Kerckhoffs's Principle
text: Kerckhoffs's principle holds that a cryptographic system should remain secure even if everything about it except the key is public knowledge. It implies that security must rest on the secrecy of the key rather than on the obscurity of the algorithm, which may become known.

title: Reframing
text: Reframing is the act of deliberately changing the way a problem or situation is conceived, altering its context, boundaries, or emphasis to reveal new options. By shifting the frame, a solver can escape an unhelpful representation and perceive possibilities that the original framing concealed.

title: Assumption Challenging
text: Assumption challenging is the practice of identifying and questioning the tacit premises taken for granted in a problem. Many apparent impasses arise from unwarranted assumptions about constraints, and explicitly testing whether each assumption truly holds can open paths to solutions previously deemed impossible.

title: Deduction Grid Puzzles
text: A deduction grid puzzle presents a set of categories and clues from which the solver must determine a unique matching of items across categories. Using a grid to mark confirmed and excluded combinations, the solver applies process of elimination and the clues' logical constraints to reach the solution.

title: Constraint Logic Puzzles
text: Constraint logic puzzles require finding an arrangement that satisfies a set of stated rules, using deduction rather than guesswork to eliminate impossibilities. Each constraint narrows the space of arrangements, and systematically combining the constraints converges on the one consistent configuration.

title: Insight Problems
text: Insight problems are tasks whose solution requires a sudden restructuring of how the problem is understood rather than incremental analysis. They typically involve breaking an implicit assumption, and solvers often experience an impasse followed by an abrupt realization when the correct representation is found.

title: Null Hypothesis of Innocence
text: In investigation, entertaining the hypothesis that no wrongdoing occurred serves as a baseline against which apparent evidence of a crime is tested. Considering this null hypothesis guards against prematurely assuming guilt and helps distinguish genuine indications of a crime from innocent coincidence.

title: Deductive-Nomological Explanation
text: The deductive-nomological model treats a scientific explanation as a valid deductive argument in which the phenomenon to be explained follows from general laws together with statements of particular conditions. On this account, to explain an event is to show that it was expected given the relevant laws.

title: Correlation Versus Causation
text: A correlation is a statistical association between two variables, whereas causation means that one variable produces changes in the other. Correlation does not establish causation, since an association may result from coincidence, reverse causation, or a common underlying factor influencing both variables.

title: Prior and Posterior Probability
text: A prior probability is the credence assigned to a hypothesis before considering new evidence, while the posterior is the revised credence after incorporating that evidence. Updating from prior to posterior according to how well the hypothesis predicts the evidence is central to probabilistic reasoning.

title: Straw Man Fallacy
text: The straw man fallacy misrepresents an opponent's position as a weaker or distorted version and then refutes that misrepresentation instead of the actual claim. It creates a false appearance of having defeated the argument, and identifying it requires comparing the criticism to the original position.

title: Ad Hominem Fallacy
text: An ad hominem fallacy attacks the person advancing an argument rather than addressing the argument itself, treating a characteristic of the speaker as though it bore on the truth of the claim. The origin of a claim is generally irrelevant to whether the claim is actually true.

title: Slippery Slope Argument
text: A slippery slope argument claims that a first step will inevitably lead through a chain of events to some extreme outcome. It becomes fallacious when the intermediate links are asserted without adequate support, since a plausible starting action need not trigger the alleged sequence.

title: Cognitive Load
text: Cognitive load is the amount of mental effort imposed on working memory by a task. Because working memory is limited, excessive load impairs comprehension and problem solving, so techniques such as decomposition, chunking, and external notes help by reducing the demands placed on it at any moment.

title: Deductive Validity Forms
text: Certain argument forms are valid by their structure alone, guaranteeing that true premises yield a true conclusion regardless of subject matter. Recognizing these forms, such as modus ponens and hypothetical syllogism, allows an argument's validity to be assessed from its logical pattern rather than its content.

title: Abduction Selection Criteria
text: In abductive reasoning, competing explanations are compared using criteria such as explanatory scope, simplicity, coherence with background knowledge, and testability. The hypothesis that best satisfies these virtues is provisionally accepted, though abduction yields plausible rather than certain conclusions and remains open to revision.

title: Counterfactual Reasoning
text: Counterfactual reasoning considers what would have happened under conditions contrary to fact, such as whether an effect would still have occurred had a suspected cause been absent. It supports causal analysis by isolating whether a factor made a difference to the outcome.

title: Overdetermination
text: Overdetermination occurs when an outcome has more than one sufficient cause present at once, so that it would have happened even if any single cause had been absent. It complicates counterfactual tests of causation, since removing one sufficient cause leaves the outcome unchanged.

title: Deductive Certainty
text: Deductive certainty refers to the guarantee that, in a valid argument with true premises, the conclusion must be true. This certainty flows from logical form and distinguishes deduction from inductive and abductive inference, whose conclusions are at most probable given their premises.

title: Inductive Generalization
text: An inductive generalization infers a general rule about a population from observations of a sample. Its reliability depends on the sample being sufficiently large and representative, since conclusions drawn from biased or small samples fail to warrant confident claims about the whole.

title: Statistical Syllogism
text: A statistical syllogism reasons from a statistical generalization about a class to a conclusion about a particular member, inferring, for example, that a given individual probably has a property common in that class. The conclusion is probabilistic and can be defeated by more specific information.

title: Sample Representativeness
text: A representative sample reflects the relevant characteristics of the larger population it is drawn from, allowing valid inductive generalizations. When a sample is skewed toward particular subgroups, conclusions extended to the whole population may be systematically mistaken, weakening any inference based upon it.

title: Levels of Measurement
text: Levels of measurement classify data as nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio, each supporting different operations. Nominal data label categories, ordinal data rank them, interval data have meaningful differences without a true zero, and ratio data add a true zero permitting meaningful ratios.

title: Occam's Razor Caveat
text: Occam's razor recommends the simplest adequate explanation but does not assert that reality is always simple; a more complex explanation can be correct when the evidence requires it. The razor breaks ties between explanations of equal fit rather than settling matters that evidence can decide.

title: Deductive Versus Inductive Contrast
text: Deductive arguments aim for conclusions that follow necessarily, evaluated as valid or invalid, while inductive arguments aim for conclusions that follow probably, evaluated as strong or weak. Deduction preserves truth without extending content, whereas induction extends content at the cost of certainty.

title: Retrieval Cues
text: A retrieval cue is a stimulus that helps bring a stored memory into awareness, working best when it matches conditions present at encoding. The effectiveness of cues explains context-dependent and state-dependent memory, and deliberately encoding distinctive cues can make later recall more reliable.

title: Encoding Specificity
text: The encoding specificity principle states that memory retrieval is most effective when the cues available at recall overlap with those present when the memory was formed. It accounts for why reinstating the original context or state can substantially improve access to a stored memory.

title: Reasoning Under Uncertainty
text: Reasoning under uncertainty involves drawing conclusions and making choices when relevant facts or probabilities are incompletely known. It relies on probabilistic estimates, expected outcomes, and heuristics, and rational approaches aim to weigh the likelihood and value of possible results rather than seeking impossible certainty.

title: Decision Under Ignorance
text: Decision under ignorance describes choices where the probabilities of outcomes are entirely unknown, precluding expected-value calculation. Criteria such as maximin, maximax, and minimax regret provide alternative rules that reflect different attitudes toward the unknown, from cautious pessimism to optimism or regret minimization.

title: Dominance Reasoning
text: Dominance reasoning simplifies a decision by eliminating any option that is worse than another in every relevant respect. Because a dominated option can never be the best choice regardless of which outcome occurs, discarding such options reduces the decision to a comparison among the survivors.

title: Cost-Benefit Analysis
text: Cost-benefit analysis evaluates a decision by systematically identifying and comparing its expected costs against its expected benefits, often expressed in common units. It supports choices by making trade-offs explicit, though its usefulness depends on accurately estimating and valuing the relevant consequences.

title: Fermi Estimation
text: Fermi estimation is a method of arriving at approximate answers to quantitative questions by decomposing them into factors that can be roughly estimated and combined. Named for physicist Enrico Fermi, it yields order-of-magnitude figures useful for sanity checks when precise data are unavailable.

title: Steganographic Techniques
text: Steganography conceals information within an ordinary carrier so that its presence is not apparent, using methods such as hidden markings, microdots, or embedding data in images or text. Unlike cryptography, which scrambles content, steganography relies on the message going entirely unnoticed by observers.

title: Rail Fence Cipher
text: The rail fence cipher is a transposition cipher that writes the plaintext in a zigzag across a set number of rows, then reads it off row by row to form the ciphertext. Its security is minimal, as the number of rails is the only key and is easily guessed.

title: Atbash Cipher
text: The Atbash cipher is a simple substitution cipher that reverses the alphabet, mapping the first letter to the last, the second to the second-to-last, and so on. It is a fixed monoalphabetic substitution with no key, making it easy to recognize and decode.

title: Cipher Versus Code
text: In cryptography a cipher operates on individual letters or symbols by a systematic rule, whereas a code replaces whole words or phrases with predefined equivalents, typically using a codebook. Codes require sharing the codebook, while ciphers depend on an algorithm and a key.

title: Cryptanalysis
text: Cryptanalysis is the study of methods for recovering the plaintext or key of encrypted messages without prior authorization to do so. Techniques include frequency analysis, exploiting patterns and repetitions, and analyzing weaknesses in the cipher's design, and they drive the development of stronger encryption.

title: Known-Plaintext Attack
text: A known-plaintext attack is a form of cryptanalysis in which the analyst has access to both some ciphertext and its corresponding plaintext, and uses the pair to deduce the key or method. The availability of matching text greatly aids breaking many classical ciphers.

title: Pigpen Cipher
text: The pigpen cipher is a monoalphabetic substitution that replaces letters with symbols derived from fragments of grids and their positions. As a simple geometric substitution, it hides text visually but offers little security, since its fixed symbol-to-letter mapping is easily learned or deduced.

title: Playfair Cipher
text: The Playfair cipher encrypts pairs of letters using a five-by-five grid built from a keyword, applying rules based on the positions of each pair within the grid. By enciphering digraphs rather than single letters, it resists simple frequency analysis better than monoalphabetic substitution.

title: Index of Coincidence
text: The index of coincidence measures how likely two randomly chosen letters in a text are identical, and it differs between monoalphabetic and polyalphabetic ciphertexts. Cryptanalysts use it to detect polyalphabetic encryption and to estimate key length in ciphers such as the Vigenere.

title: Divide and Conquer
text: Divide and conquer is a problem-solving strategy that splits a problem into independent subproblems, solves each separately, and combines the results into a solution to the whole. It is effective when a problem's structure allows clean separation into parts that can be tackled on their own.

title: Generate and Test
text: Generate and test is a problem-solving method that produces candidate solutions and checks each against the problem's requirements, keeping any that satisfy them. Its efficiency depends on generating plausible candidates and on the ease of testing, and it degrades when the candidate space is very large.

title: Backtracking
text: Backtracking is a systematic search technique that builds a solution incrementally and abandons a partial path as soon as it violates a constraint, returning to a previous choice point to try an alternative. It efficiently explores constraint problems by pruning branches that cannot lead to a solution.

title: Problem Space
text: A problem space is the abstract set of all states reachable in a problem, together with the initial state, goal state, and operators that transform one state into another. Framing a problem as a search through this space clarifies which strategies can navigate toward a solution.

title: Subgoaling
text: Subgoaling is the strategy of setting intermediate objectives that lie on the path from the current state to the final goal. By reducing a large problem into a sequence of nearer targets, it makes progress measurable and is a core mechanism within means-ends analysis.

title: Analog Versus Digital Encoding
text: In memory and information terms, analog encoding preserves continuous features of an experience, such as spatial or perceptual qualities, whereas digital or symbolic encoding represents information in discrete, categorical form. The distinction bears on how different kinds of information are stored and later retrieved.

title: Elaborative Interrogation
text: Elaborative interrogation is a study technique in which the learner asks why a stated fact is true and generates an explanation. By actively connecting new facts to prior knowledge through explanatory reasoning, it deepens encoding and improves retention compared with passive reading.

title: Interleaving Practice
text: Interleaving is a learning strategy that mixes different problem types or topics within a study session rather than practicing one type to completion before moving on. Though it feels more difficult, interleaving often improves the ability to discriminate among problems and to retain skills over time.

title: Distributed Practice
text: Distributed practice spreads learning across multiple sessions separated in time, in contrast to massed practice concentrated into a single session. Spacing study episodes generally produces stronger long-term retention, a robust finding closely related to the effectiveness of spaced repetition.

title: Recognition Versus Recall
text: Recognition is identifying previously encountered information when it is presented again, whereas recall is retrieving it from memory without such cues. Recognition is typically easier than recall because the presented item itself serves as a retrieval cue that reduces the search required.

title: Corroborating Independent Sources
text: A conclusion supported by multiple sources that arrived at their information independently is more credible than one resting on a single source or on sources that merely repeat one another. Independence matters because it reduces the chance that a shared error or bias underlies all the reports.

title: Working Hypothesis
text: A working hypothesis is a provisional explanation adopted to guide investigation, held tentatively while evidence is gathered to support, refine, or discard it. It organizes inquiry by suggesting what to look for, without committing prematurely to a conclusion before the evidence justifies one.

title: Deductive Closure
text: In investigation, a solution should account for all the established facts without contradiction; a hypothesis that leaves key evidence unexplained or conflicts with it is incomplete. Testing a proposed explanation against every known fact is a check on whether the reasoning has genuinely closed the case.

title: Elimination of Impossibilities
text: A classical maxim of deductive investigation holds that once the impossible options have been excluded, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth. The method depends on genuinely exhausting and correctly ruling out the alternatives, since a missed possibility undermines the conclusion.

title: Anagram Solving
text: An anagram is a rearrangement of the letters of a word or phrase to form another, and solving one involves finding the arrangement that yields meaningful text. Techniques include sorting letters, identifying likely letter groupings, and recognizing common prefixes and suffixes to constrain the possibilities.

title: Truth Tables
text: A truth table lists every combination of truth values for an argument's or expression's components and shows the resulting value of the whole. It provides a mechanical method for testing validity of propositional arguments and for defining logical connectives such as conjunction, disjunction, and implication.

title: Necessary and Sufficient Together
text: A condition that is both necessary and sufficient for an outcome holds exactly when the outcome does, so each implies the other. Such biconditional relationships, expressed as 'if and only if', are common in definitions, where the defining condition and the defined term coincide precisely.

title: Deductive Nesting of Conditions
text: Complex conditions can nest, so that satisfying an outer requirement depends on inner sub-conditions, each necessary or sufficient in its own right. Carefully untangling how such conditions combine, using the logic of necessity and sufficiency, is essential to reasoning correctly about layered rules and criteria.

title: Provenance Versus Content
text: Assessing information involves separating provenance, its source and how it was obtained, from content, what it actually claims. A claim's origin bears on its reliability but not directly on its truth, so both dimensions must be weighed without letting one improperly override the other.

title: Deductive Puzzle Constraints
text: In logic puzzles, each clue functions as a constraint that permits some combinations and forbids others. Solving proceeds by combining constraints to eliminate impossibilities until a single consistent assignment remains, illustrating how deductive reasoning narrows a space of possibilities to a unique answer.

title: Occam's Razor in Diagnosis
text: In diagnostic reasoning, a principle related to Occam's razor favors explaining multiple findings by a single cause rather than several independent ones when a unifying explanation fits the evidence. This preference for parsimony must still yield to evidence indicating that several distinct causes are actually present.

title: Steganography in Plain Sight
text: Some concealment techniques hide a message within ordinary communication so that it passes unnoticed, such as encoding it in the first letters of words or in seemingly innocuous details. The security of such methods rests on the hidden content escaping the attention of any observer.

title: Hypothesis Competition
text: Sound inference to the best explanation requires comparing a genuine range of rival hypotheses rather than defending a single favored one. An explanation can appear best only relative to the alternatives considered, so overlooking a plausible rival can produce a confident but mistaken conclusion.

title: Deductive Soundness Check
text: To judge a deductive argument fully, one checks both that its form is valid and that each premise is actually true, since validity alone leaves open the possibility of a false conclusion from false premises. Only a valid argument with true premises is sound.

title: Salience and Attention
text: Salience is the quality by which certain features stand out and capture attention, and it strongly influences which details are noticed and later remembered. Because salience can be driven by novelty or emotion rather than importance, relying on it can bias observation and recall toward the conspicuous.
